Chicken Pomodoro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Chicken Pomodoro
Chicken breasts cooked in a light garlicky sauce made with fresh cherry tomatoes, topped with mozzarella cheese.
Serves4
Prep10 minutes
Cook25 minutes
Why You’ll Love Our Chicken Pomodoro
- It’s simple, but packed with flavor. Pomodoro sauce typically has minimal ingredients, throwing the bright flavor of tomatoes into the spotlight. This recipe proves you can create bold flavors from just a handful of ingredients.
- Weeknight-friendly. This recipe is cooked in one skillet and requires minimal chopping, making it perfect for any night when you need dinner fast.
Every summer I look forward to tomatoes from my garden and the abundance of farmers markets bursting with different shapes, sizes, and colors of the gorgeous fruit (it’s fine if you consider it a vegetable; tomato, tom-ah-to). As peak tomato season fades, my cravings don’t stop. That’s when I turn to tomato recipes, like this chicken pomodoro, that work year-round.
Inspired by classic pomodoro sauce, this one-skillet dinner turns cherry tomatoes, a flavorful choice even in the dead of winter, into a quick, bright sauce that enlivens mild chicken breasts. To keep the sauce tomato-forward, it’s lightly flavored with garlic and basil, but you could also add a sprinkle of chili flakes for heat or oregano for a complementary herbal note. Topping the chicken with fresh mozzarella gives the dish chicken Parmesan vibes, but in a much lighter way.
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“This was like a lighter, fresher take on chicken Parmesan. I liked the bright flavors in the sauce, and the little bit of butter really brought it all together with some richness. I took the chicken out of the pan, tossed half a pound of cooked pasta in the sauce, and served it alongside. No complaints at the dinner table from my family!” —Christine, October 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
With over 15 years of experience as a professional recipe developer for national print and digital outlets, I have learned how to create recipes that are easy to follow, quick and simple to make, and don’t skimp on flavor, like this skillet dinner. Chicken recipes in particular have been a huge part of my recipe career because chicken is an affordable, versatile, and crowd-pleasing protein that can be spiced and sauced in countless ways. That means I know how to give this lean protein a boost of flavor without overcooking it, because dry, tough chicken is a no-go in my world.
Key Ingredients in Chicken Pomodoro
- Chicken: Boneless, skinless chicken breasts turn this skillet of saucy tomatoes into a meal. To get a good portion size, it’s best to halve larger pieces of chicken versus buying thin-sliced chicken breasts. Those are typically pounded into large, flat cutlets, and 4 wouldn’t fit in a skillet at once.
- Cherry tomatoes: These little round tomatoes are the best type of tomato for this recipe because of their thin skin and flavorful, juicy interior. They’re also easy to find year-round, so you can make this recipe any time you want.
- Garlic: Fresh garlic is one of the few traditional seasonings for pomodoro sauce, so you bet I was going to include it. To keep its sharpness, I add it to the skillet with the tomatoes rather than sautéing it first, which mellows the taste.
- Basil: Basil leaves are a wonderful garnish, but I also love the ease of tossing a whole sprig of basil into a sauce so it can perfume the dish as it bubbles away. Herb stems have so much flavor, so even if you have some without leaves, don’t toss them!
- Butter: I learned from some amazing Italian chefs that butter in tomato sauce is totally legit, and it’s an essential part of Marcella Hazan’s legendary tomato sauce. Here, a small amount goes a long way to add a touch of silky richness to the sauce and balance the natural tang of fresh tomatoes.
- Mozzarella: Fresh mozzarella can be too wet for some recipes, but here it works perfectly, blanketing the chicken and enhancing the dish’s saucy base. For a more rustic look, you can tear the cheese instead of slicing it.
How to Make Chicken Pomodoro
- Brown the chicken. Halve 2 large boneless chicken breasts crosswise, then season both sides with salt and pepper. Cook in olive oil in a large skillet until well-browned on both sides, but not fully cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
- Start cooking the sauce. Stir in about 3/4 of the halved tomatoes, some minced garlic, and a sprig of fresh basil, coating them in the remaining oil and gently scraping up any browned bits on the bottom of the skillet as the tomatoes release liquid.
- Add broth and simmer. Stir in chicken broth and bring to a simmer. Simmer until the tomatoes break down, and the sauce thickens slightly.
- Add more tomatoes and return the chicken to the sauce. Stir in another handful of halved tomatoes and a pat of butter. Nestle the chicken pieces into the sauce, top with cheese, cover, and simmer for a few minutes.
- Finish with cheese and basil. Uncover the skillet and simmer until the cheese is melted, the chicken is cooked through, and the sauce has thickened. Remove from the heat and top with fresh, torn basil.
Helpful Swaps
- Start with smaller chicken breasts. If you have small boneless, skinless chicken breasts (around 6 ounces each) you can skip halving them and cook them whole.
- Lighten up on the cheese. For a less cheesy meal, replace the sliced mozzarella with a sprinkle of grated Parmesan or skip the cheese entirely and top more generously with basil.
- Try a different herb. Fresh oregano is an excellent sub for basil if you are out. Add fresh leaves sparingly as a garnish; they’re more intense than basil.
- Make it extra-creamy. If you are craving penne alla vodka, you can give this dish a similar richness by adding heavy cream instead of broth when adding the second batch of tomatoes. Start with 1/4 cup, taste, and adjust from there to your liking.
Storage and Make-Ahead Tips
- Pomodoro is a quick-cooking sauce, so it’s best to make it fresh, but there are some make-ahead aspects that can trim a few minutes off the prep. Slice the tomatoes and chicken breasts up to 1 day in advance and store them separately in airtight containers in the refrigerator.
- If you want to make this a freezer-friendly meal, cook it all the way through, leaving the cheese off the chicken. Freeze the sauce and chicken in separate freezer-proof containers, thaw overnight in the refrigerator, then assemble and rewarm, covered, in a skillet, topping with cheese in the last few minutes.
What to Serve with Chicken Pomodoro
Chicken Pomodoro Recipe
Chicken breasts cooked in a light garlicky sauce made with fresh cherry tomatoes, topped with mozzarella cheese.
Prep time 10 minutes
Cook time 25 minutes
Serves 4
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
- 2 large boneless, skinless chicken breasts (1 1/2 to 2 pounds)
- 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt, divided
- 3/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, divided
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 1/2 pounds cherry or grape tomatoes (3 pints or 4 cups), halved and divided
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 sprig fresh basil, plus more for garnish
- 1/2 cup low-sodium chicken broth
- 1 tablespoon unsalted butter
- 4 ounces fresh mozzarella cheese, sliced into 1/4-inch-thick rounds
Instructions
- Slice 2 large boneless, skinless chicken breasts in half crosswise to make 4 thinner pieces. Pat dry with paper towels. Season with 1 teaspoon of the kosher salt and 1/2 teaspoon of the black pepper.
- Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the chicken in a single, tight layer and cook until golden-brown, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate (the chicken will not be cooked through).
- Reduce the heat to medium. Add three-quarters of the halved cherry tomatoes (3 cups), 2 minced garlic cloves, 1 fresh basil sprig, the remaining 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt, and 1/4 teaspoon black pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally and scraping up any bits from the bottom of the skillet, until the tomatoes start to soften and become juicy, 4 to 5 minutes. Stir in 1/2 cup low-sodium chicken broth and simmer until the sauce thickens and the tomatoes have collapsed, about 5 minutes.
- Stir in the remaining 1 cup halved cherry tomatoes and 1 tablespoon unsalted butter until the butter melts. Return the chicken to the skillet, nestling it into the sauce. Pour in any accumulated juices on the plate. Top the chicken with 4 ounces sliced fresh mozzarella cheese.
- Cover and simmer for 3 minutes. Uncover and simmer until the sauce thickens slightly, 3 to 4 minutes more. Garnish with torn fresh basil leaves.
Recipe Notes
General tip: The halved chicken pieces will inevitably be a little thicker at one end than the other, and that’s totally fine, but if there is a big difference (more than 1/2 inch), take a moment and flatten the thicker end slightly with a meat mallet or rolling pin to even it out.
Substitutions
- Instead of chicken broth, use low-sodium vegetable broth or even water (although if using water, you’ll want to add an extra pinch of salt to make up for the sodium in canned broth).
- Fresh mozzarella offers a lightly creamy taste that doesn’t dominate the tomatoes, but if all you have is low-moisture mozzarella cheese, you can use that. Top the chicken with 1 cup of shredded mozzarella cheese or 1 slice per piece of chicken.
Storage: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Reheat the chicken in sauce, covered, in the microwave or in a 350°F oven until the tomatoes bubble and the chicken is warmed through. I like to top the chicken as it warms with a bit more cheese for a fresh, creamy bite, but it’s not essential.

Image of Our Satellite-Choked Night Skies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:49:07 UTC
23:49:07 KST

Stunning Image of Our Satellite-Choked Night Skies
To create this composite image, photographer Brendan Larsen captured almost 600 photographs over a two-hour period and then manually stitched them together.
This is the most time-consuming photo edit I’ve EVER done!
I left my camera photographing the night sky over Mt Taranaki for nearly TWO HOURS, capturing 578 photographs.
The result? An estimated 14,450 satellite trail appearances, representing approximately 1,400 individual satellites! 😱
I manually masked in EVERY SINGLE TRAIL from the original photographs — approximately 45 HOURS of editing to create this one image!
The Guardian has more on how he created the image (which, despite many online commenters’ beliefs, is not AI):
Larsen, 51, says he set his camera up to take an unlimited number of eight-second-long shots, with a two-second gap in between each photo. “I left her running for two hours and captured 578 photos … That was the easy part.”
The hard part came next. Larsen spent about 45 hours layering the individual photos – each of which contained about 25 satellites – over one another, using Adobe Photoshop. Much of the time was spent painstakingly erasing stars, to reveal the satellites.
“I could start to see the pattern emerging and realised: ‘Wow, this looks really awesome.’ I knew if I carried on it would look even better and more impressive in terms of satellite numbers.”
Fellow photographer Vincent Laforet called Larsen’s image “an important photograph”:
I was initially startled. Then confused. Then fascinated all in quick succession.
And then I felt a deep sense of betrayal once I realized that what I was tracking with my eyes were a series of small satellites. And btw: that they likely had ruined my long exposure that I was capturing at the time.
I remember asking in the moment:
Who gave anyone permission do this?

SoundCloud is partnering with another generative AI music service, ElevenLabs.

You can edit your videos with AI on Instagram&#8217;s new desktop Edits app
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:46:06 UTC
23:46:06 KST

Instagram’s standalone video editing app is now available on macOS, where you can plug in your AI agent of choice to assemble your videos. Instagram’s Matthew Simari, head of product management for Edits, said in an interview with The Verge, “One of the things we’re releasing with Edits Desktop is a MCP for all the tools within Edits Desktop. You can use any agent you want, you can use Muse — we would love you to — but really any agent you want of [your] choice, to edit, tweak, work with your video.”
You can edit your videos with AI on Instagram’s new desktop Edits app
Instagram’s desktop editor has a full multi-track timeline, keyboard shortcuts, and support for connecting AI agents.
The Edits app originally launched on mobile platforms last year. Simari said creators have been “heavily” requesting a desktop version, but AI plans were also a factor in the expansion to macOS. Instagram added an AI “creative assistant” to the mobile version of Edits in September, which can give users video suggestions and feedback using data and metrics from their Instagram account like views and retention on their videos.
On the new desktop version of Edits, Simari said users can “go back and forth from agentic to manual editing.” He gave an example of a creator asking Meta’s Muse agent to use the Edits MCP to make a rough cut of a video in their downloads folder, saying, “It’ll be able just to go access that MCP, do the tool calls, make that rough cut for you, and then you can open that project file in Edits to continue editing.”
The jump to desktop follows Instagram’s push into longform, widescreen videos which tend to be a lot easier to edit on a larger screen. Meta says it’s “expanding Edits to support multiple aspect ratios” and adding support for watermark-free 4K exports. Beyond its AI features, the desktop version of Edits also has more advanced editing features like a full multi-track timeline and precise audio waveforms and color grading tools. It also supports keyboard shortcuts, which Meta says can be “carried over from another editor.”
Like the mobile Edits app, the desktop version has access to Instagram’s audio library and support for publishing videos directly to Instagram. Meta also says audio and text styles users have saved in the mobile app will be accessible from the desktop version, too.
However, the desktop app currently isn’t available on Windows or Linux, only macOS. You can’t edit the same project across both mobile and desktop yet, either. Meta says it’s working on cross-platform editing, and plans to update the new desktop app weekly.

Alpine Linux Security advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:44:20 UTC
23:44:20 KST

Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass
If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd.
Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.
If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set
PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd.
Either one closes the hole.
What is the problem?
An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.
The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is *
(an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and
needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$
password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024
bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without
one reachable.
Details are in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes. No CVE identifier had been assigned at the time of writing.
Who is affected?
You are affected if all of the following are true:
- You run the Alpine openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or
you run openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no. (openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes is not affected.)
- PasswordAuthentication is yes (the OpenSSH default, unless you changed it).
- The machine has an account whose password field is *. This includes:
  - root, which ships as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16.
OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password protects root, so
root is only reachable if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That does not help if
another account that can log in is able to become root, for example
through doas.
  - Any key-only user created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'.
  - Users coming from a directory service through musl-nscd (nslcd, winbind, sssd), since they have no shadow entry.
  - The alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images (see below).
- At least one local account has a $5$ or $6$ password hash.
Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20).
Who is not affected?
- Docker and other container users that do not run sshd in the
container.
- Systems with PasswordAuthentication no.
- Systems using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes (with UsePAM no you are affected).
- Locked accounts: those with ! as the password field in /etc/shadow (a line starting user:!:). They cannot log in with a password or a key.
- Systems where no account has a $-style password hash.
- Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes
PasswordAuthentication no.
How can I fix it?
1. Update
apk upgrade -U -a
Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 contain the fixed package (see the release announcement). The fixed package versions are:
Restart sshd after upgrading (rc-service sshd restart). Upgrading the
package does not restart a running sshd, so you must do it after.
2. If you cannot update: disable password authentication
Before you start, make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until you have tested a new login.
Run these as root. The first two commands create a drop-in file. Alpine’s
default sshd_config reads that directory from 3.19 onward; older releases
ignore it. The sed command changes yes to no on every
PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, whatever the spacing,
including lines inside a Match block. It also adds PasswordAuthentication no at the top of the file, for the case where there was no such line, and
saves the original as /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak. The last two commands check
the configuration, restart the daemon, and show the result:
mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d
echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf
sed -i.bak -e '1i PasswordAuthentication no' \
  -e 's/^\(\s*PasswordAuthentication[^y#]*\)yes/\1no/i' \
  /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sshd -t && rc-service sshd restart
sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication
The last command should print passwordauthentication no. To undo, delete
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf and copy
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak back over /etc/ssh/sshd_config.
Cloud images (tiny-cloud)
The official tiny-cloud images (the qcow2, VHD and AMI artifacts) from
3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ship an alpine user with a * password field and
passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot. They become exploitable as
soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example when an admin sets a
console password, or user-data adds a user with hashed_passwd. An attacker
then gets a shell as alpine and can use doas to become root.
Images built from 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, 3.24.4 and later include the fixed
package. Images from earlier point releases do not, so on every running
instance, update openssh or disable password authentication.
Releases that are no longer supported (3.21 and older)
These releases have the same bug. 3.21 reached its end of support on 2026-11-01, but we have published fixed packages for each release all the way back to 3.16.
How do I know if I was attacked?
Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for
an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user).
Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on
exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as
compromised.
How could this happen?
When sshd is built without PAM, it checks a password by hashing the attempt
with crypt() (the C library function that turns a password into its stored
hash) and comparing the result to the stored password field. For an account
whose stored field is too short to contain a salt (the random prefix of a
hash), sshd borrows the salt of another account.
musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is
over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for
every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.
OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. The stable-branch packages above carry a patch for the same problem.
Credits
Reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. Thanks to Damien Miller and Darren Tucker of the OpenSSH project for the fix and the 10.6p2 release, to Timo Teräs for help analyzing the issue, and to Natanael Copa, who built and uploaded the updated packages.

Alpine Linux Security advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:44:20 UTC
23:44:20 KST

Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass
If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd.
Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.
If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set
PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd.
Either one closes the hole.
What is the problem?
An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.
The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is *
(an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and
needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$
password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024
bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without
one reachable.
Details are in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes. No CVE identifier had been assigned at the time of writing.
Who is affected?
You are affected if all of the following are true:
- You run the Alpine openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or
you run openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no. (openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes is not affected.)
- PasswordAuthentication is yes (the OpenSSH default, unless you changed it).
- The machine has an account whose password field is *. This includes:
  - root, which ships as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16.
OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password protects root, so
root is only reachable if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That does not help if
another account that can log in is able to become root, for example
through doas.
  - Any key-only user created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'.
  - Users coming from a directory service through musl-nscd (nslcd, winbind, sssd), since they have no shadow entry.
  - The alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images (see below).
- At least one local account has a $5$ or $6$ password hash.
Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20).
Who is not affected?
- Docker and other container users that do not run sshd in the
container.
- Systems with PasswordAuthentication no.
- Systems using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes (with UsePAM no you are affected).
- Locked accounts: those with ! as the password field in /etc/shadow (a line starting user:!:). They cannot log in with a password or a key.
- Systems where no account has a $-style password hash.
- Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes
PasswordAuthentication no.
How can I fix it?
1. Update
apk upgrade -U -a
Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 contain the fixed package (see the release announcement). The fixed package versions are:
Restart sshd after upgrading (rc-service sshd restart). Upgrading the
package does not restart a running sshd, so you must do it after.
2. If you cannot update: disable password authentication
Before you start, make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until you have tested a new login.
Run these as root. The first two commands create a drop-in file. Alpine’s
default sshd_config reads that directory from 3.19 onward; older releases
ignore it. The sed command changes yes to no on every
PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, whatever the spacing,
including lines inside a Match block. It also adds PasswordAuthentication no at the top of the file, for the case where there was no such line, and
saves the original as /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak. The last two commands check
the configuration, restart the daemon, and show the result:
mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d
echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf
sed -i.bak -e '1i PasswordAuthentication no' \
  -e 's/^\(\s*PasswordAuthentication[^y#]*\)yes/\1no/i' \
  /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sshd -t && rc-service sshd restart
sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication
The last command should print passwordauthentication no. To undo, delete
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf and copy
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak back over /etc/ssh/sshd_config.

WhatsApp will let you invite friends to events who aren’t on the app
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:44:18 UTC
23:44:18 KST

WhatsApp is rolling out a new feature that allows you to invite friends and family members to events in the app — even if they don’t have the messenger installed. When you create an event in WhatsApp, you can share a link with a friend or family member without the app, and they can still view all the details.
WhatsApp will let you invite friends to events who aren’t on the app
You can also manage your WhatsApp RSVPs through a new Events Home.
WhatsApp will let you manage your events through a new Events Home, where you can create and send invites, as well as manage RSVPs. You can use the new hub to send custom reminders and include an option for guests to add a plus-one. WhatsApp says you can view a complete list of past and upcoming events by navigating to your Settings menu and selecting Events.
This update could make WhatsApp a viable alternative to the other event-planning platforms out there, like Facebook. While Partiful and Apple Invites can send invites to anyone, too, not all event-planners have an iPhone or want to download a new app.
WhatsApp notes that it won’t show your phone number to guests you don’t know, while invitees without WhatsApp will only see the event address after they RSVP. These new features are rolling out to all users in the coming weeks.

September in Servo: , rounded rectangles, and more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:34:18 UTC
23:34:18 KST

Servo 0.7.0 contains all of the changes we landed in September, spanning 527 commits!
The developer tools console now eagerly evaluates JS inputs, allowing faster feedback (@freyacodes, #47527).
We’ve shipped new web platform features:
- the :checked pseudoclass (@skyz1, #47987)
- the user-select property (@SimonSapin, @mrobinson, #48137, #48242)
- the <progress> element (@rayguo17, #46974)
- CSS typed arithmetic (@Loirooriol, #48338)
- the alpha() CSS function (@Loirooriol, #48344)
- the font-width property (@Loirooriol, #47914)
Plus a bunch of new DOM APIs:
- parentRule on CSSRule and CSSStyleDeclaration (@skyz1, #47743)
- version on HTMLHtmlElement (@SilvioPilato, #47786)
- getComposedRanges() and direction on Selection (@mrobinson, #47683)
- baseURL on CSSStyleSheet (@Gae24, #47783)
- CSS modules(@Gae24, #47813) and text modules (@Gae24, #47863)
- getContextAttributes() on CanvasRenderingContext2D and OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D (@Taym95, #47868)
- the Content-Language header (@TimvdLippe, #47930)
- dir on Document (@yezhizhen, #48170)
- SVGAElement, SVGPatternElement, SVGTSpanElement, SVGTextContentElement, SVGTextElement, SVGTextPositioningElement (@mu-mostafa98, #48174)
- the MLKEM768-X25519 algorithm for WebCrypto (@kkoyung, #48240, #48282, #48313, #48350)
- roundRect() on CanvasRenderingContext2D (@yezhizhen, #48293)
- paintTime and presentationTime on PerformancePaintTiming (@shubhamg13, #47926)
- getCueAsHTML() on VTTCue (@TimvdLippe, #48146)
Security
We upgraded to SpiderMonkey v153.3 and mozangle v0.7, both of which included fixes for security bugs reported upstream (@sagudev, #48176, #47655, #48259).
Real world compat
The egui.rs demo now works as expected with --pref dom._webegpu_enabled.
This Candy Crush game is now playable.
We’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion, and failures in our GitHub issues.
Work in progress
Our accessibility tree (--pref accessibility_enabled) now reports geometry bounds for inline elements (@alice, #47905) and does much less work when responding to DOM changes (@alice, @mrobinson, #47690).
Additionally, elements with display: none are reported as hidden (@alice, #47772).
We had lots of conformance improvements for our WebGL2 implementation (--pref dom_webgl2_enabled) (@mxmgorin, #48423, #48441, #48470, #48479, #48495, #48473, #48536).
Support for WSIWYG editors (which rely heavily on contenteditable) is going very well: keyboard inputs are now hooked up when --pref dom_exec_command_enabled is present, so many editors are now usable (example).
Closed captioning for video elements is making progress.
Text tracks now fire enter, exit, and cuechange events (@TimvdLippe, #47725).
Media elements now return the full sorted list of text tracks (@TimvdLippe, #47785), and adding cues to a text track now sets that track correctly (@TimvdLippe, #48012).
Text track objects now reflect the attributes of the associated <track> element.
Text track URLs are fetched at the correct time (@TimvdLippe, #48325), and active cues are computed correctly (@TimvdLippe, #48305), while text track cues are ordered as expected (@TimvdLippe, #48368).
Additionally, WebVTT parsing can now recover from errors (@TimvdLippe, #48391).
The Sanitizer API (--pref dom_sanitizer_enabled) now accepts the javascriptURLs property (@skyz1, #47867).
IndexedDB continues to improve: tables no longer error if unrelated tables contain duplicate index names (--pref dom_indexeddb_enabled) (@leowatts, #47936).
Additionally, we implemented openCursor() and openKeyCursor() on IDBIndex (@kuntal-devrat, #48281), as well as advance(), continue(), and continuePrimaryKey() on IDBCursor (@kuntal-devrat, #48400).
We implemented the getTimeline() and setTimeline() methods for the Animation interface (--pref dom_web_animations_enabled) (@simonwuelker, #48122).
Embedding API
There’s a new API for events originating from accessibility tools: Servo::forward_accessibility_action (@alice, @mrobinson, #48512).
There is also an API to clear session history: WebView::clear_session_history (@Narfinger, #47483).
The WebView::set_throttled API has been removed (@mrobinson, #39923).
Throttling automatically occurs when a WebView is hidden and is stopped when shown.
The WebViewDelegate::notify_focus_changed method was removed, along with the Servo methods focus and blur (@mrobinson, #48364).
Embedders must call WebView::set_focused whenever a WebView has gained or lost system focus.
The webgl feature has been added to the default_web_features feature (@janeoa, #47866).
If an embedding does not want to ship with WebGL support they will now need to disable default features.
Multiprocess mode is enabled at build time with the new Cargo feature multprocess (@Narfinger, #47360).
To remove support for this feature (reducing binary size by ~2MB), build Servo with default features disabled.
Two new preferences exist to tune garbage collector behaviour: js_mem_gc_malloc_threshold_base_mb and js_mem_gc_urgent_threshold_mb (@mxmgorin, #47999).
These can help on memory-constrained devices, and more information is available in the SpiderMonkey source (base, urgent).
The JVM compatibility target was raised to 11 on Android (@veyndan, #48414).
For users and developers
It is now possible to cross-compile the OpenHarmony build from Windows hosts (@jschwe, #48392).
Unhandled promise rejections are reported to the JS console (@TTyChud, #48486), making it easier to narrow down web compatibility issues in Servo.
The OpenHarmony SDK was updated to API level 23 (@Narfinger, #48505).
Pressing Control+A (or Command+A on macOS) now selects all the content in a document (@dzfrias, @mrobinson, #48025). It is no longer possible to copy text inside of password inputs (@dzfrias, #48404).
Embedder-originating JS (e.g. devtools console or embedding APIs) will always execute, even in documents that disable scripting via sandboxing or CSP (@derdilla, #48394).
Performance and stability
We improved performance by removing unnecessary allocations (@Narfinger, @TimvdLippe, @yezhizhen, #47689, #47839, #47838, #47982, #48006, #48036, #48099, #48204, #48127, #48218, #48357, #48386, #48422, #48440, #48452, #48508), preallocating more when building vectors (@jschwe, @Narfinger, @sagudev, @webbeef, #47455, #47613, #48026, #48398), and avoiding IPC in single process mode (@leowatts, @Narfinger, @Uiniel, @TTyChud, #47691, #47718, #48002, #48073, #48476, #48435).
We also sped up Servo by reducing interactions with the GC (@TimvdLippe, @Narfinger, #47818, #48257, #48396), and doing less work when modifying selections (@SimonSapin, #47579), dispatching events (@webbeef, #48078), calculating font metrics (@RichardTjokroutomo, #48238), and indexing window frames (@mrobinson, #47832).
We reduced memory usage in common cases by reusing buffers (@Narfinger, #47751), clearing more page-specific data (@Radeonares32, @Narfinger, @jschwe, @mrobinson, @mxmgorin, #47651, #47806, #47805, #48166, #48295, #48297, #48016), compacting data structures (@Narfinger, @webbeef, @SimonSapin, @mrobinson, #47776, #48039, #48050, #47742, #48301, #48296, #48105), and sharing more buffers (@jdm, #47998).
We also fixed a memory leak involving <audio> and <video> elements (@TTyChud, #48371).
We turned on thread affinity boosting on Linux, which can improve performance on some CPU architectures (@jschwe, #47058).
We’re working on statically preventing a footgun that can lead to uncollectible GC cycles and leaking memory (@Gae24, @jdm, @lumiscosity, @SilvioPilato, @sahilnyk, @TTyChud, @kuntal-devrat, @MohamedAli00949, #47941, #48013, #48021, #48035, #48033, #48051, #48072, #48171, #48209, #48248, #48246, #48264, #48285, #48311, #48408, #48053, #48156, #48186, #48223, #48315, #47872, #47698, #47682, #47735, #47816, #47817, #47794, #47909, #47934, #47935, #47954, #48022, #47955, #48058, #48228, #48247, #48261, #48280, #48302, #48316, #48328, #48346, #48355, #48262, #48377, #48304, #48378, #48388, #48432).
We fixed panics in WebRTC (@MunishMummadi, #4772), execCommand() on Document (@TimvdLippe, #47784), <video> (@calvaris, #46148), <iframe> (@jdm, #48465), SharedWorker (@mrobinson, #47940), ancestorOrigins on Document (@mrobinson, #48009), about:memory (@mxmgorin, #47686, #48001), and EGL 1.4 configurations (@mxmgorin, #47803).
We also fixed a very ironic panic triggered by the about:crash page that loads when a normal page triggers a panic (@mrobinson, #48055)
The JS console no longer hangs when primitive values as thrown as exceptions (@FatCat560, #47629). Servo no longer hangs on shutdown in multiprocess mode (@Narfinger, #48523), when certain pages use IntersectionObserver (@mxmgorin, #47693), when closing a browsing context with pending WebDriver commands (@yezhizhen, #48131, #48172), or when closing SharedWorkers (@nicoburns, #48477).
about:memory got more improvements: we measure more memory for SVG rendering (@Narfinger, @mrobinson, #47061), WebAudio (@jdm, #47996), and identify globals that have been leaked (@jdm, #48237).
More on the web platform
CSS images now delay the load event, leading to more consistent behaviour for engine users performing visual rendering (@TimvdLippe, #48199).
Interactive selections in documents continued to improve! They now can span shadow trees (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, #47931, #47694, #47895), and have consistent heights and positions (@mrobinson, #47937), plus there are new context menu entries to copy and select all (@mrobinson, #48101). Additionally, image-based content shows when it is part of a selection (@mrobinson, #48149).
Window.open() respects sandbox flags that prevent popups (@mrobinson, #47653).
LargestContentfulPaint now reports the loadTime for image content (@shubhamg13, #48286), ignores cross-origin frames (@shubhamg13, #48094), ignores invisible text (@shubhamg13, #48010), and reports null elements when they are removed from the tree (@shubhamg13, #48125).
select() on a text input now focuses the control (@dzfrias, @mrobinson, #48475).
Our WebDriver server now automates setting permissions (@xbwwj, @yezhizhen, #47623), while sending click events and keyboard actions uses fewer delays (@yezhizhen, #48066).
There are more useful error messages for methods on Document (@eachra-bawn, #47835) and CSS-related interfaces (@eachra-bawn, @jdm, #47746).
We upgraded our stylo dependency, which improves compatibility with contrast-color(), color-mix(), vertical-align, list-style, place-items, at-rule(), calc(), alpha(), attr(), content: attr(), and named-feature() (@Loirooriol, #46987, #47942).
We also fixed bugs related to visibilityState on Document (@yezhizhen, #47908), containsNode() on Selection (@mrobinson, #47938), setKeyframes on KeyframeEffect (@simonwuelker, #48103), selections when focusing a text input (@mrobinson, #48107), AudioParam clamping and automation (@kevlu93, #48351, #48347), PannerNode outputs (@kevlu93, #48510), the muted attribute on HTMLMediaElement (@TimvdLippe, #48403), placeholders in text inputs (@jdm, #47761, #47797), animations when modifying document stylesheets (@SharanRP, #48000), gradient color stops (@BudiArb, #48288), sticky table rows (@TTyChud, #48380), ::first-letter (@Loirooriol, #48307), text-wrap-mode (@mrobinson, #48469), OTF fonts (@wood-ghost, #47904), CSS and nosniff (@sahvx655-wq, #45481), Sec-Fetch- headers and redirects (@TimvdLippe, #48203), moveBefore() on Node (@mrobinson, #47692), supports() on WebCrypto (@kkoyung, #47768, #47891, #47953, #47984, #48410, #47545), cross-origin windows (@mrobinson, @jdm, #47632, #48411, #48038), origins of about:blank and about:srcdoc (@mrobinson, #47630), keypress events (@mrobinson, #48324), text and media documents (@SilvioPilato, #47823), body() on Response (@TTyChud, #48409), <details> with <summary> (@TimvdLippe, #48224), editing hidden inputs (@dzfrias, #48165), attribute nodes in XPath (@leowatts, @mrobinson, #47912), absolutely positioned boxes (@mxmgorin, #48081), CSS Grid containers with absolutely positioned nodes (@nicoburns, #47519), WebDriver wheel/pointer actions (@yezhizhen, #48143), and blob: URLs (@Gae24, #47910).
New contributors

Work in progress
Our accessibility tree (--pref accessibility_enabled) now reports geometry bounds for inline elements (@alice, #47905) and does much less work when responding to DOM changes (@alice, @mrobinson, #47690).
Additionally, elements with display: none are reported as hidden (@alice, #47772).
We had lots of conformance improvements for our WebGL2 implementation (--pref dom_webgl2_enabled) (@mxmgorin, #48423, #48441, #48470, #48479, #48495, #48473, #48536).
Support for WSIWYG editors (which rely heavily on contenteditable) is going very well: keyboard inputs are now hooked up when --pref dom_exec_command_enabled is present, so many editors are now usable (example).
Closed captioning for video elements is making progress.
Text tracks now fire enter, exit, and cuechange events (@TimvdLippe, #47725).
Media elements now return the full sorted list of text tracks (@TimvdLippe, #47785), and adding cues to a text track now sets that track correctly (@TimvdLippe, #48012).
Text track objects now reflect the attributes of the associated <track> element.
Text track URLs are fetched at the correct time (@TimvdLippe, #48325), and active cues are computed correctly (@TimvdLippe, #48305), while text track cues are ordered as expected (@TimvdLippe, #48368).
Additionally, WebVTT parsing can now recover from errors (@TimvdLippe, #48391).
The Sanitizer API (--pref dom_sanitizer_enabled) now accepts the javascriptURLs property (@skyz1, #47867).
IndexedDB continues to improve: tables no longer error if unrelated tables contain duplicate index names (--pref dom_indexeddb_enabled) (@leowatts, #47936).
Additionally, we implemented openCursor() and openKeyCursor() on IDBIndex (@kuntal-devrat, #48281), as well as advance(), continue(), and continuePrimaryKey() on IDBCursor (@kuntal-devrat, #48400).
We implemented the getTimeline() and setTimeline() methods for the Animation interface (--pref dom_web_animations_enabled) (@simonwuelker, #48122).
Embedding API
There’s a new API for events originating from accessibility tools: Servo::forward_accessibility_action (@alice, @mrobinson, #48512).
There is also an API to clear session history: WebView::clear_session_history (@Narfinger, #47483).
The WebView::set_throttled API has been removed (@mrobinson, #39923).
Throttling automatically occurs when a WebView is hidden and is stopped when shown.
The WebViewDelegate::notify_focus_changed method was removed, along with the Servo methods focus and blur (@mrobinson, #48364).
Embedders must call WebView::set_focused whenever a WebView has gained or lost system focus.
The webgl feature has been added to the default_web_features feature (@janeoa, #47866).
If an embedding does not want to ship with WebGL support they will now need to disable default features.
Multiprocess mode is enabled at build time with the new Cargo feature multprocess (@Narfinger, #47360).
To remove support for this feature (reducing binary size by ~2MB), build Servo with default features disabled.
Two new preferences exist to tune garbage collector behaviour: js_mem_gc_malloc_threshold_base_mb and js_mem_gc_urgent_threshold_mb (@mxmgorin, #47999).
These can help on memory-constrained devices, and more information is available in the SpiderMonkey source (base, urgent).
The JVM compatibility target was raised to 11 on Android (@veyndan, #48414).
For users and developers
It is now possible to cross-compile the OpenHarmony build from Windows hosts (@jschwe, #48392).
Unhandled promise rejections are reported to the JS console (@TTyChud, #48486), making it easier to narrow down web compatibility issues in Servo.
The OpenHarmony SDK was updated to API level 23 (@Narfinger, #48505).
Pressing Control+A (or Command+A on macOS) now selects all the content in a document (@dzfrias, @mrobinson, #48025). It is no longer possible to copy text inside of password inputs (@dzfrias, #48404).
Embedder-originating JS (e.g. devtools console or embedding APIs) will always execute, even in documents that disable scripting via sandboxing or CSP (@derdilla, #48394).
Performance and stability
We improved performance by removing unnecessary allocations (@Narfinger, @TimvdLippe, @yezhizhen, #47689, #47839, #47838, #47982, #48006, #48036, #48099, #48204, #48127, #48218, #48357, #48386, #48422, #48440, #48452, #48508), preallocating more when building vectors (@jschwe, @Narfinger, @sagudev, @webbeef, #47455, #47613, #48026, #48398), and avoiding IPC in single process mode (@leowatts, @Narfinger, @Uiniel, @TTyChud, #47691, #47718, #48002, #48073, #48476, #48435).
We also sped up Servo by reducing interactions with the GC (@TimvdLippe, @Narfinger, #47818, #48257, #48396), and doing less work when modifying selections (@SimonSapin, #47579), dispatching events (@webbeef, #48078), calculating font metrics (@RichardTjokroutomo, #48238), and indexing window frames (@mrobinson, #47832).
We reduced memory usage in common cases by reusing buffers (@Narfinger, #47751), clearing more page-specific data (@Radeonares32, @Narfinger, @jschwe, @mrobinson, @mxmgorin, #47651, #47806, #47805, #48166, #48295, #48297, #48016), compacting data structures (@Narfinger, @webbeef, @SimonSapin, @mrobinson, #47776, #48039, #48050, #47742, #48301, #48296, #48105), and sharing more buffers (@jdm, #47998).
We also fixed a memory leak involving <audio> and <video> elements (@TTyChud, #48371).
We turned on thread affinity boosting on Linux, which can improve performance on some CPU architectures (@jschwe, #47058).
We’re working on statically preventing a footgun that can lead to uncollectible GC cycles and leaking memory (@Gae24, @jdm, @lumiscosity, @SilvioPilato, @sahilnyk, @TTyChud, @kuntal-devrat, @MohamedAli00949, #47941, #48013, #48021, #48035, #48033, #48051, #48072, #48171, #48209, #48248, #48246, #48264, #48285, #48311, #48408, #48053, #48156, #48186, #48223, #48315, #47872, #47698, #47682, #47735, #47816, #47817, #47794, #47909, #47934, #47935, #47954, #48022, #47955, #48058, #48228, #48247, #48261, #48280, #48302, #48316, #48328, #48346, #48355, #48262, #48377, #48304, #48378, #48388, #48432).
We fixed panics in WebRTC (@MunishMummadi, #4772), execCommand() on Document (@TimvdLippe, #47784), <video> (@calvaris, #46148), <iframe> (@jdm, #48465), SharedWorker (@mrobinson, #47940), ancestorOrigins on Document (@mrobinson, #48009), about:memory (@mxmgorin, #47686, #48001), and EGL 1.4 configurations (@mxmgorin, #47803).
We also fixed a very ironic panic triggered by the about:crash page that loads when a normal page triggers a panic (@mrobinson, #48055)
The JS console no longer hangs when primitive values as thrown as exceptions (@FatCat560, #47629). Servo no longer hangs on shutdown in multiprocess mode (@Narfinger, #48523), when certain pages use IntersectionObserver (@mxmgorin, #47693), when closing a browsing context with pending WebDriver commands (@yezhizhen, #48131, #48172), or when closing SharedWorkers (@nicoburns, #48477).
about:memory got more improvements: we measure more memory for SVG rendering (@Narfinger, @mrobinson, #47061), WebAudio (@jdm, #47996), and identify globals that have been leaked (@jdm, #48237).
More on the web platform
CSS images now delay the load event, leading to more consistent behaviour for engine users performing visual rendering (@TimvdLippe, #48199).
Interactive selections in documents continued to improve! They now can span shadow trees (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, #47931, #47694, #47895), and have consistent heights and positions (@mrobinson, #47937), plus there are new context menu entries to copy and select all (@mrobinson, #48101). Additionally, image-based content shows when it is part of a selection (@mrobinson, #48149).
Window.open() respects sandbox flags that prevent popups (@mrobinson, #47653).
LargestContentfulPaint now reports the loadTime for image content (@shubhamg13, #48286), ignores cross-origin frames (@shubhamg13, #48094), ignores invisible text (@shubhamg13, #48010), and reports null elements when they are removed from the tree (@shubhamg13, #48125).
select() on a text input now focuses the control (@dzfrias, @mrobinson, #48475).
Our WebDriver server now automates setting permissions (@xbwwj, @yezhizhen, #47623), while sending click events and keyboard actions uses fewer delays (@yezhizhen, #48066).
There are more useful error messages for methods on Document (@eachra-bawn, #47835) and CSS-related interfaces (@eachra-bawn, @jdm, #47746).
We upgraded our stylo dependency, which improves compatibility with contrast-color(), color-mix(), vertical-align, list-style, place-items, at-rule(), calc(), alpha(), attr(), content: attr(), and named-feature() (@Loirooriol, #46987, #47942).
We also fixed bugs related to visibilityState on Document (@yezhizhen, #47908), containsNode() on Selection (@mrobinson, #47938), setKeyframes on KeyframeEffect (@simonwuelker, #48103), selections when focusing a text input (@mrobinson, #48107), AudioParam clamping and automation (@kevlu93, #48351, #48347), PannerNode outputs (@kevlu93, #48510), the muted attribute on HTMLMediaElement (@TimvdLippe, #48403), placeholders in text inputs (@jdm, #47761, #47797), animations when modifying document stylesheets (@SharanRP, #48000), gradient color stops (@BudiArb, #48288), sticky table rows (@TTyChud, #48380), ::first-letter (@Loirooriol, #48307), text-wrap-mode (@mrobinson, #48469), OTF fonts (@wood-ghost, #47904), CSS and nosniff (@sahvx655-wq, #45481), Sec-Fetch- headers and redirects (@TimvdLippe, #48203), moveBefore() on Node (@mrobinson, #47692), supports() on WebCrypto (@kkoyung, #47768, #47891, #47953, #47984, #48410, #47545), cross-origin windows (@mrobinson, @jdm, #47632, #48411, #48038), origins of about:blank and about:srcdoc (@mrobinson, #47630), keypress events (@mrobinson, #48324), text and media documents (@SilvioPilato, #47823), body() on Response (@TTyChud, #48409), <details> with <summary> (@TimvdLippe, #48224), editing hidden inputs (@dzfrias, #48165), attribute nodes in XPath (@leowatts, @mrobinson, #47912), absolutely positioned boxes (@mxmgorin, #48081), CSS Grid containers with absolutely positioned nodes (@nicoburns, #47519), WebDriver wheel/pointer actions (@yezhizhen, #48143), and blob: URLs (@Gae24, #47910).

His companies have continued to rake in billions in government contracts, his busted AI has been integrated into critical government systems, and the cuts led by his “Department of Government Efficiency” has, conservatively, killed many thousands of people around the world. He has installed manosphere podcasters, X trolls, and conspiracy theorists into top administration roles; they have performed even worse than their already low expectations. He has leveraged commercial surveillance companies to build a brutal, tech-powered mass deportation campaign. His government’s communications strategy can be described in no other way than inscrutable AI slop shitposting. This is to say nothing of the cost of living crisis Trump has caused as he’s started an illegal war in Iran that has driven up gas and diesel prices and levied tariffs on America’s allies for reasons that defy explanation. This has driven up the price of everything even as Trump’s administration slashes regulations on fossil fuel companies and big corporations.

Tech is about to get hammered in Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:11:27 UTC
23:11:27 KST

Tech CEO hearings. Tougher AI and data center guardrails. Investigations of Elon Musk’s DOGE cuts. The gates are open for Democrats once they regain control of committee gavels come January after a historic win of majorities in both the House and Senate on Tuesday.
Tech is about to get hammered in Congress
Democrats have promised to drag CEOs to testify under oath and investigate corporate influence.
“LAWYER UP,” the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee wrote on X in a message aimed at the Trump administration as well as “corporate corruption” shortly after networks like NBC News projected Democratic control of the House. “Subpoenas,” Senate Finance Ranking Member Ron Wyden (D-OR) posted. It’s clear tech executives will also be caught in Democrats’ crosshairs. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA) posted in response to a comment that asked, “Live televised trials of Big Tech executives when?”
“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing”
Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX), chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and an Oversight member, made clear that AI companies are well within his sights. “AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath,” he said in a statement. “The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics.” Rep. Frank Pallone, the top Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, the clearinghouse for tech policy issues ranging from digital privacy to kids online safety to AI, pledged to advance policies that “protect consumers and the environment, prioritize clean energy, and rein in Big Tech.” Silicon Valley Congressman Ro Khanna said taxing billionaires should be among Democrats’ top goals. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) has called to “PAUSE AI NOW.”
Democrats have already used their position in the minority to signal what would be at the top of their committee agendas. House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (D-MD), for example, held a “shadow” hearing earlier this year after the Trump administration’s Justice Department settled its Live Nation-Ticketmaster antitrust trial, which state attorneys general who continued to litigate went on to win.
At the time, Raskin told reporters that it was important to get a head start on administration oversight. “The corruption permeates the administration so much that we have to start building the record because it’s such an overwhelming task,” he said. “We will be using the products of all of these shadow hearings to figure out where to go.” More recently, Raskin demanded information from Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle about nondisclosure agreements for public officials considering data center proposals.
“AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath”
Democrats are also itching to investigate Tesla and SpaceX CEO Musk over all manner of issues. Musk spent record-breaking amounts trying to elect Republicans this cycle and held an unprecedented role in the second Trump administration as the public face of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), responsible for slashing federal jobs and eliminating the country’s soft diplomacy arm, USAID. Powerful Democratic lawmakers recently told Politico they’re eyeing issues like Musk’s role in DOGE, his alleged conflicts of interest, and his role in reportedly disrupting Starlink service to Ukraine.
Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-CA), a lawmaker from Silicon Valley who just won reelection, says while he’s all for probing things like DOGE, he also doesn’t want his party to get lost in endless calls for tech CEOs to testify without significant legislating to back it up. “I think what is imperative for Democrats is to come to the table with solutions, not with slogans. Not with a lot of performative ranting, but actual solutions,” Liccardo tells The Verge in an interview.
With full control of Congress by a significant margin, Democrats may be able to push forward legislation that would have otherwise been difficult to pass under current Republican leadership. They will still likely run into vetoes by President Donald Trump over things like more heavy-handed AI safeguards that the president has resisted. TD Cowen’s Washington Research Group wrote in a note Wednesday that it still firmly believes Trump “will veto any AI safety bill passed by Congress that would slow the AI model releases cycle.” The group also anticipates that Democrats will take another stab at tech antitrust legislation, which has been more or less on hold for years, but suspects those efforts will either stop short of a floor vote or get vetoed.
Liccardo thinks AI safety rules should be at the top of Democrats’ tech agenda, followed closely by data centers and AI’s impact on jobs. Despite Trump’s aversion to many AI safeguards, he says Congress may be able to get Trump’s signature if they can muster enough bipartisan support. “Pushing Trump out of the way requires that we show strength,” Liccardo says. “We saw that in the past with, for example, the Epstein files.” When some Republicans broke away from him, Liccardo says, Trump realized “that he had to get out of the way of the train because he was not going to stop it.”
Trump told The New York Times on election night he’d at least aim to work with Democrats, which could indicate a potential path for measures with a broad coalition of bipartisan support. The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA), for example, passed overwhelmingly in the Senate in 2024, but was blocked by Republican leadership in the House. While Trump has not endorsed the Kids Online Safety Act, which was cosponsored by his ally Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), it’s conceivable it could pass the House if given the floor time, and Trump could consider signing it should it pass both chambers. “Big Tech’s lawless disregard for our children and our communities will be among my top priorities this Congress,” KOSA cosponsor Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said in a statement. “Whether it’s the industry trading kids’ lives for greater profits or its wealthiest leaders trying to buy influence from a corrupt Trump Administration, Big Tech’s reign of impunity must come to an end. Frankly, this issue has always been bipartisan, and I’m hopeful that I’ll have strong partners on both sides of the aisle as we pursue a strong oversight agenda.”
Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) says Democrats should pass bills like those he’s introduced to make app stores responsible for imposing age requirements and keep kids under 16 off of social media to give parents back a sense of control. “Democrats should give voice to parents who feel powerless against social media corporations that treat their children like free labor for the dopamine economy,” he says in a statement.
Data center developers are also likely to hit obstacles and have to slow their breakneck pace. “For tech investors the big focus is will these mid-term elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution…the answer in our view is a clear YES,” Yorkville Ives analysts wrote in a note on Wednesday. “There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years. While Trump will likely veto any major draconian AI safety or regulatory laws, this will force the tech industry (Big Tech CEOs) to the negotiating table to try to come up with compromises around legislation in Congress surrounding AI related legislation.”
“Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation”
Center-left tech policy coalition Chamber of Progress is already warning Democrats not to “confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate,” with CEO Adam Kovacevich saying that Democratic governor candidates who opposed data center bans won at higher rates than supporters. Liccardo says “it’s not a secret that data centers poll about as well as measles, mumps, and rubella, but I don’t think that’s what suddenly drove the midterms.” He hopes to leverage the data center buildout to make developers pay for needed investments in the energy grid.
One company that could get a slightly warmer welcome in Congress may be Anthropic, which notably stood up to the Trump administration when the Pentagon demanded it agree to let it use Anthropic’s AI for domestic mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. The company is still likely to face many of the same questions and skepticism about its AI safety proposals as other leading AI companies, but its positioning over the past several months may help differentiate it from peers.
Democrats’ recent messaging has promised a Big Tech and AI crackdown. Between 2020 and 2024, the party spent about $2 million to run six political ads that referenced keywords relating to the tech industry, according to public policy group Reset Tech; between 2025 and 2026, they ran 387, spending more than $100 million to do so. If the results from Tuesday are any indication, the rewards for following through with that message could be high.

NASA’s new experimental X-70 plane will be used to test next-gen aviation technologies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:10:12 UTC
23:10:12 KST

Yesterday NASA announced the latest addition to its X-series of experimental aircraft that have included the Bell X-1 that first broke the sound barrier nearly 80 years ago, and the more recent X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator. The new X-70 Fractal is designed to be a “high-performance, highly adaptable research platform” that NASA can use as a testbed for the development and testing of next-generation aviation technologies.
The X-70 is NASA’s next experimental X-plane
The X-70 Fractal is expected to take flight within the next two years.
The agency only released an AI-generated image of the X-70 shrouded in smoke and shadows, but confirmed several of the plane’s capabilities. It will be a crewed aircraft with a cruising speed of Mach .75 that can reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet and will provide an “operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles.” The X-70 will be able to carry up to 2,000 pounds of experimental equipment either inside or outside the aircraft, and will feature “advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight.”
“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics.”

MCP Explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:08:35 UTC
23:08:35 KST

Model Context Protocol
What is MCP?
An open standard for connecting AI apps to the tools and data they use. A server says what it can do, the app shows that to the model, and when the model wants something the app calls the server and hands the result back.
- Host
- the AI app you use: Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, an agent
- Server
- a small program exposing tools, data or prompts
- Model
- decides what to use; never talks to a server directly
- Not REST
- JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout or one HTTP endpoint, and servers can talk back
- Not just JSON-RPC
- JSON-RPC is the envelope. MCP defines what goes in it: the methods, capability negotiation, transports and auth
or jump to Tools · the spec time machine · Break it
Model Context Protocol
Spec

The hidden supply chain costs of the AI boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
14:03:27 UTC
23:03:27 KST

Today, I’m talking with Willy Shih, an economist, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, and the author of the upcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains.
The hidden supply chain costs of the AI boom
Economist Willy Shih on his new book Where Does My Stuff Come From?, RAMageddon, and why we still can’t make the iPhone in America.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Willy is one of my all-time favorite Decoder guests — his way of looking at the world through our supply chains is just a fascinating way of making sense of the global economy. I first met Willy in 2019, while The Verge was covering Foxconn’s promise to build an LCD fab in Wisconsin. That obviously never happened, but Willy called it right away because he could see the supply chain to support a fab simply wasn’t in place. We also had Willy on the show in 2021 to talk about what was then the pandemic-era chip shortage.
Now, five years later, we’re in another manufacturing mess, as we stand in the middle of a political fight over whether globalization is coming to an end. Trumps’ tariffs keep changing, the factories that were supposed to reshore in America mostly haven’t materialized, and AI is devouring the planet’s computing resources during an unprecedented infrastructure buildout.
Willy’s new book is all about the economics underlying these complex systems, which our politicians and regulators seem to insistently ignore. You’ll hear us talk about why the markets have reacted to all these disruptions the way they have, and why China remains a global manufacturing powerhouse even though every other country thinks that’s so risky. I loved this conversation — it’s in the weeds, and Willy really knows his stuff.
Okay: economist Will Shih on his new book Where Does My Stuff Come From? Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Willy Shih, you’re an economist and professor of management practice at Harvard. You’re also the author of the new book, Where Does My Stuff Come From: The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains. Welcome back to Decoder.
Well, thanks for having me back.
I am very excited to talk to you. You and I first started talking ages ago when The Verge was covering Foxconn in Wisconsin. You are a reliable source of information on what it takes to actually build an LCD plant anywhere, not just in Wisconsin.
The Foxconn in Wisconsin thing was funny because I tend to go on first principles on these things. Once I knew they weren’t going to build a glass plant across the street, it’s like there’s no way there’s going to be a factory.
Now, what happened afterwards, of course, is people heard your show, and then I started getting calls from people who live in the community. They went to the zoning hearings in town, then sent me the plans and asked, “Is this going to be a panel factory?” I said, “No, I told you it’s not going to be a panel factory.” So they sent me the plans. I said, “Well, there’s not enough concrete to make this a panel factory.” For a panel factory, you need stability, so you gotta have all this structural steel, and you have to have all this concrete.
