Why This Obscure Audio Codec Is a Perfect Fit for the N64
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
12:51:48 UTC
21:51:48 KST

Why this Obscure Audio Codec is a Perfect Fit for the N64
Sorry for the clickbait title. I promise this post delivers: 44100 Hz stereo with near-Opus bitrates using about 4% of the N64’s CPU time.
But first, some history: The options for playing and storing audio data on the N64 were dire. The PlayStation could just stream uncompressed redbook audio straight from the CD. On the N64, cartridge space was at a premium and time on the 93 MHz CPU was limited.
Worse, access to the vector co-processor, the RSP, was guarded by Nintendo for the longest time. Nintendo's own platform library, Libultra, internally used the RSP for various graphics and sound-related tasks, but Nintendo didn't allow third-party developers to directly write code for it.
Libultra provided some functions to transparently play back compressed audio using an ADPCM scheme (adaptive differential pulse code modulation). The RSP handled decompression on the fly, just before the audio was sent to the output buffer.
This works well enough and cuts the space needed for a sample by a factor of 4. Still, a 5-minute stereo audio track at 44100 Hz will land at about 12MB – way too much for an N64 cartridge, even when you cut the sample rate in half. The whole Mario 64 ROM is just 8MB in total. The biggest N64 games were 64MB.
So N64 games produced music similarly to a tracker: short samples were scheduled and played back with some limited effects at the right time. With the space constraints on the cartridge, fully “recorded” audio was pretty much out of the question.
Later in the N64's life, some blessed developers were allowed by Nintendo to directly access the RSP. Most famously, Conker's Bad Fur Day used this to decompress MP3 audio for the myriad of speech samples in the game. Decoding MP3 is quite expensive and the frame rate of the game suffered. It was good enough for cutscenes, but just too much for continuous background music or sound effects during gameplay.
Audio in the Open Source Libdragon
Similar to Nintendo's Libultra, Libdragon, the open source alternative, has a real-time ADPCM decoder running on the RSP. So with ROM space being cheaper these days, I just compressed all music for Xibalba 64 with ADPCM. About 31MB of the 32MB ROM are used for sound and music. Remember that Mario 64 just used an 8MB ROM and Xibalba 64 is a much simpler game with only 15 minutes of music. It worked, but storing music this way is a gratuitous waste of space.
Now, Libdragon also has a real-time, RSP-accelerated Opus decoder. It's a marvel in itself. The Opus format was published 16 years after the N64 and yet Giovanni Bajo managed to make it work on this “obsolete” hardware. Compression and audio quality are excellent, but again – it's too slow to be used during gameplay.
What's the alternative then? We could build an RSP-accelerated MP3 decoder, but the performance gain over Opus would be marginal, and quality and compression would be worse.
QOA would be a slight improvement over ADPCM, but it's just a poor fit for the vector co-processor: each sample relies on the previous decoded sample. Hard to vectorize.
A simple transform codec, something like MP3, but without all the design-by-consortium baggage, may work…
The Ultra Low Complexity Codec
During some late-night “research”, I stumbled across an old Game Boy Advance demo that plays recorded music at just 70kbps. That's less than a typical MP3, but at comparable quality. I repeat: On a GBA. With a 16 MHz ARM CPU. With no vector instructions and, according to the GitHub page, some headroom to spare.
Time-domain codecs (such as ADPCM) need significantly higher bitrates for this quality. Subband codecs, such as MP2, have much worse quality at comparable bitrates, and more “modern” transform codecs, such as MP3, usually need at least an 80–100 MHz CPU. For this GBA demo, no existing codec would fit the bill.
So Aikku93 not only wrote a decoder in ARM assembly, but also created a whole new codec: The Ultra Low Complexity Codec (ULC).
ULC is a transform codec and somewhat similar to MP3. ULC transforms slices of PCM data into the frequency domain. Like MP3, it uses the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) to do so. But unlike MP3, it does not split the signal into multiple bands (ULC's MDCT is “full-band”). Where MP3 uses classic entropy encoding (Huffman specifically), ULC does… not. Instead, transformed coefficients are stored with a very simple nibble-based syntax.
In short: ULC is what MP3 could have been. The same core idea, but without the cruft around it. The “ultra low complexity” does not come from a different algorithm, but by carefully applying and packaging it.
The nibble-based packaging is maybe the most elegant idea of ULC. Each coefficient is stored in just 4 bits, interpreted as a signed integer. Some values are reserved to indicate zero fill, noise fill, or a quantizer change:
- -7 … -2, 2 … 7 - coefficient value
- 0 - zero run, run length (1 … 16) follows in the next nibble
- 1 - long zero run, run length (17 … 288) follows in the next two nibbles
- -1 - quantizer change, value follows in the next nibble
- -8 - noise fill, length and amplitude follow in the next three nibbles
Everything is nibble aligned. This means the whole codec works without any arbitrary bit reads or entropy decoding. Reading and unpacking a block of coefficients takes just ~150 lines of C.
Also note that noise fill is a valuable addition. Cymbals, hi-hats and snare drums greatly benefit from that. MP3 does not have anything similar and needs to encode quasi-random coefficients as is.
ULC can produce usable results even at 16kbps. Quality of course suffers, but it might still be good enough for some applications.
Aikku93 has been working on ULC since 2019 and has steadily improved the encoding quality. All code is permissively licensed. Time to try this on the N64 then!
ULC on the N64
I spent an evening in pre-LLM days compiling the ULC reference decoder for the N64 and producing a small demo. It worked without a hitch.
The only problem: it was keeping the CPU very busy. Nothing was offloaded to the RSP. As a proof of concept, it wasn't doing much: we already knew the 93 MHz CPU was enough to decode a transform-based codec, but we don't need a “music player” that does nothing else. We need this for background music and spoken dialog during gameplay. It cannot hog the CPU.
Float to 16-bit Fixed Point
Obviously the IMDCT needs to be moved to the RSP coprocessor instead. We could just DMA one block of decoded coefficients to the RSP's memory, do the transform and DMA the completed samples back to RDRAM into the output buffer.
That's easier said than done, though. The RSP has only 4096 bytes of data memory (DMEM) and another 4096 bytes for instructions (IMEM). The vector instructions work in 16-bit or 32-bit fixed point, with no floats. The IMDCT will only be efficient if all the data for a transform fits into the RSP's DMEM at once. We also need some of the DMEM for temporary values and – if possible – the lapping buffer: half of the previously decoded block. So with the default 2048-sample block size of ULC, we're out of luck, even with 16-bit fixed point.
While ULC can work with smaller MDCT block sizes, it was optimized for 2048, so
we should keep it as large as possible. On top of that, the ULC reference 
encoder/decoder uses floats, so the obvious choice would be 32-bit fixed point to
maintain quality, but 16-bit may work. So we have two options, both arriving
at 3072 bytes:
- 32-bit values, a 512-sample block size (256-sample lap buffer): (512 + 256) * 4 bytes
- 16-bit values, a 1024-sample block size (512-sample lap buffer): (1024 + 512) * 2 bytes
Using 16-bit fixed point would not only reduce the DMA traffic, but also speed up computation on the RSP. The trade-off would be a higher noise floor. How high? No idea. So I carefully refactored the reference decoder, still running on the N64 CPU, to work in 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14).
After almost blowing my ears off a bunch of times, I got it working and could only hear (or imagine?) the faintest white noise when cranking it up. Case settled: 16-bit it is.
Cramming it into the RSP
Now I just needed to port this C code to the RSP. My knowledge of MIPS assembly is very basic, and writing an RSP decoder would be a serious endeavor.
This is where I took a hiatus from this project – I had a game to finish. When I returned earlier this year LLMs have improved quite a bit. Still, I didn't exactly trust GPT-5 with it. In some previous experiments it did a very bad job, often ignoring delay slots and other intricacies of the RSP, never finishing the job.
(Aside: GPT-6 or Opus-5 would probably one-shot this now)
So instead I opted for a more iterative approach. Max Bebök created a small C-like language to write code for the RSP, aptly named RSPL. Armed with the language documentation, I asked Codex to translate the C code to RSPL piece by piece, always verifying the result. It took a few days to port and land on an API design that made sense. Then in subsequent steps Codex further optimized the RSPL assembly output by first rewriting some parts (directly in assembly this time), then minimizing pipeline stalls by adapting the RSPL's optimizer.
The end result is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling the IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling. It barely fits into the 4096 byte IMEM of the RSP.
The C side of the decoder is still handwritten, but only because LLMs have no taste. The whole process took me a few weeks, but I'm still amazed that it worked at all.
To make ULC easily seekable, I added a sparse table at the end of the file that contains the byte offset of every eighth frame. The decoder quickly skips ahead from the nearest frame to the desired one. This adds about 20 bytes per second – manageable even for 16kbps audio.
ULC proved to be a very viable alternative to ADPCM and Opus on the N64. Quality and bitrate are close to those of Opus, but complexity is only 4x that of ADPCM. A single 44100 Hz stereo track costs about 4% of CPU time and 5% of RSP time. Perfectly usable for background music, speech, ambience and longer sound effects.
The decoder works transparently in Libdragon, just like all other audio codecs. It has been merged into the preview branch a while ago.
Addendum
A few days ago an excellent port of Half-Life for the N64 was published. 
The README states:
[...] libdragon's ULC audio codec for the 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks, is what makes everything fit in one 64 MB cartridge image.
~ github.com/ToxyCola/Half-Life-Nintendo-64-Port
Many thanks to Aikku93 for creating ULC. It's a wonderful codec. I merely found and adapted it. I seek simplicity and elegance in everything I do and ULC is something I can truly adore. Kudos!

For this GBA demo, no existing codec would fit the bill.
So Aikku93 not only wrote a decoder in ARM assembly, but also created a whole new codec: The Ultra Low Complexity Codec (ULC).
ULC is a transform codec and somewhat similar to MP3. ULC transforms slices of PCM data into the frequency domain. Like MP3, it uses the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) to do so. But unlike MP3, it does not split the signal into multiple bands (ULC's MDCT is “full-band”). Where MP3 uses classic entropy encoding (Huffman specifically), ULC does… not. Instead, transformed coefficients are stored with a very simple nibble-based syntax.
In short: ULC is what MP3 could have been. The same core idea, but without the cruft around it. The “ultra low complexity” does not come from a different algorithm, but by carefully applying and packaging it.
The nibble-based packaging is maybe the most elegant idea of ULC. Each coefficient is stored in just 4 bits, interpreted as a signed integer. Some values are reserved to indicate zero fill, noise fill, or a quantizer change:
- -7 … -2, 2 … 7 - coefficient value
- 0 - zero run, run length (1 … 16) follows in the next nibble
- 1 - long zero run, run length (17 … 288) follows in the next two nibbles
- -1 - quantizer change, value follows in the next nibble
- -8 - noise fill, length and amplitude follow in the next three nibbles
Everything is nibble aligned. This means the whole codec works without any arbitrary bit reads or entropy decoding. Reading and unpacking a block of coefficients takes just ~150 lines of C.
Also note that noise fill is a valuable addition. Cymbals, hi-hats and snare drums greatly benefit from that. MP3 does not have anything similar and needs to encode quasi-random coefficients as is.
ULC can produce usable results even at 16kbps. Quality of course suffers, but it might still be good enough for some applications.
Aikku93 has been working on ULC since 2019 and has steadily improved the encoding quality. All code is permissively licensed. Time to try this on the N64 then!
ULC on the N64
I spent an evening in pre-LLM days compiling the ULC reference decoder for the N64 and producing a small demo. It worked without a hitch.
The only problem: it was keeping the CPU very busy. Nothing was offloaded to the RSP. As a proof of concept, it wasn't doing much: we already knew the 93 MHz CPU was enough to decode a transform-based codec, but we don't need a “music player” that does nothing else. We need this for background music and spoken dialog during gameplay. It cannot hog the CPU.
Float to 16-bit Fixed Point
Obviously the IMDCT needs to be moved to the RSP coprocessor instead. We could just DMA one block of decoded coefficients to the RSP's memory, do the transform and DMA the completed samples back to RDRAM into the output buffer.
That's easier said than done, though. The RSP has only 4096 bytes of data memory (DMEM) and another 4096 bytes for instructions (IMEM). The vector instructions work in 16-bit or 32-bit fixed point, with no floats. The IMDCT will only be efficient if all the data for a transform fits into the RSP's DMEM at once. We also need some of the DMEM for temporary values and – if possible – the lapping buffer: half of the previously decoded block. So with the default 2048-sample block size of ULC, we're out of luck, even with 16-bit fixed point.
While ULC can work with smaller MDCT block sizes, it was optimized for 2048, so
we should keep it as large as possible. On top of that, the ULC reference 
encoder/decoder uses floats, so the obvious choice would be 32-bit fixed point to
maintain quality, but 16-bit may work. So we have two options, both arriving
at 3072 bytes:
- 32-bit values, a 512-sample block size (256-sample lap buffer): (512 + 256) * 4 bytes
- 16-bit values, a 1024-sample block size (512-sample lap buffer): (1024 + 512) * 2 bytes
Using 16-bit fixed point would not only reduce the DMA traffic, but also speed up computation on the RSP. The trade-off would be a higher noise floor. How high? No idea. So I carefully refactored the reference decoder, still running on the N64 CPU, to work in 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14).
After almost blowing my ears off a bunch of times, I got it working and could only hear (or imagine?) the faintest white noise when cranking it up. Case settled: 16-bit it is.
Cramming it into the RSP
Now I just needed to port this C code to the RSP. My knowledge of MIPS assembly is very basic, and writing an RSP decoder would be a serious endeavor.
This is where I took a hiatus from this project – I had a game to finish. When I returned earlier this year LLMs have improved quite a bit. Still, I didn't exactly trust GPT-5 with it. In some previous experiments it did a very bad job, often ignoring delay slots and other intricacies of the RSP, never finishing the job.
(Aside: GPT-6 or Opus-5 would probably one-shot this now)
So instead I opted for a more iterative approach. Max Bebök created a small C-like language to write code for the RSP, aptly named RSPL. Armed with the language documentation, I asked Codex to translate the C code to RSPL piece by piece, always verifying the result. It took a few days to port and land on an API design that made sense. Then in subsequent steps Codex further optimized the RSPL assembly output by first rewriting some parts (directly in assembly this time), then minimizing pipeline stalls by adapting the RSPL's optimizer.
The end result is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling the IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling. It barely fits into the 4096 byte IMEM of the RSP.
The C side of the decoder is still handwritten, but only because LLMs have no taste. The whole process took me a few weeks, but I'm still amazed that it worked at all.
To make ULC easily seekable, I added a sparse table at the end of the file that contains the byte offset of every eighth frame. The decoder quickly skips ahead from the nearest frame to the desired one. This adds about 20 bytes per second – manageable even for 16kbps audio.
ULC proved to be a very viable alternative to ADPCM and Opus on the N64. Quality and bitrate are close to those of Opus, but complexity is only 4x that of ADPCM. A single 44100 Hz stereo track costs about 4% of CPU time and 5% of RSP time. Perfectly usable for background music, speech, ambience and longer sound effects.
The decoder works transparently in Libdragon, just like all other audio codecs. It has been merged into the preview branch a while ago.
Addendum
A few days ago an excellent port of Half-Life for the N64 was published. 
The README states:
[...] libdragon's ULC audio codec for the 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks, is what makes everything fit in one 64 MB cartridge image.
~ github.com/ToxyCola/Half-Life-Nintendo-64-Port
Many thanks to Aikku93 for creating ULC. It's a wonderful codec. I merely found and adapted it. I seek simplicity and elegance in everything I do and ULC is something I can truly adore. Kudos!

Vivaldi 8.3 for Desktop: make bad ads sad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
12:39:12 UTC
21:39:12 KST

We aren’t part of the Big Tech oligarchy, and our business doesn’t depend on knowing all about you to predict when you are ready to buy a new toothbrush. While most browser companies turn your browsing into data for harvesting, and profiles to sell, Vivaldi gives you a European alternative that respects your privacy. With 8.3, we have given our Ad and Tracker Blocker a major upgrade so you can send the surveillance machinery home empty-handed.
We aren’t against respectful advertising. A contextual ad that matches the page you’re reading, and doesn’t follow you around afterwards, is a fair way for a site to pay its writers. The ads we object to are the ones that track and profile you. They follow you from site to site and remember things about you that you never chose to share. The built-in Ad and Tracker Blocker was created to make those bad ads sad. Rad!
How much advertising you want to block depends on YOU, who you are and what you’re reading. Some people want every tracker and ad long gone, and don’t mind if it causes a site to occasionally misbehave. Others want the sites they use to work perfectly every time. Some want a bit of both, depending on the site.
For this release we have given the Ad and Tracker Blocker an extensive rebuild to handle large filter lists more efficiently. We’ve also given it an updated design and new labels.
The updated Ad and Tracker Blocker gives you four default levels of protection to choose from:
- Off: turns the built-in blocker off completely
- Light: blocks most known trackers and some ads
- Strong: blocks more trackers and ads, sites may break
- Aggressive: blocks almost all trackers and ads, sites may break
You can set your default level of blocking from settings or when onboarding to Vivaldi. The level you select from here will be applied to all sites, but in Vivaldi we always give you more. Ad blocking shouldn’t be all or nothing. In Vivaldi, you can decide how much of the web gets through, one site at a time, on every device you use. That’s the kind of control a browser should give the people who use it.
Levels really pay off when you set them per site. Put that dj-set on Youtube on full blast without ads breaking your beat with Aggressive. Keep your bank on Light so every form works as expected. Turn protection down on the small independent site you trust and whose ads you’re happy to see. To set a level for the site you’re on, click the shield icon in the Address Bar. Vivaldi remembers your choice, so each site loads the way you decided.
If you are particularly interested in the topic, we’ve also added the option to create “custom” levels. In these levels you configure everything yourself, giving you full control over which blocklists are used. You can add a custom block list either added from a remote URL or from their file manager.
The new Ad and Tracker Blocker is also available for Vivaldi on Android and iOS today, so your protection looks and works the same way on your laptop, your phone and your tablet.
Expanding our love for vertical tabs
Long before vertical tabs were a talking point in our industry, they were introduced as an option in Vivaldi, and we have continued to improve the workflows for those who prefer to have their tabs on the side. With our 8.0 update this year, we introduced a redesign that really gave the vertical tabbers a sought-after update. With 8.3 we’re stepping it up with two new additions. If you like your Tab Bar stacked the same order as your sandwiches, listen up.
With Expand Tab Bar on Hover, you can keep the vertical Tab Bar slim, with just favicons showing, and give the page as much of your screen as possible until you actually need your tabs. When you’re looking for a tab, move your cursor over the Tab Bar and it smoothly expands to show full titles. Move away and it slides right back. The feature works when the Tab Bar sits on the left or right side of the window.
Pinned tabs on a vertical Tab Bar can now sit side by side in a compact grid at the top, neatly and all in order. Your mail, calendar and project tools stay one click away, and there’s far more room for everything else you have open. This is Vivaldi, so if you instead prefer the “old” way with each pinned tab taking a row, there is obviously a setting (Settings > Tabs > Tab Features > Pinned Tabs > Show Pinned Tabs at Full Width).
If you’re yet to try vertical tabs, this is your sign. If you’re already in love with vertical tabs, you’re welcome.
What else is new in Vivaldi 8.3
Paste and Go, for a whole list of links
Someone sends you a long list of links in an email or a chat, and you want to open every one of them. The desperate times of clicking them one by one are finally over! Copy the whole list, paste it in the Address Field, and Vivaldi opens each URL in its own tab. Research sources, someone’s wishlist, the reading list a colleague shared: all of them open simultaneously in each own tab, ready to stack, tile or work through one by one.
Copy Sanitized Link
Links often carry tracking parameters that tell a site who shared them and where they came from. Copy Sanitized Link strips those out before the link reaches your clipboard, so the person you send it to gets the page and nothing else. It’s an easy habit that keeps a bit more of your browsing to yourself.
Faster Reader Mode
Reader Mode has gotten some tender love and caring for 8.3. It now opens faster and scrolls more smoothly, so you can switch from a busy page to a clean, readable article in a moment and settle in.
Support for Tab Groups API
Vivaldi now supports Chrome’s Tab Groups API for extensions, so extensions built around tab groups can now work in Vivaldi.
This is your browser
We cannot repeat this often enough: Vivaldi is an independent employee-owned European company. That means we don’t answer to advertisers or a VC firm pushing features that benefit them instead of you. We don’t collect data, we just want to make a great browser that helps you explore the web.
Every release we do is built for the people who use Vivaldi. With 8.3 we’re giving you more control over what you see, what follows you, and how your tabs look. As our marketing department said: “this is a really on-brand release”.
If Vivaldi helps you explore more, tell someone about it. Helping a friend, colleague or family member make the switch is one of the best ways to fight for a better web.
Vivaldi 8.3 is ready today!
Vivaldi 8.3 is also out today on mobile. Read what’s new in Vivaldi 8.3 on Android and iOS.
As always, thank you for being part of the Vivaldi community. Together, we’re fighting for a better web, one release at a time.
Changelog
Take a look at the full list of changes from Vivaldi 8.2 to 8.3.

1980
the first star
back in old unix your password hash just sat in /etc/passwd, right next to your username. in a file everyone could read.
in 1980 bill joy put a * there for an account called daemon. nobody's supposed to ever log in as it.
a * isn't a hash, so no password can match it. unix still does this today
3bsd · /etc/passwd · 1980
Addressgithub.com/dspinellis/unix-history-repo/blob/BSD-3/etc/passwd
the next field is the real name. he wrote "the devil himself"
1990s
how sshd checks your password
ok so these days the hash lives in /etc/shadow and looks like $6$abc$k2P9…. the $6$ means sha512, abc is the salt, the rest is the actual hash
you type your password, sshd hashes it with that same salt and checks if it comes out identical. same = you're in. that's it
and if the field is just *? there's nothing to match. type whatever you want, it's never getting you in
1990s
the fine print
one more rule. if crypt() can't do its job, it returns NULL. like if the salt asks for some algorithm the system doesn't have, there's nothing to compute, so you get NULL instead of a hash
the single unix spec · crypt() · 1997
Addresspubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/7908799/xsh/crypt.html
pretty clear.
except a lot of programs never check for NULL. they just compare whatever crypt() gives back with the stored field, hit the NULL, and crash
2012
crypt stops saying NULL
so musl (the libc under alpine) goes ok fine, crypt() just won't return NULL anymore. if it fails, it returns a single character instead. that character can never match a real password, so programs don't crash, they just see a wrong password
now guess which character they picked for that
"?"
yep. the star. again.
musl · b3c4cc12 · aug 2012
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12
"reportedly."
musl · b3c4cc12 · the diff
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12
"should not happen" gone, NULL gone, "*" in
2012
three weeks later
then musl adds sha512 crypt. the thing is, sha512crypt gets slower the longer the password is, so someone could send one giant password and keep your server busy for a long time. so musl just caps it at 256 bytes and refuses anything longer
musl · 88bf5a8a · aug 29 2012
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=88bf5a8a
twenty days after the "*" commit btw
musl · crypt_sha512.c @ 88bf5a8a
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/misc/crypt_sha512.c?id=88bf5a8a
so past 256 bytes crypt fails. and when crypt fails… it says "*".
musl · crypt_sha512.c
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha512.c
literally in the comment the whole time
2016
sshd borrows bob's salt
CVE-2016-6210. ask sshd about a user that doesn't exist and it says no instantly, cause there's nothing to hash. real users take a few ms longer. so just time it and you know who exists
the fix is kinda funny. no real hash to check? sshd grabs some other account's salt and hashes your password anyway, just to waste the same amount of time. still a no, just a slower no
openssh-commits · jul 2016
Addresslists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2016-July/005428.html
"for invalid users." and also, it turns out, real users with a *.
2019 → 2022
the fix for the fix
2019. turns out alpine's docker images had no root password. at all. CVE-2019-5021. alpine fixes it by locking root with !
but without pam, ! also kills ssh keys. and cloud images log in with keys.
2022. alpine 3.16 switches root to *. still locked, keys work again
alpine aports · fbe926af · shipped in 3.16, 2022
Addressgitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports/-/commit/fbe926af.patch
narrator: it did not.
2016 → 2026
ten quiet years
why did nobody notice? well, maybe someone did. maybe someone pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt, half a slack message or a whole ssh key, and it just let them in. you've never pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt?? amazing. a fresh box with no passwords set isn't affected. a * in shadow needs a wrong try first. openssh tests on openbsd and glibc, musl doesn't test sshd, and most distros go through pam, which never even calls crypt for a *.
so as far as anyone knows, nobody noticed. as far as anyone knows.
some people got really close though
libc-alpha · debian #714219 · 2013
Addresssourceware.org/legacy-ml/libc-alpha/2013-07/msg00046.html
a debian dev asks glibc to copy musl's "*". six years later debian moves to libxcrypt, which says "*0", and closes the bug. one character away.
musl mailing list · dec 2024
Addressopenwall.com/lists/musl/2024/12/31/2
this thread is about busybox passwd breaking on a 257 character password. same "*", same limit. nobody says "sshd"
openssh-commits · 30 oct 2026
Addresslists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2026-October/013271.html
a security review fixes pick_salt(). the bug is four lines below it. four days before i found it.
nov 2026
how i ran into it
i was messing around with openssh, mostly the boring parts where it talks to libc, like the password code. people don't really look at that stuff, they look at the crypto. so i built sshd every way i could think of (glibc, musl, pam, no pam, shadow, no shadow) and threw like 17,600 weird logins at it. weird hashes, broken accounts, passwords way too long
oh did i say "i"? sorry. i had agent swarms. a lot of them. let's not get into it
every build agreed on every login. except musl without pam. that one said yes to things it shouldn't

Agility is the first pure humanoid robot company on the stock market. Are you buying?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Almost a year ago to the day, Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock responded to some gentle social media taunting from rival robotics company Agility with a prediction: “You’ll be bankrupt in <12 months.”
Instead, Agility is going public through a reverse-merger that will see it become a publicly-traded company and raise $465 million in new capital from retail investors and a tranche of private funding. The transaction will take place through a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC.
“You don’t see a lot of dancing robots or backflipping robots from Agility,” CEO Peggy Johnson told TechCrunch ahead of the company’s market debut. “We stuck to our strategy, which [are] these manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”
Agility predates the recent boom in physical AI investment. The company was spun out of Oregon State University in 2015 by a group of researchers who made headway in figuring out how to get a robot to walk safely on two legs. The company has focused on deploying a handful of its Digit robots in industrial settings with nine different customers, including Schaeffler, GXO, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and Mercado Libre. Digits are generally used to move heavy totes, including more than 100,000 of them at a GXO logistics facility.
Compared to humanoid robots built by Figure, Tesla, 1X, or Boston Dynamics, Agility’s Digit can seem plodding, but the robot is actually doing real work, and earning money — albeit just $174,000 in the first six months of 2026, and mostly from related parties. The company lost $362 million in the same time period, which means the clock is ticking for it to successfully deploy its infusion of new capital.
The good news is that Agility has $300 million in planned contracts from 30 customers for its new generation of robot, Digit 5. The new model can safely operate around humans, not just in an isolated work cell like its previous model (and indeed most humanoid robots). That deal was “one of the driving factors” behind the decision to take the company public, Johnson said, but could not yet reveal who the customers or say if they are investors.
To close the deals, Johnson said that Digit 5 will have to hit undisclosed targets along several metrics, including throughput, uptime, and accuracy of placement. The company has yet to show off the prototypes of Digit 5, but Johnson said they will be demonstrated at CES 2027 and widely available at the end of that year.
The company’s pitch is that a robot can save $100,000 a year for companies under a robot-as-a-service model and even more if the customer purchases the robot outright. Whether those unit economics work out in the end will depend on Digit 5’s capabilities, both in terms of task accuracy, and how long it can work without pauses for recharging or maintenance.
Johnson gave the example of a single person lifting a 50-pound object — an informal threshold some workplaces use to avoid injury. “Digit can do that over and over and over,” she said. “You don’t want to give a human that job. You want to give that to the robot.”
Agility faces two key questions: How quickly can it find new customers for Digit 5, and how quickly can it improve on the robot’s capabilities? Prospective customers need to spend $500,000 for Agility to do an on-site proof of concept before a deployment is fully scaled up; there were four customers signed up in May, 2026. And while Agility can pick up heavy loads and place them with 98% accuracy, it still — like most of today’s robots — lacks the ability to do complex manipulation tasks.
It’s still not clear how quickly generative AI techniques will unlock the kind of dexterity that could allow robots to handle a wide variety of items. Training systems based on video and teleoperation data have not led to reliable general autonomy, though adapting the transformer architecture to different modalities appears promising to physical AI researchers.
“There’s no internet of physical data of robot movements, and that’s why you see so many people trying to simulate the data using a variety of things, and we use all of those techniques as well,” Johnson said. “They have their pros and cons, but we also have … 65,000 hours of real operational data from real customers in real facilities…that helps us accelerate the training of Digit.”
Johnson said the capital raised in the SPAC transaction would meet the company’s current needs, but wouldn’t project that it would be sufficient for the company to be self-sustaining. She wouldn’t share production targets for Digit 5, but the company has said its production facility could produce 10,000 of the robots annually.
“What you’ll see from us going forward is continuing to listen to our customers, understanding what they need in these facilities,” she said. “We’re taking our cue from them because we’re building a business.”
For all the open questions, Agility still finds itself further ahead of most humanoid builders by dint of simply putting its product in the field.
“Let’s start with the bins and the totes, and then let’s do the picking and the kitting,” cofounder and chief robot officer Johnathan Hurst told TechCrunch at the opening of the company’s Fremont R&D facility this summer. “And then let’s like start working on cardboard, which is really hard, and loading and unloading tractor trailers and things like that. Okay, now we’re at 100 million robots, you know? A trillion-dollar company.”
Correction: This story originally mis-identified the CEO of Figure AI; it is Brett Adcock.

OpenSSH 10.6p2 Critical workaround for alpine without PAM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
11:40:30 UTC
20:40:30 KST

Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 was released on 2026-11-05. It will be available
from the mirrors listed at https://www.openssh.com/.
OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol 2.0 implementation and
includes sftp client and server support.
Recently the OpenSSH team have received a large number of security
bug reports, many of which are findings from AI models or made with
AI assistance. While many AI reports are determined not to have
security impact when considered in the context of a realistic
threat model, we very much welcome these reports, especially when
combined with human triage, analysis, test-cases and particularly
when accompanied by proposed fixes.
** We have seen a number of cases where a security bug identified
** by AI tools is subsequently independently discovered by a
** different researcher. This suggests that adversaries who do not
** report bugs to OSS projects are likely to be able to discover
** these bugs too. Given this, the OpenSSH team will, for now, be
** making more frequent releases to get bugfixes into users' hands
** more quickly rather than batching them until the next planned
** release.
Once again, we would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their
continued support of the project, especially those who contributed
code or patches, reported bugs, tested snapshots or donated to the
project. More information on donations may be found at:
https://www.openssh.com/donations.html
Future deprecation notice
-------------------------
 * scp(1): begin deprecating the -R flag, which is used to perform a
   remote-to-remote copy by executing scp on a remote host. This
   option is a fragile optimisation that is difficult to use because
   it requires credentials on the remote host. It also creates
   security risks if the shell quoting rules on the remote system
   where the copy is performed differ from the client's expectations.
   From OpenSSH 10.6, this option will continue to work but will
   cause a deprecation warning to be emitted to standard error. In
   a future release, the option will be ignored and will leave in
   place the default remote-to-remote copy behaviour (copy via the
   host running scp).
 * sshd(8): support for platforms that do not allow file descriptor
   passing and that also require root privilege for PTY allocation
   will be removed in a future release. Affected platforms are known
   to include SCO OpenServer 5 and QNX 6 but may include other
   similarly old operating systems. This deprecation can be avoided
   if the user community for these platforms is able to assist us in
   building alternatives, such as avoiding the need for root in PTY
   allocation.
Changes since OpenSSH 10.6p1
============================
This release contains a critical security workaround that affects
Linux systems that use the musl libc and PAM disabled.
This release also includes a number of bugfixes that had already
been committed on the portable OpenSSH V_10_6 stable branch.
Security
========
 * sshd(8): avoid password authentication bypass that is exploitable
   through sshd(8) that affects some Linux systems when built and run
   with PAM support disabled. We consider the root cause of this bug
   to be outside sshd, but it is exploitable via sshd and can be
   avoided there.
   This bug was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield
   (wakefield.co)
Bugfixes
--------
 * sshd(8), ssh(1): enable the post-quantum hybrid signature scheme
   ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 as an allowed CA signature algorithm.
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): fix <1 second CPU spin if ChannelTimeout was in
   use.
Portability
-----------
 * sshd(8): fix compilation on (old) platforms that set SKIP_PRIVDROP
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): fix detection of Azerbaijani locales
 * sshd(8), ssh-agent(1): fix creation of agent sockets on platforms
   without the openat(2) syscall.
 * ssh(1), ssh-add(1), ssh-keygen(1): fix some strange behaviour if
   SIGINT/SIGQUIT was received while reading a passphrase.
 * sshd(8): allow restart_syscall(2) in seccomp sandbox; bz4036

OpenSSH 10.6 was released on 2026-10-06. It is available from the
mirrors listed at https://www.openssh.com/.
OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol 2.0 implementation and
includes sftp client and server support.
Recently the OpenSSH team have received a large number of security
bug reports, many of which are findings from AI models or made with
AI assistance. While many AI reports are determined not to have
security impact when considered in the context of a realistic
threat model, we very much welcome these reports, especially when
combined with human triage, analysis, test-cases and particularly
when accompanied by proposed fixes.
** We have seen a number of cases where a security bug identified
** by AI tools is subsequently independently discovered by a
** different researcher. This suggests that adversaries who do not
** report bugs to OSS projects are likely to be able to discover
** these bugs too. Given this, the OpenSSH team will, for now, be
** making more frequent releases to get bugfixes into users' hands
** more quickly rather than batching them until the next planned
** release.
Once again, we would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their
continued support of the project, especially those who contributed
code or patches, reported bugs, tested snapshots or donated to the
project. More information on donations may be found at:
https://www.openssh.com/donations.html
Future deprecation notice
-------------------------
 * scp(1): begin deprecating the -R flag, which is used to perform a
   remote-to-remote copy by executing scp on a remote host. This
   option is a fragile optimisation that is difficult to use because
   it requires credentials on the remote host. It also creates
   security risks if the shell quoting rules on the remote system
   where the copy is performed differ from the client's expectations.
   From OpenSSH 10.6, this option will continue to work but will
   cause a deprecation warning to be emitted to standard error. In
   a future release, the option will be ignored and will leave in
   place the default remote-to-remote copy behaviour (copy via the
   host running scp).
 * sshd(8): support for platforms that do not allow file descriptor
   passing and that also require root privilege for PTY allocation
   will be removed in a future release. Affected platforms are known
   to include SCO OpenServer 5 and QNX 6 but may include other
   similarly old operating systems. This deprecation can be avoided
   if the user community for these platforms is able to assist us in
   building alternatives, such as avoiding the need for root in PTY
   allocation.
Potentially-incompatible changes
--------------------------------
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): compression will be less effective as a result
   of the change noted below in the "Security" section
 * ssh(1): destination usernames entered on the commandline are now
   more strictly checked and will refuse usernames that include
   backslash and dollar symbols. Usernames that are specified by
   the "User" directive in configuration files are not subject to
   these restrictions. The motivation for this change is mentioned
   below in the "Security" section.
 * sshd(8): on platforms that do not support file descriptor passing
   and that require root for PTY allocation, the GatewayPorts and
   StreamLocalForwarding options are forcibly disabled. The
   motivation for this change is discussed below in the "Security"
   section.
Changes since OpenSSH 10.5
==========================
This release contains a number of security fixes, several new
features and some small bugfixes.
Security
========
 * sftp(1): more strictly validate paths returned from the server to
   avoid some cases where a server could return paths that could
   manipulate a recursive copy operation into writing outside its
   target directory. Report and patch from Junghoon Cho.
 * sshd(8): when GSSAPIAuthentication is in use, only store GSSAPI
   credentials when authentication has succeeded. Avoids a situation
   where credentials from a failed GSSAPIAuthentication attempt may
   persist and be made inappropriately available if another
   authentication subsequently succeeds. Issue report and patch from
   Moritz Theile.
 * sshd(8): reset GSSAPIAuthentication before authentication, avoiding
   state from one authentication attempt being confused with that of
   a later attempt. Report and feedback from Moritz Theile.
 * sshd(8), ssh(1): disable LZ77 dictionary coder to mitigate the
   side-channel leaks described in "Crossing the Streams: SSH
   Plaintext Recovery via a Common Compression Context in
   Multiplexed Channels" by Fabian Bäumer and Marcus Brinkmann,
   preprint https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07709 (2026)
   A chosen-plaintext attack method exists which makes use of
   dictionary-based compression to recover secrets from one channel
   by interacting with the SSH session's shared compression
   dictionary through another channel.
   Attacker-controlled input can recognizably reflect into the
   total length of transmitted ciphertexts by virtue of LZ77
   replacing repeated strings with back-references into the SSH
   session's encoder search buffer, which is shared across all
   channels. For this reason, the documentation already recommended
   against enabling compression for connections that share trusted
   and untrusted traffic.
   This change will reduce the effectiveness of the Compression
   option. Users are encouraged to use application-level compression
   over the SSH protocol where possible, as this will typically be
   more effective and will be completely immune to this type of
   attack.
 * ssh(1): disallow '$' and '\' characters in usernames entered on
   the command-line to avoid usernames from untrusted sources
   yielding injection in shell context via ProxyCommand, Match exec,
   etc. Usernames specified via the configuration files are not
   subject this this control. Reported by SecBuddyF KeenLab Tencent
   (CodeBuddy Security)
   We continue to recommend against directly exposing ssh(1) and
   other tools' command-lines to untrusted input. Mitigations such
   as this can not be absolute given the variety of shells and user
   configurations in use.
 * ssh-keygen(1): correct handling of Daylight Saving Time when
   converting dates. Previous handling could cause errors of
   up to +/- 1 hour (unless you are in the Antarctica/Troll
   timezone, where the error could be +/- 2 hours). These errors
   could result in creation of certificates with incorrect expiry
   times. bz4004; from Khush Patel
 * sshd(8), ssh(1): ensure that compressed payloads don't inflate
   past the maximum supported packet length. Reported by Oleh Konko.
 * sshd(8): fully honor the authorized_keys "restrict" keyword,
   which was not being properly applied to tunnel forwarding
   (PermitTunnel, disabled by default). This is a separate problem
   to the one fixed in openssh-10.5.
 * sshd(8): correctly handle some options that accept "none". Some
   options, including AuthorizedPrincipalsFile, were documented as
   accepting "none" as a way to disable them; however, when
   overridden by an sshd_config(5) Match keyword, this argument was
   being incorrectly interpreted as a literal file.
   With Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research
 * sshd(8): On OS X SDK >= 27, sandboxing is no longer supported
   as the API we depended upon has been removed and no obvious
   alternative provided.
 * sshd(8): on platforms that do not support file descriptor passing
   and that require root for PTY allocation, the post-authentication
   sshd-session process retains root privilege, whereas on other
   platforms this process runs with the privilege of the logged-in
   user. When sshd-session was run with elevated privilege, it could
   perform certain actions as root and circumvent controls that
   would normally have applied to the user, such as making unix
   domain socket connections or binding (via -R forwarding) to low-
   numbered TCP ports.
   For this reason, this release disables the GatewayPorts and
   StreamLocalForwarding options and support for these (few)
   platforms will be removed in future if no alternatives to
   requiring privilege in the post-authentication process are found.
   Affected platforms include QNX 6, SCO OpenServer 5 and builds
   that were made with the --disable-fd-passing configure option.
   This problem was reported separately by sn0x-sharma and by Dark
   River.
New features
------------
 * All: enable hybrid post-quantum ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 signature
   algorithm. Note that this no longer uses the "@openssh.com"
   vendor extension suffix that the previous experimental
   implementation used. Keys generated with the previous experimental
   support must be regenerated and/or removed.
 * sshd(8): Add the WarnWeakCrypto option to sshd_config(5). This
   option was previously available for the client only. This option
   is enabled by default and will log when the client uses a key
   agreement scheme that is not post-quantum safe.
 * ssh-keygen(1), ssh-add(1): preserve user-verification (PIN or
   biometric) requirement for resident keys loaded from a FIDO
   token, by checking the credential's credProtect policy.
   GHPR701 from Savely Krasovsky
 * ssh(1): include local and remote version strings in the ~I
   connection information display.
 * ssh-add(1): add a -P flag to skip PIN entry for FIDO and PKCS#11
   tokens that do not require it.
 * sftp(1): add '-p' flag for mkdir/lmkdir to create directories as
   required. This flag has similar ergonomics to mkdir(1), and
   previously-existing directories do not cause an error.
 * ssh-keygen(1): add a "hexdump" key export mode that dumps the SSH
   wire-formatted key blob in hex format. Useful when writing
   documentation, tests, etc. E.g. `ssh-keygen -em hexdump -f /key`
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): ChannelTimeout now accepts timeouts with
   fractional seconds.
 * sshd(8): allow specification of the location of $SSH_AUTH_SOCK
   used for agent forwarding using a new AgentSocketPath option.
   This supports both using a user-specific path, such as the
   default of a subdirectory of $HOME ("user:.ssh/agent"), and
   the previous approach of allowing agent forwarding sockets to be
   located in a shared directory (e.g. "shared:/tmp"). Sockets
   created in shared directories will be created inside a
   subdirectory with a randomised name. bz3860
 * ssh-agent(1): allow specification of agent socket directories
   using a -A flag. It accepts "user:" and "shared:" directory
   styles similar to the sshd AgentSocketPath option.
 * sshd(8): account for public key authentication "key ok" tests
   separately to auth attempts. Add a `PubkeyAuthOptions max-pk-ok:nnn`
   option to allow a number of PK_OK tests (asking whether the
   server might accept a given public key) that do not count against
   MaxAuthTries, defaulting to 6 attempts. After these attempts are
   exhausted, further attempts count as failed authentications
   against MaxAuthTries. Practically, this allows more keys on disk
   or held in ssh-agent to be checked for use before the server
   disconnects.
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): extend the existing TCPKeepAlive option to also
   support setting keepalives on sockets created for forwarding
   connections. Previously this option controlled keepalives on the
   connection socket only. TCPKeepAlive "yes" or "transport" enables
   keepalives on the connection socket. "TCPKeepAlive all" additionally
   enables them for forwarding sockets. bz3921
Bugfixes
--------
 * sshd(8), ssh(1): fix configuration matching on more Turkic
   languages which have disjoint dotted and dotless i/I characters,
   specifically Azerbaijani and Crimean Tatar. bz3991
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): don't attempt to set TCP_NODELAY on non-IP/IPv6
   sockets. Eliminates some noise in debug logs.
 * ssh(1): fix case for ssh -G option output; bz4005
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): Fix ChannelTimeout specificity; previously a
   more specific channel type (e.g. "session:shell") could clobber
   a user-specified ChannelTimeout if it was less specific (e.g.
   "session").  Also, in some cases, the debug messages were
   printing 0 instead of the effective timeout. bz3994
 * sftp(1): avoid NULL dereference crash in some circumstances when
   a server fails a stat/lstat operation. GHPR707
 * sshd(8): close a race condition where a SIGTERM/SIGQUIT would be
   ignored if it was received by the server while it was processing a
   SIGHUP restart request. bz3981
 * sshd(8), ssh(1): check key and CA signature types during key
   parsing against allowlists (PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms, etc) as
   early as possible. This reduces the attack surface presented by
   disabled algorithms. Suggested by and with extensive feedback
   from Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic
   Research.
 * All: switch the fallback implementation of the ed25519 signature
   algorithm used when libcrypto is disabled from SUPERCOP ed25519
   to libsodium. The libsodium implementation includes a number of
   strictness checks over the original reference implementation we
   have used to this point and a more ergonomic API.
 * ssh-add(1), ssh(1), ssh-keygen(1): fix spin on password entry when
   the program attempting to read a password was started in a
   background process group, with no TTY and with certain signals
   ignored. bz3995
 * scp(1): disallow nul byte in received scp -O filename. This was
   not reachable in normal operation. Reported by Chua Wei Xun.
 * ssh-keygen(1), ssh(1), sshd(8): implement a maximum number of KDF
   rounds that will be accepted when writing an OpenSSH-format
   private key or when loading one. This limit is set quite high
   (1M), but ensures that a service that is passed a bad key with a
   ridiculously high number of rounds will eventually complete
   parsing it.
 * ssh-keygen(1): bump the default number of KDF rounds from 24 to
   32 (this is a linear increase, not like bcrypt(3) which is
   exponential).
 * ssh(1): make StreamLocalBindMask properly respect Host/Match
   blocks and make it first-match-wins as documented. bz4013
 * sshd(8): make StreamLocalBindMask properly first-match-wins.
Portability
-----------
 * All: remove the NetBSD BROKEN_READ_COMPARISON workaround. This
   appears to be no longer required and caused pre-auth CPU spinning.
 * sshd(8): don't link sshd against libselinux when SELinux support
   is enabled (note: this library is still linked for the sshd-auth
   and sshd-session helper binaries).
 * sshd(8): allow madvise(..., MADV_DONTNEED_LOCKED) in the seccomp
   sandbox; needed by GrapheneOS' hardened allocator. bz4001
 * sshd(8): restrict mremap(2) flags accepted by the seccomp
   sandbox. Only MREMAP_MAYMOVE is now accepted as other flags may
   have some utility in attack chains. Reported by: Mohammad Hossein
   Abedini.
 * sshd(8): allow PAMServiceName in Match (regressed in 10.4).
   During the refactor of server option parsing, the ability to set
   PAMServiceName in Match blocks was accidentally disabled.
 * sshd(8): the --disable-fd-passing configure option has been
   removed.

==========

 - SHA256 (openssh-10.6.tar.gz) = 0lP9h9/QH3k667vqbxKhkkusc3CN5iKUiDNI9fsR06A=

We have seen a number of cases where a security bug identified by

researcher. This suggests that adversaries who do not report bugs
to OSS projects are likely to be able to discover these bugs too.
Given this, the OpenSSH team will, for now, be making more frequent

Once again, we would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their

code or patches, reported bugs, tested snapshots or donated to the

Potentially-incompatible changes
--------------------------------
 * Portable OpenSSH now requires ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography)
   support in libcrypto, including support for the NISTP521 curve.
   ECC is included in the default build configurations of all
   versions of all libcrypto implementations currently supported by
   OpenSSH, including LibreSSL, OpenSSL, BoringSSL and AWS LC.
   The --without-openssl build configuration is not affected.
Changes since OpenSSH 10.4
==========================
This release contains a number of security fixes and small bugfixes.
Security
========
 * ssh-agent(1): fix an interaction between agent locking and the
   session-bind@openssh.com extension that is used to identify
   forwarded agents. These binding requests were refused when the
   agent was locked, with the result that operations that were
   intended to be limited to local use only could be performed
   remotely, including the ability to add PKCS#11 tokens and make
   use of keys that had destination restrictions applied.
   Reported by sn0x-sharma
 * ssh(1): avoid potential realloc use-after-free in the client if a
   remote forwarding is added via the local session multiplexing
   socket while a remote forwarding open request is pending with the
   server. Report and fix from Brian Mingus of Cognatory
 * sshd(8): make the authorized_keys "restrict" keyword apply
   correctly to tunnel forwarding too (which is administratively
   disabled by default). Reported by Erichen, Institute of Computing
   Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
    
New features
------------
 * ssh-keygen(1): add ability to set or clear the touch-required and
   verify-required flags on FIDO private keys when resetting a
   private key's passphrase.
 * ssh(1): tweak ordering of certificates tried during pubkey
    authentication to prefer FIDO keys that do not require user
    presence (touch) first, and FIDO keys that require user
    verification via PIN or biometrics last. This effectively tries
    low-friction authenticators before higher friction ones.
 * ssh(1): add a "ssh -Z user@host" mode that prints the keys that
   will be tried for public key authentication in the order that
   they will be used.
    
 * sshd(8) use setproctitle(3) to identify sshd-session when its
   acting as a post-authentication monitor.
    
Bugfixes
--------
 * ssh-keyscan(1): make reading the server banner a non-blocking
   operation to prevent a stuck server from blocking a many-host
   keyscan from proceeding.
 * sshd(8): use sshpkt_fatal() instead of plain fatal() for errors
   in the packet code as this provides context of the failing peer
   (address, port, user, etc).
 * sshd(8): when signing hostkey proofs for a client UpdateHostKeys
   request, allow each hostkey to perform at most one signature
   operation.
    
 * sshd(8) fix GSSAPI option names, that were broken during a
   servconf.c refactoring in openssh-10.4; bz3974.
    
 * ssh-keygen(1): pass back errors from ed25519 key generation, which
   theoretically can fail. GHPR702.
 * sshd(8): move check of public key type against allowed algorithms
   to before parsing of the key sent by the peer. This removes at
   least some key parsing and verification paths from the pre-auth
   attack surface. Suggested by Christopher Paul Rohlf of Anthropic.
    
 * ssh-keygen(1): fix double frees (impossible to reach outside of a
   test harness), and also use freezero where possible. From
   Christopher Paul Rohlf at Anthropic.
 * sshd(8): fix ChannelTimeout and RekeyLimit not being applied in
   sshd_config Match blocks.
 * sshd(8): in sshd config dump mode, write all directives in mixed
   case for consistency
    
Portability
-----------
 * sshd(8): re-allow PAMServiceName inside a Match block, which
   was incorrectly disabled during a refactoring in openssh-10.4.
   bz3987

OpenSSH 10.4 was released on 2026-07-06. It is available from the
mirrors listed at https://www.openssh.com/.
OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol 2.0 implementation and
includes sftp client and server support.
Once again, we would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their
continued support of the project, especially those who contributed
code or patches, reported bugs, tested snapshots or donated to the
project. More information on donations may be found at:
https://www.openssh.com/donations.html
Potentially-incompatible changes
--------------------------------
 * sshd(8): configuration dump mode ("sshd -G") now writes directives
   in mixed case (e.g. "PubkeyAuthentication") whereas previously it
   emitted only lower-case names.
 * sshd(8): on Linux systems with the seccomp sandbox enabled,
   failures to enable SECCOMP or NO_NEW_PRIVS are now fatal.
   Previously sshd(8) would log the error but continue operation,
   to support systems that lacked these features. Now systems that
   lack these should instead disable the sandbox at configure time.
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): make the transport protocol stricter by
   disconnecting if the peer sends non-KEX messages during a post-
   authentication key re-exchange. Previously a malicious peer could
   continue sending non-key exchange messages without penalty. These
   would be buffered, causing memory to be wasted up until the
   connection terminated or the server/client hit a memory limit.
   Implementations that do not restrict messages sent during key
   exchange as per RFC4253 section 7.1 may be disconnected.
   Reported by Marko Jevtic.
Changes since OpenSSH 10.3
==========================
This release contains a number of security fixes as well as general
bugfixes and a couple of new features.
Security
========
 * sftp(1): when downloading files on the command-line using
   "sftp host:/path .", a malicious server could cause the file to
   be downloaded to an unexpected location. This issue was identified
   by the Swival Security Scanner.
 * scp(1): when copying files between two remote destinations, do
   not allow a malicious server to write files to the parent
   directory of the intended target directory.  This issue was
   identified by the Swival Security Scanner.
 * sshd(8): when using the "internal-sftp" SFTP server implementation
   (this is not the default), long command lines were previously
   truncated silently after the 9th argument. If a security-relevant
   option was in the 10th or later position, it would be discarded.
   Reported by Steve Caffrey.
 * sshd(8): add a documentation note to mention that the
   GSSAPIStrictAcceptorCheck option is ineffective when the server
   is joined to a Windows Active Directory. Reported by Yarin Aharoni
   of Safebreach.
 * sshd(8): DisableForwarding=yes didn't override PermitTunnel=yes
   as it was documented to do. Note that PermitTunnel is not enabled
   by default. Reported independently by Huzaifa Sidhpurwala of
   Redhat and Marko Jevtic.
 * sshd(8): avoid a potential pre-authentication denial of service
   when GSSAPIAuthentication was enabled (this feature is off by
   default). This was not mitigated by MaxAuthTries, but would be
   penalised by PerSourcePenalties. This was reported by Manfred
   Kaiser of the milCERT AT (Austrian Ministry of Defence).
 * sshd(8): fix a number of cases where the minimum authentication
   delay was not being enforced. Reported by the Orange Cyberdefense
   Vulnerability Team.
 * ssh(1): fix a possible client-side use-after-free if the server
   changes its host key during a key reexchange. This was reported by
   Zhenpeng (Leo) Lin of Depthfirst.
New features
------------
 * All: add experimental support for a composite post-quantum
   signature scheme that combines ML-DSA 44 and Ed25519 as specified
   in draft-miller-sshm-mldsa44-ed25519-composite-sigs.
   This scheme is not enabled by default. To use it, you'll need
   to add it to HostKeyAlgorithms, PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms, etc.
   Keys may be generated using "ssh-keygen -t mldsa44-ed25519".
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): replace the wildcard pattern matcher with an
   implementation based on an NFA. This avoids exponential worst-case
   behaviour for the old implementation.
Bugfixes
--------
 * ssh-agent(1): fix incorrect reply to "query" SSH_AGENTC_EXTENSION
   requests. bz3967
 * sshd(8): avoid sending observably different messages for valid vs
   invalid users in GSSAPIAuthentication (disabled by default).
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): fix several bugs that incorrectly
   classified bulk traffic as interactive. bz3972, bz3958
 * ssh-keygen(1), ssh-add(1): skip unsupported key types when
   downloading resident keys from a FIDO token. Previously, downloads
   would abort when one was encountered. GHPR657
 * ssh(1): fix a potential use-after-free on an error path if
   cipher_init() fails.
 * sshd(8): perform stricter encoding and validation of transport
   state passed between sshd privilege separation subprocesses. This
   somewhat further hardens the server against attacks on sshd-auth
   or sshd-session subprocesses.
 * ssh-agent(1): avoid possible runtime denial of service by
   enforcing some limits on the length of usernames in key use
   constraints.
 * sftp(1): fix two separate one-byte out-of-bounds reads, in
   SSH2_FXP_REALPATH and batch command processing.
 * sftp-server(8): disallow use of the copy-data extension to read
   and write to the same inode simultaneously.
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): avoid strlen(NULL) crash if an X11 channel was
   created before the x11-req SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST was sent.
   GHPR679
 * sftp(1), scp(1): avoid a situation where sftp_download() could get
   stuck in a loop if a broken server repeatedly returned zero length
   while reading a file.
 * ssh(1): avoid leaking DNS0x20 case-randomised names into names
   canonicalised using CanonicalizePermittedCNAMEs. bz3966
 * sftp-server(8): avoid truncation of pathnames passed to lstat()
   during SSH_FXP_REALPATH handling on systems where PATH_MAX is not
   the actual max. GHPR688
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): correct arming of poll(2) event masks for some
   socket-type channels. GHPR660
 * sshd(8): major refactor of sshd_config parsing and management
   code, to allow for more exact serialisation/deserialisation across
   privilege separation boundaries.
 * ssh-add(1): open connection to the agent only after getopt()
   processing has completed, to give options like "-v" a chance to
   display debug information about this operation.
 * crypto code: fix bounds checking when signing messages of length
   greater than will fit in a size_t. In OpenSSH, message sizes are
   bounded by SSHBUF_SIZE_MAX so this was unreachable.
 * crypto code: add signature malleability and pubkey validity checks
   to ed25519 verification. SSH doesn't depend on these properties
 * crypto code: fix ECDSA order check for curves with cofactor != 1.
   All supported EC curves have cofactor 1, so this was
   unreachable.
 * sshd(8): differentiate between execution failures and a subsystem
   that was not found when logging why a subsystem failed to start.
   GHPR637
 * All: use safer idioms for timegm(3) and mktime(3) error detection.
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): avoid accepting invalid cipher or MAC lists in
   config files or command-line arguments. This could cause runtime
   failures later.
 * ssh(1): fix NULL deref crash during pubkey auth when using a PEM
   style private key with no corresponding .pub key adjacent to it.
 * sshd(8): don't print an error message when trying to load a host
   private key when PKCS#11 keys are in use, as these don't need the
   private half on the filesystem. GHPR664
 * All: don't use deprecated ERR_load_crypto_strings(). GHPR650
 * ssh(1): properly report errors during configuration default
   setting. GHPR649
 * ssh(1): use correct directive name (Match instead of Host) in
   error message. bz3968
 * sftp(1): fix "ls -ln" which was not correctly showing numeric
   UID/GIDs but rather user and group names. bz3953
 * sshd(8): avoid possible NULL dereference if an allocation fails
   during config parsing. bz3948
 * All: fix ineffective guards against loading overly large public
   keys in several places. bz3969 and bz3970
 * sftp(1): ensure file descriptors used by sftp to communicate to
   its ssh(1) subprocess don't leak into executed subprocesses (e.g.
   via "!"). GHPR693
Portability
-----------
 * Sync fmt_scaled.c with OpenBSD upstream, picking up an exactness
   fix for large exponents (GHPR671)
 * sshd(8): remove duplicate sandbox entry for clock_gettime64.
 * ssh(1), sshd(8): use correct IPTOS_DSCP_VA value if not provided
   by the system headers.
 * Sync getrrsetbyname.c with OpenBSD upstream, picking up robustness
   fixes.

OpenSSH 10.3 was released on 2026-04-02. It is available from the
mirrors listed at https://www.openssh.com/.
OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol 2.0 implementation and
includes sftp client and server support.
Once again, we would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their
continued support of the project, especially those who contributed
code or patches, reported bugs, tested snapshots or donated to the
