Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor Part 3: Bad Update Improvements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
22:01:49 UTC
07:01:49 KST

Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor Part 3: Bad Update Improvements
Welcome to part 3 of the Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor blog series. In this part I’ll go over what happened after I released the PoC for Bad Update, and how it went from taking ~20 minutes with a ~30% success rate to being near instantaneous with a near 100% success rate. If you haven’t already I highly recommend you read (or at least skim through) part 1 and part 2 as this post will reference a lot of the material discussed there. This part will be very short but will catch you up for part 4 which covers the peer pressure exploit and will be out soon.
Rock Band Blitz
In the months following the release of Bad Update v1.0 there were two major improvements made to it by others. The first by “ihatecompvir” and “InvoxiPlayGames” is a new game save entry point in the demo version of Rock Band Blitz (RBB) called DaTArrest. The demo version of RBB is a package file that’s normally downloaded from the Xbox Live store for free and saved to your console’s HDD or memory unit. When the Xbox 360 got support for using USB sticks as storage devices all of the packages signed to boot from the HDD or memory unit were grandfathered in to also boot from USB storage devices. This means the RBB demo package can be copied to a USB stick as a normal file and launched on any console on a software version that supports it.
By exploiting some memory corruption vulnerabilities in the game’s DLC parsing code they were able to craft a game save file that when loaded would bootstrap the Bad Update stage 2 ROP chain and begin the hypervisor exploit chain. Using RBB as an entry point we no longer needed the Tony Hawk American Wasteland game disc. Running the Bad Update exploit was now as simple as copying some files to a USB stick, plugging it into your console, and launching Rock Band Blitz from the dashboard.
Hypervisor Race Condition Optimizations
Shortly after the RBB entry point was discovered I received a pull request from “Máté” who had made some improvements to the hypervisor race condition part of the exploit. These improvements included a hash table for precomputing and storing the malicious ciphertext values, a better cache flushing primitive, and improved thread scheduling between the XKE payload thread and ciphertext overwrite thread. The combination of these improvements reduced execution time down to a few seconds and the race condition had a much higher success rate.
Ciphertext Hash Table
In part 2 I talked about attacking encrypted memory by using hypervisor APIs to create encrypted memory allocations at predetermined memory addresses and used two different memory pathways to capture the ciphertext for some chosen plaintext data. Using this primitive I was able to craft ciphertext data to get kernel mode code execution as well as the ciphertext data used to attack the LZX decompression code in the bootloader update XKE payload.
The whitening value used in the memory encryption scheme is 12 bits large which gives 1024 unique ciphertext combinations for some given plaintext data. However, in my original PoC I was only generating the ciphertext for one of the 1024 possible whitening values and the reason for that was a two part failure on my end. When I originally prototyped out the ciphertext attack I did actually try using a lookup table for ciphertext combinations but I wasn’t able to get it working.
The first issue was I was using a very old ~2011 era hypervisor/kernel build (it was just what all my old research was based on) which was doing a TLB flush for the encrypted VA range in the hypervisor function that setup the memory encryption. In later hypervisor builds that TLB flush was removed because the kernel wrapper function for this hypervisor function already does a TLB flush for the VA range. However, I call the hypervisor syscall directly (skipping the kernel wrapper code which does the TLB flush) and since the TLB is lazy-loaded the whitening bits would become stale and the resulting ciphertext read out of memory was invalid.
When testing the exploit on the 17559 (latest) version hypervisor the lookup table was causing issues and rather than investigate I decided I’d fix it later and moved on. By the time I got to the end of the exploit I had become so blinded by tunnel vision chasing CPU cache issues that I had convinced myself the lookup table just wasn’t going to work. What I should have probably done (aside from investigate the lookup table issues when they surfaced) was to put this project down for a few weeks and come back with a clear mindset. Oh well, lesson learned…
Getting into the implementation details of the hash table, we use the first N bits of the ciphertext we expect to see in memory as an index into two arrays. The first array contains the first 64-bits of the oracle ciphertext which is used for validation in case there’s ever a collision in the hash table. The second array stores our malicious ciphertext we want to write into memory.
In order to make this as efficient as possible (remember we’re racing the CPU and cache here) we ignore collisions. It’s better to have a few collisions and have to skip some iterations on the race condition loop than to implement support for buckets in the hash table. Instead we compensate for collisions by choosing a sufficiently large enough number of bits for the hash table key such that the number of collisions is on the order of single digits, if we even have any (majority of the time there’s 0).
However, more bits in the hash table key means a large array to hold the entries (meaning more memory is used) which could potentially work against us as we’ll be performing more fetches from RAM since CPU cache is being thrashed. Máté’s original PR used a key size of 10 bits but I later upped this to 20 bits which seems to be a happy spot where there’s usually no collisions or if there are it’s a low single digit number. The total size of memory needed to hold both hash tables is about 24MB.
Looking at the snippet above we can see how the hash table is built. We loop 1024 times to exhaust all possible whitening values for this page of memory. Each iteration we encrypt the page (which will increment the whitening value), get the ciphertext for the LZX decoder data we expect to be in memory and the ciphertext for our malicious data, then add them to the hash tables. On lines 15-16 we can see the HvxFlushSingleTb call that thwarted my own attempt at using a hash table, and on lines 30-31 we can see how the first N bits of the expected ciphertext is used as the hash table key.
Improved Cache Flushing
In my original PoC I used a unique feature of the Xbox 360 CPU to lock away half of the available L2 cache to try and put as much pressure on it as I could. The L2 locking technique was pivotal in the original PoC but it didn’t put as much pressure on CPU cache as I would have liked. Putting pressure on CPU cache is particularly annoying because kernel mode (where the exploit code is running) cannot use certain cache flushing instructions due to them being privileged and only usable in hypervisor mode.
Additionally, the hypervisor only runs with CPU caching enabled when operating on encrypted memory which makes finding a hypervisor level cache flush primitive difficult. I tried to work around this by finding a hypervisor syscall that would read a large amount of encrypted memory, and I did find one syscall that fit the description, but it wasn’t nearly enough for what I needed. That function also had locks in it which prevented me from executing it on multiple threads simultaneously.
However, there was a kernel mode cache instruction I completely overlooked that Máté had found to work extremely well, dcbz or data cache block set to zero. Aside from just zero’ing out a CPU cache line this instruction has an interesting side effect:
If the cache block is already in the data cache, all of its bytes are cleared to zero. If it is not in the cache, the block is allocated and initialized directly in the cache to zero without reading the old contents from main memory.
So if this instruction is used on a memory address that’s not currently in CPU cache the CPU will allocate space for it and potentially evict something else to make room for it. By running the dcbz instruction over large regions of memory it can be used as a cache flush primitive and force old data in CPU cache to be evicted. In Máté’s original implementation he allocated an 0x80000 byte region of memory then looped over it and for every 0x80 bytes (the size of a cache line) called dcbz. 
This worked extremely well, however, I found that by increasing the allocation size by 3x and calling dcbz at three distinct locations I was able to assert slightly more pressure on CPU cache which would be important for another improvement I’ll get to later on. Here’s the final implementation:
Improved Thread Scheduling
In part 2 I talked about trying to schedule the exploit threads on different hardware threads and how I got the best results by putting them on CPU hardware threads 0 and 1 (which are both on core 0). I don’t really know anything about how CPUs work at a hardware level but I suspected that the load/store memory transactions from both hardware threads on the same core were being queued onto the L2 crossbar in some sort of per-core fashion. Thus by putting the exploit threads on the hardware threads for a single core the writes from the exploit thread and reads from the XKE payload thread would get queued together and reduce latency for loads/stores to RAM, or something like that.
It’s probably not very surprising to anyone reading this but CPUs often have “hidden” instructions, ones not defined by the instruction set architecture (ISA) but implemented by the CPU manufacturer. Sometimes these have a special instruction encoding and other times you’d use an existing instruction in a nonsensical way to tell the CPU to do a special operation.
In the case of PowerPC the ISA actually has some well defined instructions for changing the priority of a hardware thread by executing a special OR instruction with all 3 register operands set to the same specific register based on what priority you want the hardware thread to run at. For example:
The Xbox 360 SDK docs describe a few intrinsic macros that can be used to set the priority of the hardware thread the code is running on: __SetHWThreadPriorityLow, __SetHWThreadPriorityMed, and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh. The actual CPU instructions used by these macros are slightly different than what I listed above (these macros are xenon CPU specific) but that doesn’t really matter. 
The SDK docs describe every core as having 32 dispatch slots which are split evenly between hardware threads running at medium priority (which is the default priority). By using the __SetHWThreadPriorityLow and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh intrinsic macros you can have one hardware thread use 31 of the 32 dispatch slots and the other only use 1. How the dispatch slots relate to number of instructions fed to the CPU execution units I’m not sure (again I have no idea how a CPU pipeline actually works), but being able to go from 16/16 to 1/31 sounds pretty handy for scheduling the exploit threads.
Using these intrinsic macros Máté was able to schedule the exploit threads such that the hardware thread running the XKE payload was only getting 1 of the 32 dispatch slots while the ciphertext overwrite thread got the remaining 31 slots. The result was that the CPU was now spending the overwhelming majority of time in the ciphertext detection loop than it was actually running the XKE payload.
Improved Ciphertext Overwrite Detection
The last improvement was something I came up with while working on the Peer Pressure exploit to try and make the Bad Update exploit as stable as I could get it. In the original PoC I had discovered the compressed bootloader data the XKE payload operates on was compressed into 15 blocks with all but the last block having a decompressed size of 0x8000 bytes. If the XKE payload attack was successful part of the last segment of the hypervisor would be overwritten with the decompressed data for one or more of the compressed blocks. By observing the ciphertext for the last segment of the hypervisor in two distinct locations I could determine if the last block of compressed data was written to it by the XKE payload.
The attack was setup such that if the last block of compressed data was written to the hypervisor at a specific offset it would change the instructions for one of hypervisor syscalls to a write-what-where primitive I could use to get full hypervisor code execution. However, there was a flaw in how the ciphertext was being observed which not only led to false positives that would crash the console but also missed iterations where the last block was written to memory successfully.
Above is the original implementation for the exploit thread that ran the XKE payload and checked for ciphertext changes in the last segment of the hypervisor. The lines relevant to ciphertext observation have been highlighted. Because the same thread is both running the XKE payload and checking for ciphertext changes it can only detect if the ciphertext has changed at all and not how many times it changed. Put more simply: I could only infer if one of the compressed blocks was written to memory, but not how many blocks were written. With that in mind lets run through two scenarios that could happen when running an iteration of the XKE payload while attempting to get compressed block 14 written to memory.
Missing Successful Writes
While running the XKE payload the race attack is successful on some block N such that N < 14 (0x8000 bytes get written) and successful on block 14 (less than 0x8000 bytes). Upon returning from HvxKeysExecute we observe the ciphertext for two locations in the target write zone and see that the ciphertext has changed in both locations. We can’t infer that block 14 was written after block N because we don’t have the ability to observe how many times the ciphertext changed. Thus we consider this a failed iteration even though it was successful.
False Positive Write
Assume we have just executed an iteration of the XKE payload that exhibits the missed successful write behavior for some block N and block 14. The last segment of the hypervisor now contains the data for block 14 and the tail data for some block N. We run another iteration of the XKE payload and this time only block N is written. When we observe the ciphertext changes for this iteration we’ll see the ciphertext at the first location has change but the ciphertext at the second location hasn’t because it already contained the ciphertext for the tail data of block N from the previous iteration.
This gets detected as a write for block 14 and the exploit will try to execute some hypervisor code assuming the instruction pattern for the target syscall has been changed to the write-what-where pattern found in bock 14. However, the instruction pattern is actually random instructions found in block N and will cause the console to crash.
The New Detection Method
Now that the cache flushing primitive was significantly improved it was possible to observe the ciphertext changes for each block of compressed data that was successfully written to the target region of hypervisor memory. The solution I came up with for the detecting if block 14 was written to memory was quite simple: I created a new thread that continuously watched the ciphertext for changes and counted how many changes were observed.
If the counter reached 15 once the XKE payload was done executing then we know all 15 blocks were written to memory and thus the last block had to have been written. If we observed anything less we simply consider it a failed iteration and try again. Here’s the code for the new ciphertext detection thread:
Too Much Pressure
The new ciphertext observation function worked great but there was a new problem it introduced. Due to the amount of pressure I was putting on CPU cache the console would crash about 30% of the time when executing the XKE payload. When the XKE payload runs it takes the compressed update data buffer and does an in-place relocation to move it from unprotected memory to protected memory so it can’t be tampered with asynchronously. After the XKE payload runs its main logic it’ll do another in-place relocation to move the update data back to unprotected memory before returning.
After modifying the XKE payload and inserting a bunch of printf calls I was able to determine that the console would crash in a function I called HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical when trying to move the update data from protected memory back to unprotected memory. The function works by looping over a region of memory and for each CPU cache line worth of data (128 bytes) it will: 
- Read the entire cache line into CPU registers using the protected source address.
- Invalidate both data and instruction caches for the source address, zero the cache line for the destination address.
- Write the data back to memory using the unprotected destination address.
Here’s the disassembly for the inner loop of the HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical function:
In the modified version of the XKE payload I added a bunch of printf calls in a re-implemented version of this function so I could monitor were it would crash:
After running a few dozen iterations I was able to determine that the CPU would crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address on the line highlighted in red. As I mentioned earlier in the improved cache flushing section I made some modifications to Máté’s original implementation to put more pressure on cache which made the new ciphertext observation method more reliable.
I don’t know exactly what’s happening here that causes the CPU to crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address. Perhaps one of the cache invalidation instructions didn’t fully complete before the store instruction was executed, or maybe there’s some edge case with respect to the custom memory pathways when the CPU is starved for cache. Regardless, I did manage to find a way to work around this issue.
The New Detection Method v2
Since the crash happens after we would have been able to observe all 15 blocks of data being written to hypervisor memory the solution I came up with was to immediately stop the cache flushing thread and drop the L2 locks once the ciphertext change counter hits 15. This reduces the pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical which prevents it from crashing. Here’s the updated implementation of the ciphertext observation thread logic:
I moved the L2 cache locks into the ciphertext observation thread which we can see on line 5. Once we observe all 15 blocks of data have been written to memory we drop the L2 locks on line 36, and signal to the cache flushing thread to immediately terminate on line 40.
There’s still an edge case where we don’t observe all 15 blocks being written and thus won’t be able to reduce pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical. But this didn’t seem to matter. With all the improvements the exploit is usually successful in the first run of the XKE payload and at worst it may take 2-5 iterations, but I didn’t encounter any crashes when testing. It’s still possible it could happen but I think it’s very rare it does.
Conclusion
So there you have it, thanks to all the improvements from ihatecompvir, InvoxiPlayGames, and Máté the Bad Update exploit is now instantaneous and has nearly 100% success rate, and you only need to copy a few files to a USB stick to hack your console. When I released the original PoC I made some statements like “I don’t think this can be optimized any further” mostly to avoid endless comments from non-technical people spit balling random useless ideas. The truth is I always thought it could be optimized further but I didn’t expect it would ever reach the point it’s at now.
I think the biggest thing I learned here is that I should have taken a break after I completed the first iteration of Bad Update and came back with a clear mind to try and refine it. Having just found one of the only two bugs in the Xbox 360 hypervisor I put a lot of pressure on myself to get this exploit working at all. It took a lot of effort and sleepless days to pull it off and in the end I got tunnel vision chasing issues that didn’t really matter which distracted me from the real issues at hand. Had I taken a break after the initial PoC and came back a few weeks later I probably could have had something more refined for the initial release even if it wasn’t as refined as it is now.
Any ways, that does it for part 3. You can find the source code for the Bad Update improvements on my GitHub. Part 4 which covers the Peer Pressure exploit will be out soon so stay tuned for that!

Improved Cache Flushing
In my original PoC I used a unique feature of the Xbox 360 CPU to lock away half of the available L2 cache to try and put as much pressure on it as I could. The L2 locking technique was pivotal in the original PoC but it didn’t put as much pressure on CPU cache as I would have liked. Putting pressure on CPU cache is particularly annoying because kernel mode (where the exploit code is running) cannot use certain cache flushing instructions due to them being privileged and only usable in hypervisor mode.
Additionally, the hypervisor only runs with CPU caching enabled when operating on encrypted memory which makes finding a hypervisor level cache flush primitive difficult. I tried to work around this by finding a hypervisor syscall that would read a large amount of encrypted memory, and I did find one syscall that fit the description, but it wasn’t nearly enough for what I needed. That function also had locks in it which prevented me from executing it on multiple threads simultaneously.
However, there was a kernel mode cache instruction I completely overlooked that Máté had found to work extremely well, dcbz or data cache block set to zero. Aside from just zero’ing out a CPU cache line this instruction has an interesting side effect:
If the cache block is already in the data cache, all of its bytes are cleared to zero. If it is not in the cache, the block is allocated and initialized directly in the cache to zero without reading the old contents from main memory.
So if this instruction is used on a memory address that’s not currently in CPU cache the CPU will allocate space for it and potentially evict something else to make room for it. By running the dcbz instruction over large regions of memory it can be used as a cache flush primitive and force old data in CPU cache to be evicted. In Máté’s original implementation he allocated an 0x80000 byte region of memory then looped over it and for every 0x80 bytes (the size of a cache line) called dcbz. 
This worked extremely well, however, I found that by increasing the allocation size by 3x and calling dcbz at three distinct locations I was able to assert slightly more pressure on CPU cache which would be important for another improvement I’ll get to later on. Here’s the final implementation:
Improved Thread Scheduling
In part 2 I talked about trying to schedule the exploit threads on different hardware threads and how I got the best results by putting them on CPU hardware threads 0 and 1 (which are both on core 0). I don’t really know anything about how CPUs work at a hardware level but I suspected that the load/store memory transactions from both hardware threads on the same core were being queued onto the L2 crossbar in some sort of per-core fashion. Thus by putting the exploit threads on the hardware threads for a single core the writes from the exploit thread and reads from the XKE payload thread would get queued together and reduce latency for loads/stores to RAM, or something like that.
It’s probably not very surprising to anyone reading this but CPUs often have “hidden” instructions, ones not defined by the instruction set architecture (ISA) but implemented by the CPU manufacturer. Sometimes these have a special instruction encoding and other times you’d use an existing instruction in a nonsensical way to tell the CPU to do a special operation.
In the case of PowerPC the ISA actually has some well defined instructions for changing the priority of a hardware thread by executing a special OR instruction with all 3 register operands set to the same specific register based on what priority you want the hardware thread to run at. For example:
The Xbox 360 SDK docs describe a few intrinsic macros that can be used to set the priority of the hardware thread the code is running on: __SetHWThreadPriorityLow, __SetHWThreadPriorityMed, and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh. The actual CPU instructions used by these macros are slightly different than what I listed above (these macros are xenon CPU specific) but that doesn’t really matter. 
The SDK docs describe every core as having 32 dispatch slots which are split evenly between hardware threads running at medium priority (which is the default priority). By using the __SetHWThreadPriorityLow and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh intrinsic macros you can have one hardware thread use 31 of the 32 dispatch slots and the other only use 1. How the dispatch slots relate to number of instructions fed to the CPU execution units I’m not sure (again I have no idea how a CPU pipeline actually works), but being able to go from 16/16 to 1/31 sounds pretty handy for scheduling the exploit threads.
Using these intrinsic macros Máté was able to schedule the exploit threads such that the hardware thread running the XKE payload was only getting 1 of the 32 dispatch slots while the ciphertext overwrite thread got the remaining 31 slots. The result was that the CPU was now spending the overwhelming majority of time in the ciphertext detection loop than it was actually running the XKE payload.
Improved Ciphertext Overwrite Detection
The last improvement was something I came up with while working on the Peer Pressure exploit to try and make the Bad Update exploit as stable as I could get it. In the original PoC I had discovered the compressed bootloader data the XKE payload operates on was compressed into 15 blocks with all but the last block having a decompressed size of 0x8000 bytes. If the XKE payload attack was successful part of the last segment of the hypervisor would be overwritten with the decompressed data for one or more of the compressed blocks. By observing the ciphertext for the last segment of the hypervisor in two distinct locations I could determine if the last block of compressed data was written to it by the XKE payload.
The attack was setup such that if the last block of compressed data was written to the hypervisor at a specific offset it would change the instructions for one of hypervisor syscalls to a write-what-where primitive I could use to get full hypervisor code execution. However, there was a flaw in how the ciphertext was being observed which not only led to false positives that would crash the console but also missed iterations where the last block was written to memory successfully.
Above is the original implementation for the exploit thread that ran the XKE payload and checked for ciphertext changes in the last segment of the hypervisor. The lines relevant to ciphertext observation have been highlighted. Because the same thread is both running the XKE payload and checking for ciphertext changes it can only detect if the ciphertext has changed at all and not how many times it changed. Put more simply: I could only infer if one of the compressed blocks was written to memory, but not how many blocks were written. With that in mind lets run through two scenarios that could happen when running an iteration of the XKE payload while attempting to get compressed block 14 written to memory.
Missing Successful Writes
While running the XKE payload the race attack is successful on some block N such that N < 14 (0x8000 bytes get written) and successful on block 14 (less than 0x8000 bytes). Upon returning from HvxKeysExecute we observe the ciphertext for two locations in the target write zone and see that the ciphertext has changed in both locations. We can’t infer that block 14 was written after block N because we don’t have the ability to observe how many times the ciphertext changed. Thus we consider this a failed iteration even though it was successful.
False Positive Write
Assume we have just executed an iteration of the XKE payload that exhibits the missed successful write behavior for some block N and block 14. The last segment of the hypervisor now contains the data for block 14 and the tail data for some block N. We run another iteration of the XKE payload and this time only block N is written. When we observe the ciphertext changes for this iteration we’ll see the ciphertext at the first location has change but the ciphertext at the second location hasn’t because it already contained the ciphertext for the tail data of block N from the previous iteration.
This gets detected as a write for block 14 and the exploit will try to execute some hypervisor code assuming the instruction pattern for the target syscall has been changed to the write-what-where pattern found in bock 14. However, the instruction pattern is actually random instructions found in block N and will cause the console to crash.
The New Detection Method
Now that the cache flushing primitive was significantly improved it was possible to observe the ciphertext changes for each block of compressed data that was successfully written to the target region of hypervisor memory. The solution I came up with for the detecting if block 14 was written to memory was quite simple: I created a new thread that continuously watched the ciphertext for changes and counted how many changes were observed.
If the counter reached 15 once the XKE payload was done executing then we know all 15 blocks were written to memory and thus the last block had to have been written. If we observed anything less we simply consider it a failed iteration and try again. Here’s the code for the new ciphertext detection thread:
Too Much Pressure
The new ciphertext observation function worked great but there was a new problem it introduced. Due to the amount of pressure I was putting on CPU cache the console would crash about 30% of the time when executing the XKE payload. When the XKE payload runs it takes the compressed update data buffer and does an in-place relocation to move it from unprotected memory to protected memory so it can’t be tampered with asynchronously. After the XKE payload runs its main logic it’ll do another in-place relocation to move the update data back to unprotected memory before returning.
After modifying the XKE payload and inserting a bunch of printf calls I was able to determine that the console would crash in a function I called HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical when trying to move the update data from protected memory back to unprotected memory. The function works by looping over a region of memory and for each CPU cache line worth of data (128 bytes) it will: 
- Read the entire cache line into CPU registers using the protected source address.
- Invalidate both data and instruction caches for the source address, zero the cache line for the destination address.
- Write the data back to memory using the unprotected destination address.
Here’s the disassembly for the inner loop of the HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical function:
In the modified version of the XKE payload I added a bunch of printf calls in a re-implemented version of this function so I could monitor were it would crash:
After running a few dozen iterations I was able to determine that the CPU would crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address on the line highlighted in red. As I mentioned earlier in the improved cache flushing section I made some modifications to Máté’s original implementation to put more pressure on cache which made the new ciphertext observation method more reliable.
I don’t know exactly what’s happening here that causes the CPU to crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address. Perhaps one of the cache invalidation instructions didn’t fully complete before the store instruction was executed, or maybe there’s some edge case with respect to the custom memory pathways when the CPU is starved for cache. Regardless, I did manage to find a way to work around this issue.
The New Detection Method v2
Since the crash happens after we would have been able to observe all 15 blocks of data being written to hypervisor memory the solution I came up with was to immediately stop the cache flushing thread and drop the L2 locks once the ciphertext change counter hits 15. This reduces the pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical which prevents it from crashing. Here’s the updated implementation of the ciphertext observation thread logic:
I moved the L2 cache locks into the ciphertext observation thread which we can see on line 5. Once we observe all 15 blocks of data have been written to memory we drop the L2 locks on line 36, and signal to the cache flushing thread to immediately terminate on line 40.
There’s still an edge case where we don’t observe all 15 blocks being written and thus won’t be able to reduce pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical. But this didn’t seem to matter. With all the improvements the exploit is usually successful in the first run of the XKE payload and at worst it may take 2-5 iterations, but I didn’t encounter any crashes when testing. It’s still possible it could happen but I think it’s very rare it does.
Conclusion
So there you have it, thanks to all the improvements from ihatecompvir, InvoxiPlayGames, and Máté the Bad Update exploit is now instantaneous and has nearly 100% success rate, and you only need to copy a few files to a USB stick to hack your console. When I released the original PoC I made some statements like “I don’t think this can be optimized any further” mostly to avoid endless comments from non-technical people spit balling random useless ideas. The truth is I always thought it could be optimized further but I didn’t expect it would ever reach the point it’s at now.
I think the biggest thing I learned here is that I should have taken a break after I completed the first iteration of Bad Update and came back with a clear mind to try and refine it. Having just found one of the only two bugs in the Xbox 360 hypervisor I put a lot of pressure on myself to get this exploit working at all. It took a lot of effort and sleepless days to pull it off and in the end I got tunnel vision chasing issues that didn’t really matter which distracted me from the real issues at hand. Had I taken a break after the initial PoC and came back a few weeks later I probably could have had something more refined for the initial release even if it wasn’t as refined as it is now.
Any ways, that does it for part 3. You can find the source code for the Bad Update improvements on my GitHub. Part 4 which covers the Peer Pressure exploit will be out soon so stay tuned for that!

Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
21:56:01 UTC
06:56:01 KST

Very few people are using personal AI agents to order Ubers, apparently. On the transportation giant’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, the company said that only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during its busiest week in October: the week of Halloween.
While more people used an AI agent to order food through its delivery service, Uber Eats, the volume was still fairly small compared to the overall number of trips.
Uber’s chief financial officer, Balaji Krishnamurthy, told Wall Street analysts on the call that the company handled around 320 million trips and orders across Uber and Uber Eats during the week of Halloween, but only 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by an AI agent.
“It is very, very early and very limited traction that we are seeing so far,” said CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, referring to the low number of orders placed by AI agents. “Listen, we hope that there will be more traction.”
The surprisingly low numbers of AI-initiated transactions come amid growing hype for a new wave of AI agents that don’t just answer questions but also handle tasks on users’ behalf. There’s been an explosion of personal AI startups, including one of the buzziest, Instinct, which was founded last year and raised its most recent round of funding at a $10 billion valuation. Meta’s Muse also became the No. 1 app in Apple’s U.S. App Store last month, topping 10 million users, per Meta’s own reporting. The company said many were using it to shop and transact with businesses.
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and SpaceXAI (Grok) are also now offering their own AI agents, as are numerous smaller startups.
Still, early numbers from public companies indicate the agentic web still has a long way to go. DoorDash, for instance, said last week on its earnings call that it has only received a few hundred orders from AI agents so far, as most customers are still placing orders through the DoorDash app.
Uber is seeing the same behavior, it seems. Khosrowshahi pointed out that the average time to book a ride is only 50 seconds in the company’s app, and re-ordering a favorite food only takes 90 seconds. That suggests an AI agent isn’t necessarily saving anyone time.
Despite the low number of AI-driven transactions, Khosrowshahi seemed bullish on the idea of agents in general. “We think that is another opportunity to reach our platform. We think it will be a net positive in terms of demand on the ecosystem,” he said.
Right now, there are around eight major AI assistants on the market, Khosrowshahi noted, and he expects that number to grow to more than 10 in time.
“Every single AI system company is talking to us,” he added.

Snap has surpassed 30 million paid Snapchat+ subscribers, the company announced Wednesday in its third-quarter 2026 earnings release. The milestone marks an increase of 5 million subscribers since February, when Snap reported crossing the 25 million mark.
Launched in 2022, Snapchat+ gives subscribers access to exclusive and pre-release features for $3.99 per month. Following a successful launch, Snap introduced additional paid tiers beyond the core Snapchat+ subscription to further diversify its revenue streams. These include Lens+, an $8.99-per-month plan that unlocks exclusive Lenses and AR experiences, and Snapchat+ Platinum, a $15.99 monthly tier that offers an ad-free experience.
The milestone comes a year after Snapchat announced a controversial limit on free storage for its Memories feature and informed users it would start requiring users to pay $1.99 per month for additional storage or subscribe to Snapchat+ to retain their Memories.
“We surpassed 30 million paid subscribers across Snapchat+, Memories Storage, and Lens+,” Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said in a letter to investors. “Innovative AI-powered features have helped Lens+ exceed our expectations, demonstrating how new creative experiences can drive demand for our paid products. Paid subscribers still represent a small share of our monthly community, giving us room to grow through broader adoption and new premium experiences.”
As for the company’s broader earnings release, Snap’s shares fell 12% after missing ad revenue and user growth estimates.
Snap reported 495 million daily active users for the quarter, up from 493 million in the previous quarter. However, the figure fell short of analysts’ expectations of 499 million.
“Daily engagement has historically been stable as a percentage of monthly engagement, but we do not intend to optimize Snapchat around daily use at the expense of long-term value for our community,” the investor letter said. “A longer-term horizon better aligns our reported metrics with the product and safety decisions that strengthen relationships, create lasting utility, and support broader, more durable audience growth.”
Spiegel said in the letter than while advertising revenue growth remains below the company’s target, the company plans to prioritize improving advertiser performance and expanding the ways businesses can reach its users.

OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
21:25:44 UTC
06:25:44 KST

OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election could be a defining moment for AI. And he wants politicians to start developing policies that address Americans’ concerns about the technology, rather than simply paying lip service to anti-AI sentiment and the backlash against data centers.
In a new essay, Lehane compares AI’s potential to reshape the economy to President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, the 1930s set of federal programs and reforms enacted after industrialization and the Great Depression shattered the old economic order. He observes that Americans today feel similarly anxious about losing control over their economic futures and urges politicians to find a “compelling third path” that allows people to share in AI’s benefits. He lays out five policy priorities, spanning worker protections and education to AI safety and data center development.
The essay comes on the heels of a stunning Democratic victory in the midterm elections, in which Democrats flipped control of Congress amid widespread voter frustration over the cost of living. Kate Brennan, who leads AI and corporate power policy at the AI Now Institute, told TechCrunch that Lehane’s rhetoric marks a notable shift from OpenAI’s policy agenda last year, which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding infrastructure.
Unsurprisingly, many of Lehane’s proposals would encourage wider AI adoption and support the infrastructure expansion companies like OpenAI need to grow. The original New Deal established protections for workers and placed constraints on corporate power. It’s less clear how Lehane’s vision would hold AI companies accountable for the economic disruption their technology could create.
“Invoking a New Deal metaphor is to invoke state capacity to actually benefit the public,” Brennan said. “This is written by a private company that is trying to advocate for policies for its own benefit. It is ahistorical at best and harmful at worst.”
While AI wasn’t a dominant issue in the midterms, opposition to data centers emerged as a major bipartisan concern in several races in the midterms. And Lehane may be right that AI will become a bigger part of the conversation over the next two years.
Affordability is already shaping up as a key issue for the 2028 election as Americans grapple with inflation, tariffs, and the rising cost of living. AI could become an increasingly large part of that conversation as voters stress about data centers hiking up electricity bills, AI replacing their jobs, and technology’s economic gains flowing only to a handful of wealthy companies.
Lehane acknowledges many of these concerns, but he offers few concrete proposals to prevent AI’s gains from becoming concentrated. Instead, he largely pitches AI as a path to greater prosperity for Americans willing to embrace it.
Take his proposals for the tax code. He suggests incentives for workers to learn AI skills, easier capital access for entrepreneurs, and new approaches to employee ownership and profit-sharing. Those are not the same as binding requirements that would ensure workers share in AI-generated wealth or that companies pay the costs of displacing workers.
“I was struck by how much of this policy is for a future…that is already predicated on mass AI adoption and AI benefiting society, which we have yet to see,” Brennan said. “All of it is predicated on benefiting from AI’s upside.”
Brennan said it would make more sense to see things like a revised corporate tax rate or tax incentives for hiring human beings rather than automating jobs, as well as ways to keep companies from amassing outsize market power.
Lehane’s emphasis on expanding AI’s economic opportunities, rather than limiting potential harms, extends to data centers. He notes concerns about data centers while emphasizing the construction jobs and local tax revenue they could generate. He then warns that politicians who support a data center moratorium could jeopardize America’s lead over China, going so far as to compare that stance to the 2002 vote to authorize the Iraq war.
Lehane also makes child safety and education central to his proposed agenda, stressing the importance of age-appropriate protections and safeguards around AI companions for minors. He also warns against keeping AI out of classrooms, arguing that doing so could lead to inequality between wealthy students and “children in rural communities.” But the argument takes for granted that AI improves learning, a claim that remains unproven and one critics say deserves more examination than more funding or individualized attention from human teachers.
Lehane also calls for enforceable AI safety standards, independent evaluations, public oversight, and the ability to restrict AI systems or use a kill switch to shut them down — though recent studies show that OpenAI and other AI labs haven’t published comprehensive plans for what they would do if a model escaped human control.
Brennan called these stances “disingenuous,” pointing to OpenAI’s history of opposing legislation designed to impose such measures. In 2024, for example, OpenAI opposed California’s AI safety bill, SB 1047, which would have mandated catastrophic risk evaluations and shutdown capabilities. Last year, OpenAI also sought to limit state regulation, arguing that states could undermine American innovation. The company has more recently shifted some of those positions, backing several state safety laws and saying it would be open to independent evaluators embedded in the company.
Lehane also argues that people should maintain control over consequential decisions made using AI, rather than handing off judgment entirely to machines. But that raises the question of what human control really looks like in a society where humans are increasingly being required to use AI in education, work, healthcare, and government.
Throughout his essay, Lehane frames AI as a technology that could give Americans back their sense of agency and economic opportunity. But he ties average Americans’ “middle class” success to participation in an economy increasingly shaped by companies like OpenAI. Whether his policies will meaningfully redistribute power or subtly entrench it is less clear.
TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for more specifics on Lehane’s proposals and the company’s stances, but it did not respond by the time of publication.

How I learned to love an obnoxious phone grip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
21:20:59 UTC
06:20:59 KST

Much like a great recipe, it started with a stick of butter.
How I learned to love an obnoxious phone grip
Making the case for a loud smartphone accessory.
Making the case for a loud smartphone accessory.
This wasn’t real butter; it was a friend’s new phone grip, complemented by a phone case with bold stripes. Butter is in vogue now, or at least that’s what a 12-year-old told me a few months ago. This stick of butter was labeled “unsalty” and committed to the bit by including the appropriate tablespoon markings, just like the real thing. I was enamored. “Where did you get that?” I asked. It was a PopSocket-branded combo, and I found it so irresistible I ordered an equally eye-catching grip a few weeks later. After years of carrying buttoned-up, minimalist tech, I finally said, “To hell with it. I’m gonna have some fun.” I have zero regrets, and it seems I’m not alone in this journey.
Over the past few years I’ve been a vocal, occasionally regretful, member of Team No Phone Case. A case adds bulk and collects pocket lint. Why spend $800 on a piece of tech just to cover it up? If I must use a case, I want it to barely exist. This philosophy worked great with my iPhone 13 Mini, which is perfect as-is. Its size means it’s eminently grippable — no PopSocket necessary and it feels much more secure when I hold it. But phones are big now and are only getting bigger.
Since it’s just held on by a magnet, you can take it off whenever you want to present yourself as a serious grownup
An extended period using Google’s hefty Pixel 10 Pro Fold last year convinced me to adopt a magnetic grip just to use the thing more comfortably. At first, I gravitated toward the minimalist options like low-profile ring stands. But then I saw that stick of butter, and something clicked. A chunky grip is easy to hold. It’s fun. And since it’s just held on by a magnet, you can take it off whenever you want to present yourself as a serious grownup. Why not? I put in an order for a PopSocket shaped like a hot dog, and I was so excited when it arrived I accidentally pulled it apart.
This “why not have fun” ethos has clearly been part of Bailey Hikawa’s mission for the better part of a decade. She’s been making unconventional phone grips and cases out of her Los Angeles studio since 2018. Her designs incorporate input from the disabled community, aiming to offer an easier grip for people who hold their phone differently. But they can be appreciated by anyone who’s ever felt their phone slide out of their fingers. They’re also vibrant and bold. “I would like the phone case to feel like a friend or like a new stuffed animal,” she told The Verge in 2019. Earlier this year, Apple collaborated with Hikawa on a chunky, bright MagSafe grip. Her own online shop includes other grips made of flexible, clear urethane with spaghetti noodles or baby shrimp suspended inside. They’re handmade and the very definition of one-of-a-kind.
In more conventional territory, PopSocket has a surprising number of unusual grips and cases on offer. There’s a classic tomato pincushion, the food truck collection where I found my beloved hot dog, and an aptly named “Sugar Rush” collection. I asked PopSocket founder David Barnett whether I was alone in my pursuit of a bold grip. “We’re seeing more consumers embrace color, texture and personality in their phone accessories,” he told me over email. “I think people want their everyday essentials to feel a little less ordinary. Your phone goes everywhere with you, so why not have a little fun with it?”
I think phone makers are partly to blame here, too. Aside from your stray Cosmic Orange and anything Motorola is doing, phones mostly come in shades of Boring and Light Boring. Don’t even get us started on what passes for a purple phone these days. Maybe a radical reaction to this sameness was inevitable. Whatever the reason, you can find an awful lot of punchy, vibrant grips and cases without much effort. There are color-blocked “dopamine” cases all over TikTok and Amazon, viral phone cases that hold a tube of lip gloss, and OhSnap grips in colors called things like “hazmat honey” and “electric teal.”
Me and my ridiculous PopSocket are in good company. Or we will be — I left it in the office last time I was in New York and its absence has been bumming me out ever since. We’ll be reunited soon enough, but I guess if there’s one downside to being able to take a grip off your phone easily, it’s that you can accidentally leave it behind without much effort.

Bose’s QuietComfort Headphones are more than half off

Amazon is getting back into restaurant delivery with Uber Eats team-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
21:11:07 UTC
06:11:07 KST

Amazon and Uber are teaming up to make Uber Eats the official restaurant delivery partner for Prime subscribers in the US. The news comes as Uber faces a drastically reshaped competitive landscape with the merging of rivals DoorDash and Instacart.
Amazon is getting back into restaurant delivery with Uber Eats team-up
Prime members can now order takeout straight from the Amazon app or website with waived delivery fees on orders over $25.
Under the new partnership, Amazon Prime subscribers will get $0 delivery fees on restaurant orders of $25 or more directly through Amazon’s app or website — without having to use Uber Eats or even create an account. Essentially, Amazon Prime subscribers who never bothered to sign up for Uber can now order takeout without needing to create an Uber account.
Prime members can order Uber Eats takeout directly on Amazon’s website or app using their existing Amazon payment methods. Amazon handles the ordering process and delivery alerts, while Uber Eats sends the final receipt. Uber says it’s designed to let shoppers buy meals, groceries, and everyday household items all in one place.
This is a return to restaurant delivery for Amazon, which has always aspired to be the default delivery service for all household orders. After shutting down its own internal Amazon Restaurants service years ago, the company has realized partnering is cheaper than building its own delivery service for perishable meals from scratch.
At the same time, Uber gets access to tens of millions of Amazon Prime shoppers who already love getting things delivered, without having to spend money running app store ads to win them over. DoorDash is the bigger player in restaurant delivery, so by partnering with Amazon, Uber is clearly hoping to put pressure on its much larger rival.
Amazon previously partnered with Grubhub by offering free delivery to Prime members. Adding Uber Eats as the “official” partner means Amazon is either deliberately teaming up with multiple delivery apps, or simply admitting that Grubhub has become too small to really matter to Prime members.
Whether this deal is enough to move the needle for Prime subscribers remains to be seen. While waiving the delivery fee helps, it doesn’t eliminate the largest parts of the bill. On most takeout orders, costs like service fees, local regulatory charges, driver tips, and menu markups still make up the bulk of what you pay. And setting a $25 order threshold makes this benefit less practical for solo diners or casual lunch orders, forcing customers to buy extra food just to save a $3-$4 delivery charge.
Amazon and Uber say members could save over $175 a year, but that calculation assumes you order delivery fairly often. Because the estimate is compared against paying full price on every single order, customers would likely need to order takeout several times a month to reach that total.

Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
21:10:56 UTC
06:10:56 KST

Meta has acquired Conductor, an AI coding startup that allows users to spin up software projects by deploying multiple agents into parallel workspaces.
The news was originally reported by Axios, and Conductor shared news of its acquisition on its blog.
“I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta,” wrote the startup’s founder and CEO, Charlie Holtz, on Wednesday. “We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface,” he added, teasing that the company would have “something new” for customers to use by “early next year.”
On X, Holtz also noted that he was looking forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at the company’s Superintelligence Labs. “They’ve been on an absolute tear, and I’m convinced MSL has the highest talent density of all the labs,” he added.
Meta confirmed the acquisition to TechCrunch but wouldn’t comment further or provide additional details about the deal.
Conductor, founded in 2024, only launched its core product just last summer. The company’s agentic teams, which can be deployed in the cloud, locally, or via a user’s phone, are designed to help software engineers work on separate, compartmentalized parts of a project in concert. The agents that the platform deploys aren’t developed in-house but come from major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.
Holtz said that, until early next year, Conductor’s core features would continue to work as they previously have. The exception is Conductor’s cloud service, which will shut down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data.
Meta, which previously lagged behind in AI services, has spent the last several months trying to catch up. In August, the company launched Muse Code, its own coding agent. Meanwhile, the company’s recently launched Muse agents are seeing significant adoption, with the company recently reporting that the service had surpassed 10 million users. The company has also made a number of AI-related acquisitions over the past year, including Moltbook, the viral agent platform that made headlines.

Everything is an AI scam now
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
21:05:19 GMT
06:05:19 KST

Everything is an AI scam now
Whenever you watch a video on YouTube now, you will likely get an advert for a scammy product. In the past few weeks I've seen:
- A Tai Chi training program that promises to get you ripped like someone on steroids a superhero in 20 days. (Tai chi? Really?)
- Glasses that can adapt to any prescription (not how glasses work) and are also sunglasses sometimes
- A small USB stick that offers free Internet with no limits.
- An air con unit the size of a book that can cool any room - any room! - in 90 seconds.
- Endless mobile games that probably don't exist.
This is leaking into other parts of the internet as well with adverts on the side increasingly looking like chum buckets.
What annoys me is how little verification there is for any of this. It's like we have collectively decided that AI is inevitable, and the cost is the breakdown of truth itself. Scams used to be a bad thing and there used to be measures in place to stop them. Now they've escaped the spam filter and have run wild. As long as someone can create an unconvincing advert and pay, platforms will take anything.
So we have all this poorly made junk which breaks the rules of reality, so what? Most people are aware its fake. The problem is the scammers only need to get through to a very small percentage of people to make their money back.
It's not just adverts. I have my email in my footer [1] and tend to get a lot of spam. However, the quality of the spam has gotten more sophisticated. Take this email I got the other day.
In a world of noise and uncertainty, blackout poetry does something quietly extraordinary: it finds meaning hidden within the chaos, revealing light where none seemed to exist. Our Voices in the Chaos does exactly that, drawing readers into the madness of the world and returning them with something they did not expect to find: hope. A perfect 5.0 rating from your earliest reader is a promising beginning. The question worth considering is how many more poetry lovers could discover this collection.
On first glance, this sounds pretty good! As a pitch it's clear they have engaged with reading the book... except of course they haven't. Here's how I describe the book on this site:
In these blackout poems, you will be drawn into the maddening chaos of the world and find your own voices singing within. It deals with ghosts, anxiety and complete societal collapse, but with glimmers of hope strewn throughout like the stars in the empty night sky.
Someone has clearly pointed chatGPT at the page and said create a pitch to advertise this book. It even uses some of the same phrases! Even worse, I give away Our Voices in the Chaos as a free downloadable pdf, so I'm not looking to market it or get a "perfect 5.0" rating. This email is clearly phishing for information or money. It's the new version of the Nigerian Prince scam, only more tailored to vulnerable writers and creators.
I just delete these emails now. But the scammers only need to get a few people hooked and with these emails becoming more personal and reflecting back the author's words at them, the rate of people taking them up is only going to increase.
I'm not sure what we can do about this. I guess verifying a product exists before accepting adverts for it would be a good start, but I don't expect the huge internet platforms to turn the money tap off. We need more vigilance and more awareness, but it's exhausting having to constantly evaluate things for truth.
- Come say hi if you're a human! ↩︎

Death Comes for XSLT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
20:57:10 UTC
05:57:10 KST

Death comes for XSLT
Last halloween, Google decided to kill XSLT. That was not a unilateral decision mind you, Google said “jump” and other browser vendors said “how high?”
In response, I published my Intent to Deprecate and Remove Google Chrome. A performative declaration of course, I don’t install spyware.
Fearing my parody lacked seriousness, I created XSLT.RIP to ensure the developer world was informed of Google’s death note. This did the trick, although a few commenters believed it was satire. There is subtlety to XSLT.RIP. The website itself is built with XSLT and when Google kills XSLT they’ll kill my website.
The web standards process and its stewards (Big Browser) used to adhere to a social contract. Backwards compatibility was a major design principle. Under no circumstances do you ever purposefully break the web.
Google decided to renege and break the web.
XSLT.RIP will be broken soon and I’ll sit back and watch Google break it. 17 November 2026 appears to be the date of execution. Some Chromium-based browsers have been running a man-in-the-middle attack by injecting propaganda into XSLT websites.
This site uses XSLT; that functionality is being removed from this browser very soon. When that happens, this page will likely no longer display correctly. You might be able to install a browser extension that allows you to continue viewing it. Otherwise, you should contact the maintainer of the site for further information.
Source: This site uses XSLT: what Chrome’s banner means - XSLT Playground
This appears to be an <xslt-warning-banner> custom element that fails to render when it violates content security policy.
I’m testing on ungoogled-chromium so who knows how it’s intended to look.
The line of death is another “social contract” that Google has forgotten. They’re blaming website owners and acting like questionable purveyors of free public Wi-Fi. This is arrogant and intrusive.
“contact the maintainer of the site” — you broke the web Google, own it at least.

Great Art Explained Traces the Incredible Story of Henri Matisse’s ‘The Red Studio’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
20:46:58 UTC
05:46:58 KST

Great Art Explained Traces the Incredible Story of Henri Matisse’s ‘The Red Studio’
In today’s art world, provocation and controversy are part and parcel of the market. Think recent pieces like Maurizio Cattelan’s “Comedian,” a.k.a. the duct-taped banana, or Damien Hirst’s diamond- and platinum-coated 18th-century human skull titled “For the Love of God.” And while art has never been immune to controversy, it hasn’t always been, let’s say, expected.
At the turn of the 20th century, art—especially the “high” mediums of painting and sculpture—were viewed and taught through the lens of deeply ingrained conventions about what made art good. Chief among these was representation: people look like people, landscapes look like landscapes, and rooms look like rooms. That is, until Henri Matisse created “The Red Studio.”
A prized painting in MoMA’s collection in New York, “The Red Studio,” or “L’Atelier rouge,” was so unexpected that, according to a wonderful new video from Great Art Explained, Matisse may not have really been able to grasp what he’d done either, at least not right away. The documentary short by art historian James Payne traces the history of this paradigm-shifting painting, from the artist’s personal influences to the societal and technological shifts experienced by the art-viewing public. “The painting seemed to break almost every established rule of Western painting,” Payne says.
No one else knew what to make of the work either, which stretches more than seven feet wide. Matisse flattened the picture plane, removing the usual cues about perspective and depth with a quickly applied swath of Venetian red. (Payne delves into an interesting story about that, too.) Here, color itself defines the composition in place of line and contrast, drawing on friend, mentor, and Symbolist painter Gustave Moreau’s advice that color, as Payne describes, “should be thought, dreamed, and imagined.”
“When Matisse painted ‘The Red Studio’ in 1911, it was one of the strangest pictures anyone had ever seen—a room almost completely consumed by red—furniture reduced to outlines, paintings hanging on walls that barely seem to exist, and a grandfather clock with 12 numbers but no hands,” Payne says. “Even Matisse wasn’t entirely sure what he had created, and nobody wanted to buy it.”
“The Red Studio” didn’t sell even at the famous International Exhibition of Modern Art, better known as the Armory Show of 1913, where it was in the company of experimental styles like Fauvism and Cubism, not to mention Marcel Duchamp’s proto-Dadaist “Nude Descending a Staircase (No. 2).” Although “The Red Studio” traveled to numerous exhibitions, it was broadly panned by critics. Matisse hid it away for about a decade before the piece experienced an unlikely stint at a London nightclub. It took decades for the unorthodox work to be recognized not as repulsive but revolutionary.

Residential proxies detected on White House network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
20:45:18 UTC
05:45:18 KST

Our Residential Proxy Observatory, launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.
While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650. AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.
What we observed
From October 5 to November 3:
- Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network 236 separate times.
- Those exits came from 6 addresses, on 26 of the 30 days.
- 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.
This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.
Why this is concerning
Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.
Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets, the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.
No place is too remote
The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.
Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.
We also recorded three observations from Antarctica. All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.
Other remote places with activity:
- Pitcairn: 1 Starlink address, 1 observation.
- Norfolk Island: 1 Norfolk Telecom address, 4 observations.
- Svalbard: 1 Starlink address in Longyearbyen, 3 observations.
- Also seen: the Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7).
Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

Hackers stole DreamHost customer files and inboxes during months-long attack

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
20:36:57 UTC
05:36:57 KST

Web host DreamHost has confirmed that hackers stole customer emails and credentials during a months-long cyberattack on its systems. DreamHost disclosed the breach last Thursday after it sparked an outage that spanned several days, during which it reset some customer passwords.
In a data breach notice filed with California’s attorney general, the web host said the attack began in August and allowed hackers to obtain session tokens, which keep users logged in after entering their passwords. If stolen, hackers can break into a system as if they were that user. The company said hackers exploited an unspecified vulnerability in DreamHost’s file manager, which customers use to store their files.
When reached by TechCrunch, a DreamHost spokesperson declined to say why the company did not detect the cyberattack until last week, citing an ongoing investigation. The spokesperson did not say what the vulnerability is. The company said it was unrelated to the vulnerabilities recently discovered in the PHP web software.
DreamHost’s spokesperson said that the number of affected customers is “well under 10%” but would not provide a more accurate figure. The web host touts some 400,000 paying customers across its network.
