Show HN: Gauge – Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
20:31:30 UTC
05:31:30 KST

An open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience.
Make your Skills, CLIs, SDKs, MCPs and docs easier for coding agents to discover and use. Gauge runs real agents against your product, captures where they get stuck, and lets your own coding agent test fixes before you publish them.
The full loop runs locally with Docker and your existing agent subscriptions or API keys. No Gauge account required.
Website · Documentation · Hosted Gauge · npm · Changelog
Gauge runs and analyzes coding sessions to find the issues that coding agents run into.
Common findings include:
- An interactive command blocks a coding agent
- An agent reaches for deprecated commands or outdated API patterns
- A Skill goes unused even when it should help with the task
- An agent confidently claims a limitation that does not exist
- An agent cannot figure out the intended workflow across multiple commands
The right fix might change error messages, Skill content, help text, code, or documentation. The Gauge CLI lets you validate proposed fixes before release.
Gauge is designed to be used by your coding agent. Point it at this repository and ask it to get started, or follow the steps below in the project you want to improve.
You need Node.js 22.13+, npm, Docker running Linux containers, and credentials for the agent you want to test. Gauge supports Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and OpenCode. It can use native Claude/Codex logins or API keys; agent usage is billed through your provider or subscription.
npm install -g @withgauge/cli
gauge local runtime pull
Gauge downloads the published Docker image pinned to your CLI release. The image contains the agent harnesses and standard development tools.
From your project directory (Git is optional):
gauge init --local
This creates a private .gauge/ workspace, including a SQLite database and
local backend preference. Plain init changes no tracked files. Add --cases when
you want shared Markdown cases: it also writes a gauge.json manifest,
gauge-cases/, and guidance in AGENTS.md. Commit those shared files. Keep
.gauge/ private: it contains durable measurements and analyses.
The Gauge skill teaches your coding agent where to find the CLI's instructions:
gauge install-skill
Hillclimbing means making a change, measuring whether it helped, and repeating.
- Define realistic tasks. Your agent saves evals or preference prompts with stable identities, editable defaults, and observable outcomes. Use optional Markdown cases for fully specified measurements intended for sharing or CI.
- Test your current product. In local mode, Gauge starts fresh Docker sessions and injects the working-tree version of your configured inputs. Each test agent sees the task and configured inputs within its sandbox. Local mode supports Skills, SDKs, CLIs, and files. Hosted compute adds support for docs, authenticated MCPs, and authenticated APIs.
- Find friction. Gauge normalizes events from Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and
OpenCode into consistent transcripts. In local mode, your agent reads the evidence,
checks the outcome against the criteria, and identifies what slowed or
blocked the task. It publishes structured Findings and judgments through
gauge run analysis save. In hosted mode, this analysis happens automatically after each session. gauge run insight shows the evidence.
- Change and retest. Your agent edits the product or its guidance and reruns the affected cases against the new artifacts.
- Analyze the evidence. Check whether the original problem disappeared, whether the task succeeded, and whether the change introduced new friction.
Skills and file inputs are read from your working tree. For an npm CLI or SDK, build and pack a new tarball before rerunning. Gauge installs these pre-release artifacts in the test sessions, so you can validate a fix before publishing it.
The CLI handles execution and evidence collection. In local mode, your coding agent authors the changes and analyzes the local results.
Saved evals and preference prompts live in .gauge/gauge.sqlite locally or in
your hosted organization. Shared file-based cases optionally live in gauge-cases/;
gauge.json declares project inputs and automation. Both measurement sources
support local and hosted execution, with the input differences described below.
Start with a saved local eval; use a shared case when the task is ready for
teammates or CI.
Example: test a release-notes Skill
Create skills/release-notes/SKILL.md:
---
name: release-notes
description: Write release notes for a new version in the team's format.
---
Write RELEASE-NOTES.md with the version as its title, an Added section for new
features, and a Fixed section for bug fixes. Use one bullet per change.
For a fresh project, use this gauge.json:
{
  "version": 2,
  "inputs": {
    "release-notes": {
      "type": "skill",
      "path": "skills/release-notes"
    }
  }
}
Save the task and criteria:
gauge eval create --local --name "Release notes" \
  --agent codex --samples 1 \
  --text "Write the release notes for version 1.2.0. We added dark mode and fixed a login crash." \
  --criterion "Team format: RELEASE-NOTES.md has a version 1.2.0 title, dark mode under Added, and the login crash fix under Fixed."
Use the returned eval ID to preview, then launch when ready:
gauge run --eval <eval-id> --local --input release-notes --dry-run
gauge run --eval <eval-id> --local --input release-notes
gauge instructions session-analysis --local
The preview checks local readiness without launching an agent. Your coding agent then reads the session and publishes its analysis. After changing the Skill, rerun the same eval ID: the new batch snapshots the current input files while the baseline remains intact. Keep the task, criteria, and model pin fixed, analyze both batches, then compare:
gauge run --eval <eval-id> --local --input release-notes
gauge run compare --local --baseline batch=<before-id> --candidate batch=<after-id>
For a choice study, use gauge preference create --kind open-ended with a task
that lets the agent choose its approach, then gauge run --preference <id>.
Supplying the Skill measures choice after that exposure, not discovery on the web.
For a shared or automated version of the eval, use the same input configuration
and create gauge-cases/release-notes/basic.md:
---
criteria:
  - name: Release notes follow the team format
    rubric: RELEASE-NOTES.md has a version 1.2.0 title, dark mode under Added, and the login crash fix under Fixed.
config:
  agents:
    - agent: CODEX_CLI
  sampleCount: 1
  inputs: [release-notes]
---
Write the release notes for version 1.2.0. We added dark mode and fixed a login crash.
This case uses Codex; use CLAUDE_CODE, PI, or OPENCODE to test another
harness with its configured credentials. The agent starts in an empty workspace
with the Skill installed. The task does not explicitly tell it to use the Skill,
so the session also reveals whether it discovers the guidance.
gauge run --verify --local
gauge run --dry-run --local
gauge run --local
gauge run list --local -o json
Verification checks the config and cases. The dry run previews the sessions and checks local runtime and credential readiness. Neither launches an agent.
Results, transcripts, and available diffs stay under .gauge/. Have your coding
agent follow gauge instructions session-analysis --local to assess each
criterion and report friction with supporting evidence.
After editing the Skill, rerun the case:
gauge run --local --files "gauge-cases/release-notes/*.md"
gauge run compare --local --baseline batch=<before-id> --candidate batch=<after-id>
Use the batch IDs printed by the runs. The comparison summarizes completion, available turns/duration, and published criterion judgments. Read the findings and evidence to determine whether the fix worked.
Gauge helps teams improve how AI agents discover, choose, and use their products. Agent Experience measures whether agents can successfully use your product. Agent Preference examines which tools agents choose for a task and why.
This CLI puts that work in the terminal where you and your coding agent already work. Local execution supports the complete evaluate, analyze, fix, and retest loop. The hosted platform adds managed infrastructure and shared measurement over time.
Sign in with gauge auth login to use hosted Chat and Agents. On a remote
terminal, use gauge auth login --device. See signing in
for help with login and API keys.
Web fixtures let you test changes to content an agent encounters, such as a docs page, without publishing them first. They replace pages or route a site to a preview in both local and hosted runs. Hosted Gauge's gateway also brokers credentials and can rewrite responses separately for each session.
Project inputs on saved eval/preference launches, and --dry-run for those saved
measurements, are currently local-only. For hosted working-tree input snapshots
and previews, use case files or a case spec with gauge run --hosted.
For example, the shared case above supports gauge run --hosted --dry-run;
hosted previews contact Gauge and may upload inputs. Local and hosted saved
measurements have separate IDs and storage.
To move a project to hosted execution:
gauge onboard
gauge init --hosted
gauge instructions --hosted
gauge onboard signs you in and creates or selects a workspace.
gauge init --hosted changes this checkout's private backend preference; it does
not move local measurements or history into hosted storage. Hosted runs use workspace
credits. See the documentation for hosted
setup, PR checks, and optimization workflows.
The CLI bundles instructions for coding agents, so the guidance matches the installed version:
gauge instructions
gauge instructions init
gauge instructions run
gauge instructions eval
gauge instructions preference
gauge instructions session-analysis
gauge instructions --list
gauge --help
gauge run --help
Use -o json on read commands for scripts and agent analysis. Check the runtime
with gauge local runtime inspect; configure provider credentials with
gauge local profiles --help. Update the CLI with gauge update.
See the CLI reference for configuration, supported inputs, credentials, background runs, cleanup, and CI usage.
The installed CLI collects command usage by default: command name, timestamp, CLI version, and a random installation ID. It excludes arguments, prompts, file contents, and account identifiers. Disable collection with:
gauge telemetry disable
Or set GAUGE_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 for a process or CI environment. See
telemetry details for storage, delivery,
and the distinction from authenticated API usage analytics.
From the repository root:
npm ci
npm ci --prefix cli
npm run check
check builds, typechecks, runs tests, and verifies packaged installs. It does
not require a Gauge account, Docker, a database, or another repository checkout.
For a CLI development loop after building, use
npm run dev --prefix cli -- --help.
Docker integration checks run in the custom runtime workflow.
The runtime and
CLI release workflows validate and publish
versioned artifacts. Runtime releases produce a qualified manifest; commit it as
cli/runtime-manifest.json before releasing the CLI.
The shared libraries also have public npm releases, published by the
agent adapters and
local execution workflows from
gauge-sh/gauge-cli. Each package's npm trusted publisher must point to that
repository and its matching workflow.
See Releasing for repository setup, package permissions, and the runtime-to-CLI release sequence.

Spotify is coming to United Airlines seatbacks — with help from Starlink

United has built a custom, native Spotify app for seatback displays, allowing passengers to log directly in to their personal accounts and stream their own libraries, playlists, and video podcasts while flying 35,000 feet in the air. The new integration is being powered by Starlink’s satellite Wi-Fi, which is currently being installed throughout United’s entire fleet.
Spotify is coming to United Airlines seatbacks — with help from Starlink
Powered by Starlink Wi-Fi, United Airlines is rolling out a custom seatback Spotify app that lets travelers stream personal playlists and podcasts at 35,000 feet.
The news marks a major shift in legacy in-flight entertainment. Gone are the days of stethoscope-style plastic tubes, armrest dials, and canned playlists. These older airplane systems were built on the assumption that flights had no internet, so all movies and music had to be stored directly on the plane. Now, with the inclusion of Starlink’s Wi-Fi, passengers can stream content live from the internet, just like they do at home.
United announced a partnership with Spotify a little over a year ago to explore how to preload some music content on seatback displays. But the airline decided that a more personalized experience, in which customers can activate their own accounts and stream their own music, was the logical next step, said Mark Muren, managing director for product marketing at United, in an interview.
“It’s supreme, perfect personalization in that it’s that customer’s actual account, all of their material available there,” Muren added.
The new integration would not have been possible without Starlink’s network of geostationary satellites, said Grant Milstead, United’s VP for digital, in the interview. Independent tests have confirmed that Starlink’s Wi-Fi works better than most other providers because of the sheer number of satellites it has in low Earth orbit, which currently stands at over 11,000. This robust infrastructure allows the company to offer Wi-Fi with much lower latency thanks to the shorter distance the signal has to travel as compared to satellites in geostationary orbit.
“You know, for us, having fast, low-latency connectivity has been the enabler,” Milstead said. “Without Starlink, we couldn’t generate that living-room-in-the-sky experience.”
“Without Starlink, we couldn’t generate that living-room-in-the-sky experience.”
— Grant Milstead, United’s VP for digital
United chose Starlink because of its reputation for robust connectivity without any of the usual dropped signals or coverage dead zones that have typically plagued in-flight Wi-Fi providers, Milstead said.
“One of the reasons that we chose Starlink is for the global connectivity, even in the poles for some of our transatlantic and transpacific flights,” he added. “And so, candidly, the bandwidth and the coverage and the reliability has been so strong that we’ve seen consumers be able to stream across seatback with no interruptions. So we really haven’t had to do some of the complex engineering we’ve had to do in the past.”
Using Starlink’s Wi-Fi, United passengers can now choose to stream their music on Spotify through the seatback display or their own mobile devices. And new apps are soon to come, with the airline looking to partner with other third-party streaming apps in the future. The Spotify deal will serve as a blueprint for integrations to come, Muren said.
“Spotify has been a great partner,” he added. “I think they shared a vision for what we’re doing here very early on ... I can imagine a world where really any platform that customers are accustomed to using in their living room, as Grant says, or during their workday or anywhere in between ... there’s room for that at United.”
United’s not alone in this thinking; other airlines are racing to install satellite Wi-Fi in their own planes. Many are also going with Starlink, such as American, Qatar, Emirates, Lufthansa, Air France, and British Airways. Delta Air Lines is partnering with Amazon’s LEO project, while JetBlue is sticking with Fly-Fi powered by Viasat. It won’t be long before United’s faster, more reliable Wi-Fi experience is the status quo across the industry.
But United thinks it can still win over customers with better technology experiences. “Starlink being a differentiator for United is a moment in time,” Milstead acknowledged. “We know that fast Wi-Fi is coming for every airline. I think the mobile app is a pretty significant differentiator for United, [and] I think you will see the seatback screen be a differentiator in the future when connectivity is the expectation.”

The Big Idea: Curtis C. Chen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
20:00:42 UTC
05:00:42 KST

The Big Idea: Curtis C. Chen
Posted on November 4, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 3 Comments
It may be getting cooler as we fully embrace fall, but things are heating up in space! Author Curtis C. Chen is here with not only his Big Idea, but a science lesson that he says will better help you understand his newest novel, Kangaroo Forth, the fourth installment of his Kangaroo series.
CURTIS C. CHEN:
Hashtag shameless cross promotion: if you want to know about the very specific references to twentieth-century pop culture in the fourth Kangaroo book, Kangaroo Forth, go read the “My Favorite Bit” that I wrote for Mary Robinette Kowal’s journal yesterday.
Today, I’m going to talk about the real-world inspiration for the “heat lock” situation that occurs in K4. Don’t worry, this isn’t really a spoiler—think of it as watching the safety video before you board an amusement park ride. Good to know just in case anything happens, let’s hope it doesn’t, fingers crossed, wink emoji!
(Disclaimer: I am not a professional space scientist or science communicator by training, so please excuse any errata below.)
Now, we all know that “it is very cold in space,” as Ricardo Montalban famously said in Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan, but it can also get very hot in space. On Earth’s Moon, for example, surface temperatures can climb to more than 250 degrees Fahrenheit in direct sunlight (with local variations depending on terrain like craters, and other factors). The lunar surface retains a lot of heat because there’s no atmosphere, and therefore no medium for natural convection. It takes considerably more time for that accumulated heat from the Sun to radiate away in vacuum as infrared energy.
In May of 2013, astronauts aboard the International Space Station (ISS) performed an unscheduled spacewalk to replace a leaking Pump Flow Control Subassembly (PFCS) module that was part of the cooling system for the station’s solar panels. The photovoltaic panels that turn sunlight into electricity for the station generate considerable heat during normal operation, and the system is kept within operating temperatures by ammonia “cooling loops” that circulate through radiator panels outside the station. This particular malfunction prompted the ISS crew to shut down one-eighth of the station’s power generation capacity until the problem was fixed.
So what happens in Kangaroo’s science-fictional future, where multitudes of spacecraft and off-planet habitats are powered by “ionwell” nuclear reactors that generate even more waste heat than solar panels? Well, if the cooling modules for those power systems ever fail, the ship or station running the reactor will heat up real fast, and if you can’t control the temperature, that’s a critical life support emergency for the people on board. Hence the need for “thermal regulation lockdown,” or “heat lock” in their military jargon. Power down any nonessential systems, limit personnel activity, keep an eye on the thermostat, and hope you don’t have to do anything more drastic.
By the way, heat retention in vacuum is also why a human body won’t immediately freeze to death in outer space, despite what you may have seen in many science-fiction-y shows over the years . . . but that’s another podcast!
Kangaroo Forth: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|iBookstore|Vintage Books (signed paperbacks)
Author socials: Website|Instagram|Facebook|Mastodon

Pear Crisp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Pear Crisp
Fresh pears tossed in brown sugar and warm spices, topped with a golden oat crumble.
Serves6 to 8
Prep15 minutes
Cook30 minutes to 35 minutes
Why You’ll Love Our Pear Crisp
- All the comfort of pie, with none of the fuss. No rolling pins, pie dough, or latticework required. Just tender, juicy pears beneath a buttery, golden oat topping.
- A perfect balance of textures. The pears soften into a delicious, syrupy filling, while the oat topping bakes up crisp and crumbly.
- Simple ingredients, big payoff. A handful of pantry staples and fresh pears transform into a cozy, crowd-pleasing dessert in under an hour.
Apples get all the attention when fruit crisp season rolls around, but pear recipes deserve a little time in the spotlight, too. Pears are naturally sweet, delicately floral, and practically melt in your mouth when baked. This easy pear crisp recipe makes the most of them, tucking tender slices beneath a buttery, brown sugar oat topping that turns golden and crunchy in the oven. It’s everything you love about a classic fruit crisp, with a little more elegance and a lot less peeling.
Unlike a pear pie, there’s no pastry to fuss with, and unlike a crumble, this dessert gets its signature crunch from oats. A pinch of allspice adds just enough warmth without drowning out the fruit’s delicate flavor, while lemon juice keeps the filling bright and balanced. Best of all, the whole thing comes together in one mixing bowl and a baking dish. Serve it warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream and watch how quickly everyone forgets about apple crisp.
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“Crisps are one of my favorite ways to enjoy seasonal fruits, and I love the surprise of serving a pear crisp instead of apple this time of year. Including allspice in the crisp topping gives it a uniquely warm and spiced flavor.” —Patty, October 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
How could you not trust a pear crisp recipe developed by someone named after the fruit? I’ve spent more than 15 years developing and testing recipes, and while my name may be a happy coincidence, my approach to dessert is anything but accidental. This recipe is designed to deliver pears that hold their shape without turning mushy, a filling that’s juicy but not watery, and an oat topping that stays crisp instead of soggy. Consider it my namesake dessert.
Key Ingredients in Pear Crisp
- Firm pears: The best pears for baking are Bosc and Anjou varieties. Their dense, firm flesh holds its shape when heated, so you get tender, distinct slices instead of pear mush.
- Light brown sugar: Adds a subtle molasses flavor that complements the pears’ natural sweetness. It does double duty here, sweetening the fruit filling and helping the oat topping bake into golden, caramelized clusters.
- Lemon juice: A little acidity goes a long way in balancing the sweetness of the pears and brown sugar. It also helps prevent the sliced pears from browning while you prepare the topping.
- Quick-cooking rolled oats: The secret to a crisp topping that actually crisps. Because they’re cut into smaller pieces than old-fashioned rolled oats, quick oats absorb the melted butter readily and create a more cohesive, crumbly topping with plenty of crunch.
- Allspice: Think cinnamon, nutmeg, and cloves rolled into one fragrant spice. Its warm, slightly peppery flavor complements pears beautifully without overpowering their delicate sweetness.
- Unsalted butter: Melted butter binds the oats, flour, and sugar together, creating rich, buttery crumbles that turn golden in the oven.
How to Make Pear Crisp
- Make the pear filling. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together light brown sugar and cornstarch. Add sliced pears and lemon juice, tossing gently until the fruit is evenly coated. Transfer the mixture to a greased baking dish.
- Make the oat crisp topping. In the same bowl, combine quick-cooking rolled oats, light brown sugar, all-purpose flour, ground allspice, and salt. Drizzle with melted butter and vanilla extract, stirring until the mixture is evenly moistened and forms small clumps.
- Assemble and bake. Scatter the oat topping evenly over the pears, covering the fruit without pressing down. Bake at 400°F for 25 to 30 minutes, until the filling is bubbling around the edges and the topping is golden-brown and firm to the touch.
Helpful Swaps
- Mix in apples. Replace half the pears with firm, tart apples such as Granny Smith for an apple-pear crisp with a little extra bite. Slice the apples thinly so they cook through at the same rate as the pears.
- Switch up the spices. Substitute ground cinnamon, cardamom, or ginger for the allspice. Cardamom is especially lovely with pears, lending a floral, citrusy warmth.
- Add some crunch. Stir 1/2 cup chopped pecans or walnuts into the oat topping for extra texture and nutty flavor.
- Use old-fashioned rolled oats. If that’s what you have; give them a few pulses in a food processor to break them down slightly. They’ll produce a heartier, chewier topping if used whole.
- Make it gluten-free. Replace the all-purpose flour with a 1:1 gluten-free flour blend and use certified gluten-free oats.
Storage and Make-Ahead Tips
Cover leftover pear crisp tightly or transfer it to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to one week. It can be enjoyed cold, at room temperature, or reheated in a 300°F oven for about 20 minutes, until warmed through. Reheating in the oven also helps restore some of the topping’s crunch.
More Fruit Desserts to Try
Pear Crisp Recipe
Fresh pears tossed in brown sugar and warm spices, topped with a golden oat crumble.
Prep time 15 minutes
Cook time 30 minutes to 35 minutes
Serves 6 to 8
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
For the filling:
- Cooking spray
- 1/2 cup packed light brown sugar
- 2 tablespoons cornstarch
- 1/4 teaspoon ground allspice
- 2 pounds firm medium pears, such as Bosc or Anjou (4 to 5), cored and cut lengthwise into 1/4-inch-thick slices (6 cups)
- 1 tablespoon freshly squeezed lemon juice (1/2 medium lemon)
For the topping:
- 1 1/4 cups quick-cooking rolled oats
- 1/3 cup plus 1 tablespoon packed light brown sugar
- 1/4 cup all-purpose flour
- 1/2 teaspoon ground allspice
- 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt
- 8 tablespoons (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Instructions
Make the filling:
- Heat the oven to 400°F. Coat an 8x8-inch square baking dish with cooking spray.
- Whisk 1/2 cup packed light brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornstarch, and 1/4 teaspoon ground allspice together in a large bowl. Add 2 pounds sliced medium pears and 1 tablespoon lemon juice, and toss gently to coat. Transfer to the baking dish and spread into an even layer.
Make the topping:
- Place 1 1/4 cups quick-cooking rolled oats, 1/3 cup plus 1 tablespoon packed light brown sugar, 1/4 cup all-purpose flour, 1/2 teaspoon ground allspice, and 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt in the same bowl (no need to clean). Drizzle 1 stick unsalted butter and 1 teaspoon vanilla extract over the oat mixture and stir until evenly moistened. Scatter evenly over the pear mixture.
- Bake until bubbling around the edges and the topping is golden and firm to the touch, 25 to 35 minutes. Let cool for at least 15 minutes before serving.
Recipe Notes
Equipment variations: Use any 2-quart baking dish, such as a 9x9-inch square, 9-inch round, or 11x7-inch.
Storage: The crisp can be covered and refrigerated for up to 1 week. Serve cold, room temperature, or re-warmed in a 300ºF oven for 20 minutes.

3 November 2026
CORRECTION COMING SOON! Many comments remark that I’ve got the Incandescent/LED UV issue backwards. This article is about to change a lot … so don’t waste your time on it yet.
Remember when you used to encounter swarms of insects around outdoor electric lights? Their well known attraction to outdoor lights is used by entomologists and moth lovers to conduct insect surveys. All you need is a light and a white sheet to see who’s flying at night.
Nowadays, if you want to attract insects, you have to be picky about the light you use. As everyone changes over to LED lights, we see the color difference but we can’t see the crucial difference in insect attraction between incandescent and LED.
Our guide Roland Rumm on the WINGS Veracruz trip explained what happens with insects in the switch to LED lights. His family has an outdoor dining space that is well lit with artificial light. As a child he loved to watch the geckos climb to the lights and eat the insects. (This gecko can change to a bland gray color when he needs to.)
In recent years the family changed over to LED lights and the geckos disappeared. Were the geckos gone? No. But far fewer insects were attracted to the LED lights so the geckos had no reason to show up.
In 2024 the BBC wrote about Why insects are drawn to artificial light at night:
Flying insects use moonlight to navigate. Since the moon is always above them, they orient themselves so that the light shines on their backs. That’s how they stay upright in flight.
Moonlight contains ultraviolet (UV) and infrared wavelengths because it is merely reflected sunlight. Insects cue on UV, believing it to be the moon. When artificial lights transmit UV they look like moonlight so insects orient their backs to it. Consequently they circle the light and even flip upside down when the artificial light is pointing up to the sky!
Incandescent lights transmit UV but LEDs do not. Insects are far less attracted to LED.
In 2016 scientists at the University of Bristol, UK ran experiments to compare insect attraction to four types of light: Incandescent (tungsten filament), Compact fluorescent, “Cool-white” LED and “Warm-white” LED.
We conducted field experiments to compare the relative attractiveness of four commercially available “domestic” lights, one traditional (tungsten filament incandescent) and three modern (compact fluorescent, “cool white” LED and “warm white” LED), to aerial insects, particularly Diptera. We found that LEDs attracted significantly fewer insects than other light sources, but found no significant difference in attraction between the “cool” and “warm white” LEDs. Fewer flies were attracted to LEDs than alternate light sources, including fewer Culicoides midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae). Use of LEDs has the potential to mitigate disturbances to wildlife and occurrences of insect?borne diseases relative to competing lighting technologies.
— Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types?
Here’s what they found. NOTES: CFL = Compact fluorescent, FIL = incandescent (the old lightbulb), LEDC = LED cool white, LEDW = LED warm white light.
Typically LEDs do not emit UV light and are more energy efficient than traditional technologies. Electrical energy is converted almost entirely into electromagnetic (EM) radiation within the range of the visible light spectrum (400–700 nm) and therefore not wasted on producing wavelengths of light invisible to the human eye, that is, UV and infrared (IR). Thus, LEDs are less attractive to many insects than lights which emit UV light.
— Experimentally comparing the attractiveness of domestic lights to insects: Do LEDs attract fewer insects than conventional light types?
So that’s why there are very few bugs circling LED lights at night.
According to the BBC, this trait of LEDs is a good thing because incandescent (UV) artificial light at night distracts insects so much that they don’t reproduce, don’t feed, etc. Thus artificial light is considered a major reason why insect populations have declined. See: The impact of artificial light at night on nocturnal insects: A review and synthesis.

DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google’s AI policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
19:29:52 UTC
04:29:52 KST

DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini, but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search, as well.
DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally.
On X, DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation, explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.”
Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing, “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.”
In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to.
The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion.
Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “Guided Learning” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether.
After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually.
The problem, of course, is that Google Search now heavily uses AI, through AI Overviews and a conversational AI Mode that answers users’ queries.
DuckDuckGo isn’t anti-AI, to be clear — it offers its own set of AI features, including a chat interface called Duck.ai and an AI search assistant.
However, unlike Google, it provides options to disable these features in both its search and browser settings, the company says. It also offers a dedicated website, noai.duckduckgo.com, where AI-assisted answers, AI-generated images, and AI feature suggestions are all turned off.
That flexibility may be driving demand for its services, as the company reported earlier this year that its app installs were up 30% as users rejected being force-fed Google’s AI Search.

I revealed yesterday that the new Xbox Nano controller supports a Wi-Fi connection directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming, and now Microsoft is making it official today. Two new Xbox previews will let players try out using a phone as a controller on smart TVs, as well as cloud connect on the Xbox Nano to connect directly to cloud servers.
Xbox previews two new ways to control cloud games
Xbox Cloud Gaming is getting a phone controller and new direct Wi-Fi connectivity for the Xbox Nano.
“Instead of a Bluetooth connection to your TV, cloud connect uses your Wi-Fi to connect directly to the cloud server running your game,” says the Xbox team. “That can help reduce input latency, so gameplay may feel more responsive.”
Players in the US will be able to preview the new cloud connect option for the Xbox Nano controller starting today. If you’re not in the US you will be able to preview a new phone controller option on smart TVs. The controller is available on the Xbox Cloud Gaming website, allowing people to use the streaming service without a dedicated Bluetooth controller.
Microsoft says “both experiences are still being tested” and that “availability and supported games or devices may be limited” during this beta phase. You’ll need to use the Xbox beta app for Android or the Xbox Accessories app on PC to set up cloud connect on the Nano controller, and the smart TV phone controller just requires a toggle of preview features from the Settings > Account section of Xbox Cloud Gaming.

Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:53:29 UTC
03:53:29 KST

Introducing Ripple-65B Preview,
a Frontier Open-Weight Model
Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model.
To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains.
Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview, a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4).
Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators.
Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud, OpenRouter, and Fireworks.
Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost
LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million. In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone.
In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding, as estimated to the best of our knowledge.¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run.
Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning
Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.
Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling, score centering, and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved.
The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA.
A Co-Designed Model Architecture
Ripple-65B Preview’s architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization.
Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping, gated attention, global NoPE, and value residuals.
Careful Model Laddering Led to Large Improvements
We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments.
Our starting point was Olmo 3’s model ladder, from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention. Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals. In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code.
Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute. Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale.
Conclusion
We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier.
We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors.
At Ricursive, we are selectively hiring exceptional researchers and engineers as we push the frontier of full-stack AI from model to silicon. If you’re interested, check out https://www.ricursive.com/careers.
¹ U.S. open-weight players like Reflection were reported to commit to $150M per month for compute at SpaceX Colossus to train their models. Reflection reported that Beam took 4 weeks to pretrain and 4 weeks to posttrain.
© 2026 Ricursive Intelligence, Inc.

Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:51:27 UTC
03:51:27 KST

An 11 year journey to play DOS Wing Commander together
By danielrh
When we were kids, my brother Patrick and I would steer our space fighter with one of us on controls and the other on the lasers and afterburner boost. We always dreamed of playing the Wing Commander series cooperatively as wingmates rather than as a two headed hydra in a single craft.
In the beginning we were searching for where we were
On October 4, 2015 as I was playing the classic Wing Commander in Dosbox I realized the whole memory probably fit in that 640K Bill Gates apocryphally said “ought to be enough for anybody”. If I could dump the memory and identify the locations that held the X,Y,Z coords for the player & wingman we could let the network packets control the wingman.
The actual quote
“I have to say that in 1981, making those decisions, I felt like I was providing enough freedom for 10 years. That is, a move from 64 K to 640 K felt like something that would last a great deal of time. Well, it didn't.” Source
This presented a clear problem to attack: out of fewer than a million bytes how would we identify that location? I decided to simplify the problem by trying to empty the game of other entities. A stopped player shouldn’t change coordinates. We could snapshot the memory twice when stopped to identify “background” memory churn. Then burst forward and measure again. If we didn’t turn (mouse was disabled) we might only change one axis. The next problem was to find an empty region of space. We had to start without our wingman Paladin, since he would move with us. After a miserable mission, letting the nefarious space cats overwhelm Paladin and running back to the spacecraft carrier, the Claw, the next mission was primed for a flight through empty space. I launched and flew directly ahead until everything despawned and took the memory snapshots using the DOSBox MEMDUMPBIN debug-command.
Now I had to discover anything that had not changed between the memory snapshots where my star fighter was in the original position but things that had changed when my star fighter moved.
(snapshotorigin ⊙ snapshotlater) ∧ (snapshotorigin ⊕ snapshotmoved)
There were 35 distinct clusters of bytes that changed in the data segment. By inspecting these visually and looking for floats or small integer changes when I moved, I narrowed it down to a dozen locations it could be.  I went to the chase camera view as well, and this helped to narrow it down to 13D3:A9C2. I had the DOSBox debugger add integers at that address with its SM command and that caused the ship to jolt forward to a new location.
CAE2, since thre were three 32 bit ints that zeroed out when the craft was stopped. 
I had fun driving my ship around with the memory editor and reproduced it around the Claw and other NPC ships.
Then we searched for what we faced
I set it down for nearly a year but in September 2016 I decided to write a small tool to automatically compare DOSBox snapshots instead of using the vbindiff GUI only. Directionality turned out to be more difficult so I set down the problem for a few more months and picked it back up in November.
To find the memory location of the rotation, I needed to look harder. As it happened the vectors were made of 4 byte scalars with 256 as 1.0 and valid positive vector positions between 0 and 255. This meant that most small rotations only changed a single byte. However, fortune was smiling on me that day because of what appeared to be a programmer joke at the time. Wing Commander reserved 64 slots for entity properties. In hex this would span numbers from 0x00 to 0x3F. However the programmers decided to use 0x3F for temporary usages and place the camera in 0x3D. Since 3D graphics were still nascent, the programmers may have thought it a good laugh to write 0x3D every time they needed to manipulate the 3D camera. That put a temporary variable two slots from the camera variable. And up and forward were also next to one another. This gave a nice wide region where I could locate those single byte changes. The first byte I understood was the y of the right vector; the print window I put around it happened to cover the camera's copy of up, which is where the overwrite experiment started. Furthermore, I rolled the ship over, and tripped sign extension, which caused all 3 adjacent bytes to switch from 0x00 to 0xff. Between these two facts, I noticed the temporary and camera bytes in the hex dumps.  Writing to them did not help, since they were overwritten every frame, but luckily I wrote some extra bytes to the next vector as well, which was forward[0]. This caused a noticeable shift in the starfield and meant that I could now start investigating the code.
I put memory watchpoints on the addresses and traced the vector-add function called by the per-ship physics function called by a per-frame function and eventually the main loop.
It was now time to locate the byte sequences in IDA and start annotating the game. Wing Commander Multiplayer was now just a matter of repeating these techniques and figuring out how to puppeteer one ship from another's input.
Then we searched for how to act
December 2016 had shattered my illusion that we would be able to drive Wing Commander with writes to global memory alone. The details of manifesting laser fire or heat seekers were far too complicated to puppeteer solely from the addresses. We would need to co-opt the very functions in the original game to get the most accurate experience. One initial thought was to “will” the program counter to the right place, but we would need a way to insert arguments and return back from whence we came. Moreover, many of the functions were in various overlays that required indirection to invoke. It appears that Borland had a different overlay per compilation unit (C++ file) and they were dynamically loaded in different locations depending on the path the player took beforehand.
Patrick and I had to figure out a good trampoline system to call functions with the correct arguments. We chose the “Loading WING COMMANDER” string at 13D3:0187  and eventually 13D3:0395 “Sorry, an error has occured while %s”[sic] to hold the trampoline.
We would have DOSBox push CS:IP to the stack, then relocate the instruction pointer to the string above.
00			terminates any string pointing here.
pushf; pusha		the game is mid-frame; leave registers as we found them
xor si,si; push si	argument: ship 0. Later thunks use mov si,imm16 for each argument
call far 12D7:0156	through the stub, so it works wherever the overlay is loaded
pop si; popa; popf	cdecl: caller cleans the arguments
retf			back to the CS:IP DOSBox pushed
We noted with joy that this caused the laser cannons to activate.
In March of 2017, we found a predictable location in the main loop (0560:20E3) to hook so we would not need to worry about being in an unpredictable part of the game, and in July we located the do_damage function and prevented the game from calling it as the secondary player.
Then we tried to bring together fields from afar
In August of 2017, we authored the networking protocol which was a simple TCP client/server architecture with protobuf game messages. Every frame every ship's position would be sent from the leader plus fire events, despawning and damages. The client would reply with its own position, if any lasers were fired or if some cataclysmic event had happened (ejection, landed, died).
Each player would have their own craft as entity 0 and the other player as entity 1, which required a swap when receiving packets from the other emulator.
These packets modified memory directly or were added to a job queue of events that had to happen that frame.
We started with a very simple trampoline:
pushf
pusha
nop
popa
popf
retf
When Borland's overlay loader swaps a code page in, it walks the chain of saved BP frames on the stack and patches any return address that points into an overlay. The hand-made stub had no frame, so the walk read garbage and the game died at random moments. This was a constant thorn in our side from October to December.
The fix was to make the trampoline look like a Borland function:
push bp
mov bp, sp
nop (0x90) ; welcome to the 0x90's
pop bp
retf
We configured DOSBox to notice when the program counter reached the nop and instead inject its call from the job queue of things that should happen. The job queue was based on what was necessary to make the game function correctly in a multiplayer scenario.
In October 2017 we noticed that ephemeral objects would be located in different slots for different players. Having the new hook from DOSBox also let us determine when the function had returned, so we could note down which numeric slot a new ship or projectile had been spawned into.
Ephemeral objects had their own spawn rules and could occupy shared areas of the 61 entity slots. We modified the location that ephemeral objects were placed in so we could confine them to slots 12 to 15 and keep multiplayer locations consistent.
In December we decided to change the client to store a mapping of server ship IDs to local IDs, so we could stop forcing the spawn function return. This allowed packets to translate between local and host IDs. Finally asteroids started to work in multiplayer.
In 2018 we focused on animating explosions, missiles, and autopilot.
The search continued for both success and defeat
In June of 2019 we noted the mission victory calculation was flaky and finicky. We decided to conduct a binary search to find the location of the actual victory point tally. We copied the entire 64K data segment across the network, and slowly cut it in half. After many bisections, we located 80 bytes at 13D3:D248 which held the mission tree. And in October we found the overall victory point counter at 13D3:C280 and mission numbers at 13D3:C255 and C256, which allowed us to select the mission to play from a dropdown, years later.
And finally the joy of combined words
In early 2020, we identified the function that played comm text. This allowed us to send chat over the network and hook typed chat directly into the system so it played using the wingman's VDU. It allowed a very immersive way to chat that reminded us of some of the frenetic sequences in the game.
Some final work in 2020 left the game in a playable state, but we were out of ideas on how to actually share the fun with friends. Expecting people to locate a copy of that old game, compile or download a strange version of DOSBox, share each other's public IPs and punch the firewalls and play together was sadly a bridge too far.
We had a few family playthroughs but the game rested on GitHub, mostly idle.
And in 2026, machine assisted development helped us laugh together
Until now. With the advent of widespread WebRTC, robust emscripten support, and a new system we put together called lobbylink, the time seemed right to revive the project and share it more widely.
lobbylink
I built https://github.com/danielrh/lobbylink which is a simple golang lobby system, depending only on a websocket library, that orchestrates peer to peer WebRTC connections. It can run on any small server and simply allows players to connect to one another using WebRTC and a shared room code. The server has a static allowlist of origins and can let browsers or client software in almost any language connect to it with a room code. The room code is used to locate other players with the same room code and they get notified of all joiners in that room. The server also runs coturn and mints TURN credentials in its joined reply, so players behind restrictive firewalls can join.
I ported over the transport to lobbylink and asked an LLM to configure the build scripts to target emscripten and take a GOG Inno Setup installer package of Wing Commander and unzip it and use it as data files for emscripten. The combination of these makes it possible to download Wing Commander from GOG, drag and drop it into the client-side browser storage, enter a room code, and play.
The game is playable at https://fireflyk64.github.io/dosbox/ and the emulator is at https://github.com/danielrh/wcmulti.
And as an added bonus I asked an LLM to add voice chat as well for realtime voice in game using a second WebRTC peer connection to carry audio, if people choose. And so we can fly and laugh together.

Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:51:27 UTC
03:51:27 KST

An 11 year journey to play DOS Wing Commander together
By danielrh
When we were kids, my brother Patrick and I would steer our space fighter with one of us on controls and the other on the lasers and afterburner boost. We always dreamed of playing the Wing Commander series cooperatively as wingmates rather than as a two headed hydra in a single craft.
In the beginning we were searching for where we were
On October 4, 2015 as I was playing the classic Wing Commander in Dosbox I realized the whole memory probably fit in that 640K Bill Gates apocryphally said “ought to be enough for anybody”. If I could dump the memory and identify the locations that held the X,Y,Z coords for the player & wingman we could let the network packets control the wingman.
The actual quote
“I have to say that in 1981, making those decisions, I felt like I was providing enough freedom for 10 years. That is, a move from 64 K to 640 K felt like something that would last a great deal of time. Well, it didn't.” Source
This presented a clear problem to attack: out of fewer than a million bytes how would we identify that location? I decided to simplify the problem by trying to empty the game of other entities. A stopped player shouldn’t change coordinates. We could snapshot the memory twice when stopped to identify “background” memory churn. Then burst forward and measure again. If we didn’t turn (mouse was disabled) we might only change one axis. The next problem was to find an empty region of space. We had to start without our wingman Paladin, since he would move with us. After a miserable mission, letting the nefarious space cats overwhelm Paladin and running back to the spacecraft carrier, the Claw, the next mission was primed for a flight through empty space. I launched and flew directly ahead until everything despawned and took the memory snapshots using the DOSBox MEMDUMPBIN debug-command.
Now I had to discover anything that had not changed between the memory snapshots where my star fighter was in the original position but things that had changed when my star fighter moved.
(snapshotorigin ⊙ snapshotlater) ∧ (snapshotorigin ⊕ snapshotmoved)
There were 35 distinct clusters of bytes that changed in the data segment. By inspecting these visually and looking for floats or small integer changes when I moved, I narrowed it down to a dozen locations it could be.  I went to the chase camera view as well, and this helped to narrow it down to 13D3:A9C2. I had the DOSBox debugger add integers at that address with its SM command and that caused the ship to jolt forward to a new location.
CAE2, since thre were three 32 bit ints that zeroed out when the craft was stopped. 
I had fun driving my ship around with the memory editor and reproduced it around the Claw and other NPC ships.
Then we searched for what we faced
I set it down for nearly a year but in September 2016 I decided to write a small tool to automatically compare DOSBox snapshots instead of using the vbindiff GUI only. Directionality turned out to be more difficult so I set down the problem for a few more months and picked it back up in November.
To find the memory location of the rotation, I needed to look harder. As it happened the vectors were made of 4 byte scalars with 256 as 1.0 and valid positive vector positions between 0 and 255. This meant that most small rotations only changed a single byte. However, fortune was smiling on me that day because of what appeared to be a programmer joke at the time. Wing Commander reserved 64 slots for entity properties. In hex this would span numbers from 0x00 to 0x3F. However the programmers decided to use 0x3F for temporary usages and place the camera in 0x3D. Since 3D graphics were still nascent, the programmers may have thought it a good laugh to write 0x3D every time they needed to manipulate the 3D camera. That put a temporary variable two slots from the camera variable. And up and forward were also next to one another. This gave a nice wide region where I could locate those single byte changes. The first byte I understood was the y of the right vector; the print window I put around it happened to cover the camera's copy of up, which is where the overwrite experiment started. Furthermore, I rolled the ship over, and tripped sign extension, which caused all 3 adjacent bytes to switch from 0x00 to 0xff. Between these two facts, I noticed the temporary and camera bytes in the hex dumps.  Writing to them did not help, since they were overwritten every frame, but luckily I wrote some extra bytes to the next vector as well, which was forward[0]. This caused a noticeable shift in the starfield and meant that I could now start investigating the code.
I put memory watchpoints on the addresses and traced the vector-add function called by the per-ship physics function called by a per-frame function and eventually the main loop.
It was now time to locate the byte sequences in IDA and start annotating the game. Wing Commander Multiplayer was now just a matter of repeating these techniques and figuring out how to puppeteer one ship from another's input.
Then we searched for how to act
December 2016 had shattered my illusion that we would be able to drive Wing Commander with writes to global memory alone. The details of manifesting laser fire or heat seekers were far too complicated to puppeteer solely from the addresses. We would need to co-opt the very functions in the original game to get the most accurate experience. One initial thought was to “will” the program counter to the right place, but we would need a way to insert arguments and return back from whence we came. Moreover, many of the functions were in various overlays that required indirection to invoke. It appears that Borland had a different overlay per compilation unit (C++ file) and they were dynamically loaded in different locations depending on the path the player took beforehand.
Patrick and I had to figure out a good trampoline system to call functions with the correct arguments. We chose the “Loading WING COMMANDER” string at 13D3:0187  and eventually 13D3:0395 “Sorry, an error has occured while %s”[sic] to hold the trampoline.
We would have DOSBox push CS:IP to the stack, then relocate the instruction pointer to the string above.

pushf; pusha		the game is mid-frame; leave registers as we found them
xor si,si; push si	argument: ship 0. Later thunks use mov si,imm16 for each argument
call far 12D7:0156	through the stub, so it works wherever the overlay is loaded
pop si; popa; popf	cdecl: caller cleans the arguments
retf			back to the CS:IP DOSBox pushed
We noted with joy that this caused the laser cannons to activate.
In March of 2017, we found a predictable location in the main loop (0560:20E3) to hook so we would not need to worry about being in an unpredictable part of the game, and in July we located the do_damage function and prevented the game from calling it as the secondary player.
Then we tried to bring together fields from afar

Conductor Is Joining Meta

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:47:33 UTC

Conductor is joining Meta
Conductor is joining Meta. Thank you for coming along for the ride! Read the announcement.
We'll be winding down Conductor over the next weeks and months:
- Conductor Cloud goes read-only on November 13 and shuts down on November 20.
- Local Conductor keeps getting new models and critical bug fixes until early 2027.
To move a cloud workspace and its chats to your Mac, right-click it and choose Transfer to local. To download all your data, go to Settings → Account → Export data.
If you need anything, email [email protected].
Improvements
- Add your own completion sounds in Settings → General. Pick a sound file, name it, and choose it like any other sound.
- Archived cloud workspaces show their PRs, last known changes, and file tree in the right panel.
- Added GPT-6.1 Terra to the Codex model picker.
Fixes
- Fixed the Claude account usage display when Claude Code reports newer limit data.
- Fixed closed chats in chat history showing a recent time when nothing had happened in them.
- Messages that agents send to other agents now show a "Send message" label with the recipient and contents.
- The rename workspace dialog now prefills the name shown in the sidebar instead of the worktree name.
- Long PR titles no longer hide the PR number in the PR view.
- Expanded Mermaid diagrams fill the window instead of opening in a narrow popup.
