This is especially problematic when AI "hallucinates" or fabricates information.
Educators should get to decide when and how AI shows up for their students. Not a vendor. And certainly not under threat of losing basic access to web search.
Follow the incentives
Google is a successful company because they do a great job serving their customers. Unfortunately for educators and students, Google’s customers are advertisers, not users.
Google is the world's largest advertising company, so it's important to understand that when a search engine is funded by ads, it makes every user the product. Google's own founders saw this coming. In a 1998 Stanford paper they warned that advertising-funded search engines "will be inherently biased towards the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers."
So when Google tells schools that Search and AI can't be separated, we need to ask who this serves. Is it because it isn’t technically feasible or simply because it isn’t in the best interest of Google advertisers and shareholders?
When educators ask for choice or a slowdown of AI in education, it isn’t because it benefits them directly. It’s because their incentives are aligned with student incentives and they believe in slower, evidence-based approaches over experimenting on kids with brand-new technologies.
At Kagi, we believe in choice
Like Google, Kagi also does a great job serving our customers. The difference is that Kagi’s customers are the users. We build tools that are in the best interest of the people using them. That's why we created Kagi Search with a different user-aligned model. Instead of building at the expense of users, we seek to empower our users with choice.
Our users pay us in order to NOT be the product. And in return we give them the best search with no ads, no tracking and no selling of data. Because when the user is the customer, the user's interests and the company's interests are aligned and in harmony.
For schools, this means:
- AI is optional, not required. Quick Answer only appears when a student asks for it, and schools can turn AI features on or off for the students who are ready.
- Schools stay in control. Block low-quality or distracting sites for everyone, raise trusted sources, and build custom Lenses with teacher-approved resources for class projects
- Fewer dead ends. Students can see when a result is paywalled before they click, instead of hitting a wall mid-research.
- Less noise. Kagi has no ads and no clickbait thumbnails. But it does have filters that hide AI-generated slop images, so students can focus on the information itself.
- Tools that guide, not answer. We're building features that empower students to refine their research questions and search better.
Our ask
To Google and the rest of the industry: Let’s stop putting corporate profits over the civilizational imperative to truly educate students. Let’s give schools choice over coercion and lock-in.
To schools facing this choice: You don't have to accept it. There are alternatives to mandatory AI, and Kagi is one of them.
Kagi for Education
Your students shouldn't have to accept AI to use search. Kagi gives schools clean, ad-free results with AI off by default, and the controls to decide when it comes on.

From wild to mild: Friendly foxes show changes in brain region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:24:16 UTC
03:24:16 KST

From wild to mild: Friendly foxes show changes in brain region
By Krishna Ramanujan, Cornell Chronicle
Scientists studying the neurology of tame foxes identified changes in a part of the brain that has previously been associated with aggression, according to a new paper that compared the brains of domesticated, aggressive and wild foxes.
The changes occurred in an area at the base of the brain called ventromedial hypothalamus, which is known to drive aggression, control decisions related to energy use and is important for maternal instincts and social behaviors in mice.
The study, published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology, takes advantage of a classic experiment that started in Siberia in the late 1950s where Russian geneticists noticed some foxes on silver fox farms were friendlier toward human caretakers while others were more aggressive.
They then selectively bred friendlier foxes with each other and after only six generations of this selection, they had litters of puppies that interacted with humans. The cuddlier foxes also had physical features characteristic of animal domestication, including floppy ears and shorter snouts.
“We wanted to understand, what are the neurological underpinnings of these changes in behaviors that occurred very rapidly with this selection,” said Eirene Markenscoff-Papadimitriou, assistant professor of molecular biology and genetics in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS), a Rita Allen Foundation Scholar and the paper’s senior author.
The research has implications for how environmental pressures of all kinds can alter brain structure on short timescales, Markenscoff-Papadimitriou said.
In the study, the authors decided to focus on the ventromedial hypothalamus because previous research had already identified different cell types there that control aggression in mice.
Working with Russian fox colony scientists, the study’s authors received a shipment of nine silver fox brains: three from foxes bred to be tame, three from foxes similarly bred for aggressive traits and three wild foxes. The brains were preserved and very thinly sliced. In the ventromedial hypothalamus, a fluorescent RNA scope allowed them identify markers for different cell types there.
Previously, other scientists had employed a technique called optogenetics in experiments with mice where light was used to activate specific neurons that express a receptor protein called estrogen receptor alpha in the ventromedial hypothalamus.
“If you activate them, the mouse will immediately attack another mouse,” Markenscoff-Papadimitriou said. “We hypothesized that there would be differences in the abundance of this particular cell type, and we did find that the tame fox hypothalamus had fewer of these estrogen receptor expressing neurons, which are known to be part of the aggression circuit,” she said.
Now that the paper’s authors observed this difference, next steps will involve trying to understand why domestication leads to these changes in the ventromedial hypothalamus, a brain area has not been well studied before this work.
Study co-author Anna Kukekova, an associate professor of genomic biology and animal sciences at the University of Illinois-Urbana-Champaign, may explore how mutations in different parts of the fox genome affect the development of these particular neurons.
Jared Klein ‘25, a former research technician in Markenscoff-Papadimitriou’s lab, is the paper’s first author. Co-authors include Andrew Miller, professor of population medicine and diagnostic sciences in the College of Veterinary Medicine; and Anastasiya Kharlamova, Anastasiya Vladirimova and Darya Shepeleva at the Institute of Cytology and Genetics of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
The study was funded by Cornell’s Center for Vertebrate Genomics.

Benchfmt.rs: Bringing Go's benchmarking and benchstat workflow to Rust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
18:20:06 UTC
03:20:06 KST

benchfmt.rs: Bringing Go's Benchmarking and benchstat Workflow to Rust
TL;DR: I built benchfmt.rs, a zero-dependency Rust benchmark runner and Criterion converter for Go’s benchstat. It adds /key=value projections, heap tracking for allocated bytes (B/op) and objects (allocs/op) per op, and pprof profiling.
In this post, I am benchmarking varint and Prometheus Remote Write 2.0 decoding across Go and Rust to showcase the benefits of benchstat-like flow in Rust. I’m also sharing some fun learnings on the way (e.g., yes Rust is faster).
Recently, I’ve been working on a few Rust projects across Google and open source. I came to Rust after years of writing performance-sensitive Go in Prometheus, Thanos, and teaching Go in the “Efficient Go” book. For me, much of Rust’s performance story is really good, until…. I wanted to run A/B microbenchmarks.
Perhaps I was spoiled by the Go benchmarking ecosystem, with the go tool -bench and benchstat in the center. To me, Rust standard benchmarking tools are lacking:
- Standard format for case comparison projections.
- Standard heap allocation measurements.
- Standard pprof support.
- Simple to understand reliability scoring.
DISCLAIMER: A standard here means something that will be familiar to large number of developers, and I biased on Go experience for sure!
As a result, I asked myself: can we get benchstat-compatible output for Rust microbenchmarks? Wouldn’t that make A/B testing easier and unlock fun Go vs Rust comparisons?
Here we are! I built benchfmt.rs, a zero-dependency Rust benchmark runner with a thread-local heap allocation counter, pprof profiler integration, and the same CLI flags as go test -bench. For those who don’t trust a new benchmarking runtime (you shouldn’t from the start!), it also ships a Criterion and libtest converter that emits Go’s benchfmt format directly.
In this blog post, we will implement the same pieces of code in Go and Rust, benchmark them across different Rust frameworks, and compare the results. We might learn something new along the way (I did when building this!). Enjoy!
All benchmark code and raw outputs live in bwplotka/benchmarks/benchmarks/rust-go-decode.
Benchmarking two workloads
Let’s pick two workloads to implement and benchmark in both Go and Rust. I am particularly curious about protobuf decoding performance, which, funny enough, is often one of the main costs of running distributed systems these days. Thus, let’s decode our Prometheus Remote Write 2.0 protocol. Because protobuf code generators have different maturity and trade-offs across languages, let’s also measure something simpler alongside it, a standalone varint decoder.
Workload details:
- DecodeVarints. A 36-line unsigned LEB128 varint stream decoder. Varints are the integer encoding underneath Protocol Buffers. Our fixture varints_2000.bin is 4,798 bytes and packs 2,000 uint64 values mixing 1-byte symbol indices, 2-byte bucket offsets, 4-byte deltas, and 6-byte millisecond Unix timestamps. The function writes into a preallocated 2,000-element slice with zero heap allocations.
- DecodeRemoteWrite2. A full HTTP request body decoder for Snappy-compressed Remote Write 2.0 (io.prometheus.write.v2.Request) payloads. We test batches of 200 and 2,000 series, where 2,000 matches Prometheus’s default max_samples_per_send. The 2,000-series fixture mixes counters, gauges, classic and native histograms, 1,000 trace exemplars, and metric metadata. Remote Write 2.0 interns all strings into a top-level symbols table and stores packed varint labels_refs per series. That shrinks the 2,000-series batch to 244.9 KiB uncompressed and 57.0 KiB Snappy-compressed.
Implementing and benchmarking in Go
Let’s start with Go. First, DecodeVarints writes straight into a caller-provided slice, with a fast path for single-byte values below 0x80:
func DecodeVarints(src []byte, dst []uint64) (int, error) {
	n := 0
	i := 0
	for i < len(src) {
		if n >= len(dst) {
			return n, ErrDstTooSmall
		}
		b := src[i]
		i++
		if b < 0x80 {
			dst[n] = uint64(b)
			n++
			continue
		}
		x := uint64(b & 0x7f)
		shift := uint(7)
		for {
			if i >= len(src) {
				return n, ErrUnexpectedEOF
			}
			b = src[i]
			i++
			x |= uint64(b&0x7f) << shift
			if b < 0x80 {
				break
			}
			shift += 7
			if shift >= 64 {
				return n, ErrOverflow
			}
		}
		dst[n] = x
		n++
	}
	return n, nil
}
Second, for DecodeRemoteWrite2, we tune the Go implementation the way Prometheus runs in production rather than benchmarking slow reflection-based unmarshaling. We pair github.com/golang/snappy, which uses x86-64 assembly on linux/amd64, with vtprotobuf and its generated, optimized UnmarshalVT decoder:
func DecodeRemoteWrite2(compressed []byte) (*writev2.Request, error) {
	raw, err := snappy.Decode(nil, compressed)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	req := &writev2.Request{}
	if err := req.UnmarshalVT(raw); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return req, nil
}
Now let’s measure the efficiency of our Go code!
Notice Go’s /key=value sub-benchmark names (samples=2000/lang=go), which let Go’s official benchstat tool pivot across /lang or /samples later, along with b.SetBytes, b.ReportAllocs, and for b.Loop():
func BenchmarkDecodeVarints(b *testing.B) {
	manifest := ensureFixtures(b)
	raw, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join("testdata", "varints_2000.bin"))
	if err != nil {
		b.Fatalf("read varints: %v", err)
	}
	dst := make([]uint64, manifest.VarintsCount)
	// Encode dimensions as /key=value so benchstat can pivot across /samples or /lang.
	b.Run("samples=2000/lang=go", func(b *testing.B) {
		b.SetBytes(int64(len(raw)))
		b.ReportAllocs()
		// NOTE: b.Loop() resets the timer on its first call, stops it on exit, and keeps
		// call arguments and results alive without package-level sink variables.
		for b.Loop() {
			n, err := DecodeVarints(raw, dst)
			if err != nil || n != manifest.VarintsCount {
				b.Fatalf("unexpected decode result: n=%d err=%v", n, err)
			}
		}
	})
}
func BenchmarkDecodeRemoteWrite2(b *testing.B) {
	ensureFixtures(b)
	for _, samples := range []int{200, 2000} {
		file := fmt.Sprintf("rw2_%d.snappy", samples)
		compressed, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join("testdata", file))
		if err != nil {
			b.Fatalf("read %s: %v", file, err)
		}
		b.Run(fmt.Sprintf("samples=%d/lang=go", samples), func(b *testing.B) {
			b.SetBytes(int64(len(compressed)))
			b.ReportAllocs()
			for b.Loop() {
				req, err := DecodeRemoteWrite2(compressed)
				if err != nil || len(req.Timeseries) != samples {
					b.Fatalf("unexpected v2 decode: err=%v", err)
				}
			}
		})
	}
}
Finally, let’s run 6 benchmark runs (“epochs”) for 2s each at -cpu 2 on a 24-core Intel Xeon 2.20GHz Linux workstation (Go 1.26.8, Rust 1.99.1):
go test -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkDecode' \
    -benchtime 2s -count 6 -cpu 2 -timeout 999m -benchmem \
| tee results/go.txt
One epoch looks as follows:

BenchmarkDecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=200/lang=go-2        8467    264321 ns/op    31.43 MB/s   195296 B/op     2189 allocs/op
BenchmarkDecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000/lang=go-2        976   2448633 ns/op    23.84 MB/s  1643970 B/op    19297 allocs/op
Implementing and benchmarking in Rust with Criterion
Now let’s port both decoders and benchmarks to Rust. First, decode_varints mirrors the Go loop line for line:
pub fn decode_varints(src: &[u8], dst: &mut [u64]) -> Result<usize, VarintError> {
    let mut n = 0usize;
    let mut i = 0usize;
    while i < src.len() {
        if n >= dst.len() {
            return Err(VarintError::DstTooSmall);
        }
        let mut b = src[i];
        i += 1;
        if b < 0x80 {
            dst[n] = u64::from(b);
            n += 1;
            continue;
        }
        let mut x = u64::from(b & 0x7f);
        let mut shift = 7u32;
        loop {
            if i >= src.len() {
                return Err(VarintError::UnexpectedEof);
            }
            b = src[i];
            i += 1;
            x |= u64::from(b & 0x7f) << shift;
            if b < 0x80 {
                break;
            }
            shift += 7;
            if shift >= 64 {
                return Err(VarintError::Overflow);
            }
        }
        dst[n] = x;
        n += 1;
    }
    Ok(n)
}
Second, decode_remote_write2 pairs the snap crate with prost compile-time generated Message structs:
pub fn decode_remote_write2(compressed: &[u8]) -> Result<proto::v2::Request, String> {
    let raw = snap::raw::Decoder::new()
        .decompress_vec(compressed)
        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    proto::v2::Request::decode(raw.as_slice()).map_err(|e| e.to_string())
}
Now, let’s write both Rust benchmarks using Criterion, the default choice for stable-Rust microbenchmarking. We keep the same /key=value benchmark IDs and configure Throughput::BytesDecimal to match Go’s decimal MB/s:
fn bench_varints(c: &mut Criterion) {
    // Resolve testdata/ from the crate directory baked in at compile time.
    let root = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("testdata");
    let raw = fs::read(root.join("varints_2000.bin")).unwrap();
    // Preallocate the output buffer outside the timed loop so each op does 0 heap allocs.
    let mut dst = vec![0u64; 2000];
    // Group + function ID join into "DecodeVarints/samples=2000/lang=rust" to match Go's b.Run.
    let mut group = c.benchmark_group("DecodeVarints");
    // Report decimal MB/s (1e6 B/s) to match Go's b.SetBytes; Throughput::Bytes prints MiB/s.
    group.throughput(Throughput::BytesDecimal(raw.len() as u64));
    group.bench_function("samples=2000/lang=rust", |b| {
        // b.iter runs the closure across Criterion's warmup and 100 linear-ramp samples.
        b.iter(|| {
            // std::hint::black_box is an LLVM optimization barrier: Unlike Go's b.Loop(), Rust
            // would constant-fold known inputs or delete unused work without black_box hints.
            let n = decode_varints(black_box(&raw), black_box(&mut dst)).unwrap();
            assert_eq!(n, 2000);
            // Observe the written buffer so LLVM cannot optimize away stores into dst.
            black_box(dst[n - 1]);
        });
    });
    group.finish();
}
fn bench_remote_write2(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let root = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("testdata");
    let mut group = c.benchmark_group("DecodeRemoteWrite2");
    for samples in [200usize, 2000usize] {
        let file = format!("rw2_{samples}.snappy");
        let compressed = fs::read(root.join(file)).unwrap();
        group.throughput(Throughput::BytesDecimal(compressed.len() as u64));
        let id = format!("samples={samples}/lang=rust");
        group.bench_function(&id, |b| {
            b.iter(|| {
                let req = decode_remote_write2(black_box(&compressed)).unwrap();
                assert_eq!(req.timeseries.len(), samples);
                // Force req to materialize before dropping at the end of the iteration.
                black_box(req);
            });
        });
    }
    group.finish();
}
// Generate the benchmark group runner and custom main() required by harness = false in Cargo.toml.
criterion_group!(benches, bench_varints, bench_remote_write2);
criterion_main!(benches);
Finally, let’s run the Criterion benchmark suite:
cargo bench --bench criterion_decode

                        time:   [5.2789 µs 5.3369 µs 5.4014 µs]
                        thrpt:  [888.29 MB/s 899.02 MB/s 908.90 MB/s]
DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=200/lang=rust
                        time:   [237.09 µs 238.48 µs 239.95 µs]
                        thrpt:  [34.620 MB/s 34.833 MB/s 35.037 MB/s]
DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000/lang=rust
                        time:   [2.0712 ms 2.0831 ms 2.0968 ms]
                        thrpt:  [27.835 MB/s 28.018 MB/s 28.179 MB/s]
Criterion downsides
Criterion is convenient when you want confidence intervals and HTML plots from a single cargo bench command without external tools. However, compared to go test and benchstat, four design choices get in the way:
- Compile weight. Pulling in criterion with default-features = false still compiles clap, regex-automata, ciborium, oorandom, itertools, tinytemplate, and anes. That adds 42 transitive crates and ~19s to a cold cargo bench build.
- Linear-ramp sampling vs steady-state epochs. 
  - Go’s testing.B calibrates a fixed iteration count N for -benchtime 2s and runs -count 6 equal steady-state epochs, which benchstat summarizes using the outlier-resistant median and Mann-Whitney U test.
  - Criterion defaults to Linear sampling: after a 3-second warmup, it collects 100 batches of [1d, 2d, ..., 100d] iterations and fits a least-squares line y = m * x through the origin. Because the line is forced through zero, it does not subtract a fixed timer-overhead intercept. Instead, it computes a k^2-weighted average where batch 100 carries 10,000x the weight of batch 1 and late OS spikes pull the slope up.
Comparing those two models directly introduces two measurable distortions: 
  - First, grouping Criterion’s 100 ramp samples into 6 benchstat epochs gives epoch 1 11.5x fewer iterations than epoch 6 (24,888 vs 286,212 on DecodeVarints). Mixing short bursts with long runs inflates variance to ± 5%, compared to ± 1-2% in steady-state epochs.
  - Second, timing 100 separate closure batches adds +8.6% overhead on microsecond loops (5.36 µs vs 4.90 µs, p=0.002) and skews early allocating samples with cold allocator caches (+2.3% on DecodeRemoteWrite2).
- No heap allocation tracking. Criterion reports wall-clock time and throughput only. On DecodeVarints at 0 allocs/op, that is fine. On DecodeRemoteWrite2, we cannot tell whether prost made 500 heap allocations or 500,000, or whether a refactor doubled heap churn.
- Pairwise baseline folders vs multi-dimensional tables. Criterion compares target/criterion/<id>/base against new. You cannot feed a single run file into a table that pivots -col /samples or -col /lang across Go and Rust.
Converting Criterion output with the benchfmt CLI
If a Rust codebase already uses Criterion, rewriting benchmarks just to get a benchstat table is not ideal. That is why benchfmt.rs includes a standalone benchfmt CLI binary. It reads benchmark.json and sample.json directly from target/criterion, extracts Throughput::BytesDecimal (or Throughput::Bytes) as decimal MB/s, and groups Criterion’s 100 samples into 6 contiguous epochs via --epochs 6:
cargo install --git https://github.com/bwplotka/benchfmt.rs
benchfmt criterion target/criterion \

Now, with this view we finally have a readable, standard benchstat output Go developers love. It clearly shows the Go vs Rust efficiency for our example functions. Rust is 37.16% faster on DecodeVarints (5.36 µs vs 8.54 µs) and 13.37% to 15.72% faster on DecodeRemoteWrite2.
Unfortunately, there are some gaps:
- The B/op and allocs/op tables only have a go column because Criterion never recorded allocations
- Criterion’s linear-ramp epochs still leave ± 5% variance on DecodeVarints.
Native benchfmt runs with benchfmt::Suite and CountingAlloc
For new Rust benchmarks, we can skip Criterion and use benchfmt::Suite with harness = false in Cargo.toml. Registering CountingAlloc as #[global_allocator] tracks every alloc, alloc_zeroed, and realloc in a thread_local! Cell<(u64, u64)> with zero atomic contention and zero external dependencies:
// Wrap Rust's System allocator globally so every heap alloc/realloc on the benchmark thread
// increments thread-local (allocs, bytes) counters for B/op and allocs/op.
#[global_allocator]
static ALLOC: CountingAlloc = CountingAlloc::new();
fn main() {
    let root = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("testdata");
    let raw_varints = fs::read(root.join("varints_2000.bin")).unwrap();
    let rw2_200 = fs::read(root.join("rw2_200.snappy")).unwrap();
    let rw2_2000 = fs::read(root.join("rw2_2000.snappy")).unwrap();
    let mut dst = vec![0u64; 2000];
    // Parse go-test-compatible CLI flags (-bench, -benchtime, -count, -cpu, -benchmem,
    // -cpuprofile, -memprofile) from std::env::args() and set the default "pkg:" header.
    // Using the same pkg path as Go's go.mod lets `benchstat -col /lang` join Go and Rust rows.
    Suite::from_env("github.com/bwplotka/benchmarks/benchmarks/rust-go-decode")
        // Attach ALLOC so each benchmark snapshots thread-local allocation deltas per epoch.
        .with_alloc(&ALLOC)
        // Suite prepends "Benchmark" in benchfmt output, matching Go's BenchmarkDecodeVarints.
        .bench("DecodeVarints/samples=2000/lang=rust", |b| {
            b.set_bytes(raw_varints.len() as u64);
            b.report_allocs();
            // Go b.Loop() equivalent: starts timing, alloc snapshots, and any pprof capture on the
            // first call, runs the calibrated N steady-state iterations, then stops all three.
            while b.keep_running() {
                let n = decode_varints(black_box(&raw_varints), black_box(&mut dst)).unwrap();
                assert_eq!(n, 2000);
                black_box(dst[n - 1]);
            }
        })
        .bench("DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=200/lang=rust", |b| {
            b.set_bytes(rw2_200.len() as u64);
            b.report_allocs();
            while b.keep_running() {
                let req = decode_remote_write2(black_box(&rw2_200)).unwrap();
                assert_eq!(req.timeseries.len(), 200);
                black_box(req);
            }
        })
        .bench("DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000/lang=rust", |b| {
            b.set_bytes(rw2_2000.len() as u64);
            b.report_allocs();
            while b.keep_running() {
                let req = decode_remote_write2(black_box(&rw2_2000)).unwrap();
                assert_eq!(req.timeseries.len(), 2000);
                black_box(req);
            }
        })
        .run();
}
Does CountingAlloc work with Tokio and custom allocators? Mostly yes. You can wrap custom allocators like jemalloc or mimalloc via CountingAlloc::with_allocator(Jemalloc). Because CountingAlloc uses thread-local counters on the benchmark thread, single-threaded Tokio current_thread works out of the box, while multi-threaded pools like tokio::spawn or rayon need a process-wide atomic AllocTracker passed to Suite::with_alloc.
Suite::from_env reads std::env::args(), auto-detects goos, goarch, and cpu, and writes the passed string as the pkg: metadata line (matching Go’s module path so benchstat joins Go and Rust rows into one table). Passing flags after -- mirrors go test:
cargo bench --bench suite_decode -- \
    -bench '^BenchmarkDecode' -benchtime 2s -count 6 -cpu 2 -benchmem \
| tee results/rust_suite.txt
First, let’s verify that benchfmt::Suite agrees with Criterion on timing, even with CountingAlloc active on every allocation:
benchstat criterion=results/rust_criterion.txt suite=results/rust_suite.txt
                                            │  criterion  │               suite               │
                                            │   sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base              │

DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=200/lang=rust-2    235.1µ ± 4%   231.5µ ± 1%  -1.55% (p=0.004 n=6)
DecodeVarints/samples=2000/lang=rust-2        5.364µ ± 5%   4.902µ ± 2%  -8.60% (p=0.002 n=6)
geomean                                       138.0µ        132.1µ       -4.21%
On DecodeRemoteWrite2, Criterion and benchfmt::Suite agree within 1.6% to 2.3%, while Suite’s steady-state 2s epochs tighten worst-case variance from ± 4-5% down to ± 1-2%. On DecodeVarints, while b.keep_running() runs 490,000 back-to-back iterations in one tight loop instead of 100 short ramp batches, clocking 4.90 µs vs 5.36 µs.

Look closely at the B/op and allocs/op tables. That is the kind of surprise you miss without allocation counters:
- Rust makes 14.55% fewer heap allocations at 2,000 series (16,490 vs Go’s 19,297 allocs/op). Go’s protoc-gen-go generates pointer slices such as []*TimeSeries and []*Sample, allocating every nested struct separately on the heap. Rust’s prost stores Vec<TimeSeries> and Vec<Sample> inline by value.
- Yet Rust requests 30.98% more heap bytes at 2,000 series (2.05 MiB vs Go’s 1.57 MiB) and 42.59% more at 200 series (271.9 KiB vs 190.7 KiB)!
Bonus: go tool pprof profiling to tell WHERE certain overhead exists benchmarks in Go and Rust
benchstat tells us what changed, while pprof tells us why. With features = ["pprof"] and [profile.bench] debug = 1 in Cargo.toml, benchfmt::Suite supports the same -cpuprofile, -memprofile, and -memprofilerate flags as go test. Every .pb.gz file opens directly in go tool pprof -http=:8080 or pprof.me.
CPU profiling DecodeVarints
DecodeVarints does zero heap allocations in both languages, yet Rust finishes in 4.90 µs while Go takes 8.54 µs for the same loop. Let’s capture single-threaded CPU profiles from both runners:
go test -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkDecodeVarints$' -benchtime 5s -count 1 -cpu 1 \
    -cpuprofile /tmp/go_varints_cpu.pb.gz
cargo bench --bench suite_decode -- \
    -bench '^BenchmarkDecodeVarints/' -benchtime 3s -count 1 -cpu 1 \
    -cpuprofile /tmp/rust_varints_cpu.pb.gz
Opening the source view in pprof shows where each compiler spends its cycles:
Both languages spend over 99% of CPU inside the varint loop. Go, however, burns 1.74s (32.3%) on x |= uint64(b&0x7f) << shift alone and 1.24s (23.0%) on the outer loop checks. Inspecting go tool objdump and objdump -d shows two codegen differences behind the 42.56% gap:
- Loop unrolling and 64-bit shift masking. Because shift steps by 7 up to 64 (at most 9 bytes), LLVM unrolls Rust’s inner continuation loop. Every variable << shift becomes a constant shift (shl $0x7, shl $0xe, shl $0x15, …) with no shift counter or shift >= 64 branch. Go keeps the inner loop rolled and defines x << shift as 0 when shift >= 64, whereas x86 SHLQ CL masks modulo 64. That forces Go to emit SHLQ CL, CMPQ $64, SBBQ, and ANDQ on every continuation byte.
- Signed int vs unsigned usize indices. Go’s i and n are signed int, so i < len(src) and n >= len(dst) do not prove non-negativity across the loop back-edge. Go emits duplicate unsigned CMPQ/JBE slice bounds checks before src[i] and dst[n], while LLVM removes the inner checks on Rust’s unsigned usize indices and inlines decode_varints into while b.keep_running().
CPU and heap profiling DecodeRemoteWrite2
Next, let’s collect -cpuprofile and exact -memprofile captures on the 2,000-series Remote Write 2.0 benchmark:
# CPU profiles: 3s at -cpu 1.
go test -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkDecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000/' -benchtime 3s -count 1 -cpu 1 \
    -cpuprofile /tmp/go_rw2_cpu.pb.gz
cargo bench --bench suite_decode -- \
    -bench 'DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000' -benchtime 3s -count 1 -cpu 1 \
    -cpuprofile /tmp/rust_rw2_cpu.pb.gz
# Exact heap profiles: 50 iterations with every allocation sampled.
go test -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkDecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000/' -benchtime 50x -count 1 -cpu 1 \
    -memprofile /tmp/go_rw2_mem.pb.gz -memprofilerate 1
cargo bench --bench suite_decode -- \
    -bench 'DecodeRemoteWrite2/samples=2000' -benchtime 50x -count 1 -cpu 1 \
    -memprofile /tmp/rust_rw2_mem.pb.gz -memprofilerate 1
The two CPU flamegraphs show very different bottlenecks:
Go’s x86-assembly snappy.Decode at ~0.12 ms/op actually beats pure-Rust snap at ~0.18 ms/op, and vtprotobuf’s own wire parsing takes only ~0.95 ms/op. Go still loses overall because runtime.mallocgc and GC assist take 54.1% of all on-CPU time, or ~1.34 ms/op, allocating and scanning 19,297 heap objects.
In Rust, 71.1% of CPU time goes to prost field decoding, 8.9% to snap decompression, and 18.7% to RawVecInner::grow_amortized under Vec::push and Vec::reserve. The alloc_space heap profiles show why RawVecInner::grow_amortized is so busy and why Rust allocates 30.98% more B/op than Go:
Go’s UnmarshalVT preallocates slices and structs close to their final size, totaling 1.57 MiB/op. Rust allocates 2.05 MiB/op, and 88.4% of those bytes come from RawVec capacity doubling inside prost:
- prost decodes packed repeated uint32 labels_refs one u32 at a time with Vec::push instead of pre-sizing from the wire byte length. Every series grows its Vec<u32> through capacities 4 -> 8 -> 16 -> 32, accounting for 23.0% of all allocated bytes.
- Growing Vec<v2::TimeSeries> from 0 to 2,048 copies inline 112-byte structs at each power of two, which is 21.3% of allocated bytes. Go only grows an 8-byte []*TimeSeries pointer slice.
- Pushing one 24-byte Sample into an empty Vec<Sample> jumps straight to capacity 4 due to RawVec::MIN_NON_ZERO_CAP, adding another 8.5% of allocated bytes across 1,900 series.
However, even with that extra Vec churn, glibc thread-cache reallocations in Rust cost ~3.5x less CPU than Go’s mallocgc and GC assist, so -memprofile points straight to a Vec::with_capacity fix.
Checking our microbenchmarks with a standalone binary and /usr/bin/time -v
Ok, those microbenchmarks are great, but let’s verify our efficiency numbers against the real program!
Microbenchmarks run inside an artificial loop with a hot instruction cache, a warm allocator, and a custom #[global_allocator] wrapper in suite_decode. Do those ns/op and B/op numbers hold up in an unmodified release binary?
To check, I wrote two standalone CLI binaries:
Each binary runs N iterations, accumulates a checksum, and optionally keeps K decoded messages alive via --retain K to simulate an ingestion queue. I ran both under GNU /usr/bin/time -v with GOMAXPROCS=2 on Go to match -cpu 2:
cargo build --release --bin verify_decode
/usr/bin/time -v ./target/release/verify_decode --case rw2_2000 --iters 1000 --retain 0
/usr/bin/time -v ./target/release/verify_decode --case rw2_2000 --iters 1000 --retain 1000
Here is what /usr/bin/time -v reported across all runs:
The process-level numbers show a few important details:
- CountingAlloc did not distort latency. The standalone Rust binary ran rw2_2000 at 2.22 ms/op across 1,000 cold-start iterations, close to 2.03 ms/op in benchfmt::Suite while counting 16,490 allocations per iteration.
- B/op measures allocator churn, not live memory. Over 1,000 iterations of rw2_2000, Rust requested 2.00 GiB from the allocator, yet peak RSS with retain=0 stayed at 4.21 MiB. Dropping each Request at the end of the loop lets glibc reuse the freed thread-cache chunks on the next iteration without asking Linux for new pages. Keeping all 1,000 batches alive with --retain 1000 raised RSS to 1,292.4 MiB (1.29 MiB per retained message after temporary Snappy and Vec-doubling buffers were freed) and split CPU into 2.12s user + 1.06s kernel sys time for page faults.
- Wall-clock ns/op hides Go’s background GC cost. In benchstat, Rust was 17.68% faster than Go on rw2_2000. Under /usr/bin/time -v at GOMAXPROCS=2, Rust used 99% of one core and 4.21 MiB RSS, while Go hit 144% CPU, 4.28 ms of CPU time per op, and 15.98 MiB RSS. Leaving GOMAXPROCS unrestricted on all 24 cores pushed Go to 220% CPU, or 7.13 ms of CPU time per op, and 18.53 MiB RSS as background GC threads swept heap objects. Across the whole process, Rust used 1.9x to 3.2x less CPU and 3.8x to 4.4x less RAM per request.
Summary
In general I think Rust has real potential in this AI era:
- It has extreme compile-time verification, including strict ownership and memory safety checks, which is ideal when AI generates code.
- It takes ages and can be annoying to program in by hand (sorry!), but AI writes a lot of code nowadays. Code mostly has to be readable for reviews, and Rust is good enough at that.
- It has a strong columnar storage ecosystem around crates like arrow-rs.
- It has no garbage collector, gives more control over memory allocations, and is clearly faster!
In terms of benchmarking, having both benchfmt tools in Rust lets you match the workflow to the job:
- Run benchfmt criterion target/criterion on existing Criterion suites when you want benchstat A/B tables across commits or languages without editing benchmark code.
- Use benchfmt::Suite and CountingAlloc with features = ["pprof"] for new Rust microbenchmarks to get fast std-only compiles, steady-state epochs, B/op and allocs/op tracking, and pprof profiles.
Give benchfmt.rs a spin and let me know on GitHub what breaks or what is missing!

Waymo confirms it will start splitting with Uber in January 2028

Waymo will end its exclusivity with Uber in the Austin and Atlanta markets starting in January 2028, co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana told Bloomberg News in a report published Wednesday.
The robotaxi company will offer rides directly through its own smartphone app, like it does in other cities. Uber confirmed to TechCrunch Wednesday that it still plans to host Waymo robotaxis on its app for as long as the two companies agree. Waymo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Mawakana’s comments come after reporting earlier this year by the Financial Times that Waymo was looking to get out of its deal with Uber, which was set to expire in May 2028. Mawakana told Bloomberg that Waymo initially partnered with Uber because the ride-hail giant offered scale. But the experience for riders has been “a little bit of a crapshoot,” she said, especially because riders never know for sure if they’re going to hail a robotaxi or a human-driven car.
“It’s important for us to have that relationship with the rider. We’ve gotten that feedback from the riders in those markets,” Mawakana said.
Uber — which has many robotaxi and other autonomous vehicle partners — told Bloomberg that it was Waymo’s idea not to add an option in the ride-hail giant’s app to book a robotaxi directly.

This Month in Ladybird – October 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
17:59:35 UTC
02:59:35 KST

Hello friends! In October, we moved style and layout off the main thread, built a JavaScript JIT, replaced our WebAssembly engine, redesigned the browser UI, and passed Safari Technology Preview on Web Platform Tests. :^)
Sponsors
Ladybird is entirely funded by companies and individuals who believe in the open web. You can see everyone supporting the project on our sponsors page, and we’re grateful to all of them. If you’re interested in sponsoring, please contact us.
Style and layout no longer wait for JavaScript
Browsers normally run JavaScript, style, and layout on one main thread, one at a time. While a script runs, the page can’t update. A few simple animations can keep going on the compositor, but everything else has to wait.
We moved style and layout to their own thread, and paint recording to another (#12377, #12400). They now run at the same time as JavaScript (#12396, #12432, #12460). If a script asks for layout information, like an element’s size, it waits until pending layout work is finished, so it never gets stale data.
So two things now work during a long script:
-   CSS animations keep running while JavaScript is busy.  This includes animations that change layout, like width and font-size (#12433, #12447, #12451).
- :hover keeps working while JavaScript is busy.  The render thread finds the element under the mouse, applies its hover styles, starts any transitions, updates the cursor, and draws a new frame. When the script ends, the main thread catches up and fires the hover events (#12530).
As far as we know, no other browser can do this today. Here’s a text animation while JavaScript blocks the main thread in 1.5 second bursts, with Ladybird in the top left:
And here’s :hover on a page running JavaScript for 250ms at a time, with Ladybird on the left and Chrome on the right:
You can also try it yourself. The button blocks the main thread for three seconds. Most browsers keep the square spinning, but freeze the bar and the hover target.
transform width :hover A JavaScript JIT
On Linux and macOS, LibJS now compiles hot JavaScript to machine code, on both x86-64 and AArch64 (#12613).
We decided against a JIT in the past, and did what we could to push and tune the interpreter instead. It’s already competitive, so making it twice as fast would be a huge effort, and that would only turn a 300ms hang into a 150ms hang, which you’d still notice. So we needed an optimizing JIT.
The design is deliberately boring: speculative optimization based on runtime type profiling, like other JavaScript engines. For now, we just want to go reasonably fast.
While code warms up, we record things like which types and object shapes it sees (#12588). The compiled code uses those recordings to make guesses, like “this value is always an integer”, and inlines small functions (#12595, #12598).
To find bugs during development, we used a fuzzer that ran the same code in the JIT and the interpreter and compared the results (#12601).
A new WebAssembly engine
We replaced our C++ Wasm engine and Cranelift with a new engine that has its own interpreter and JIT (#12963). It supports newer parts of WebAssembly that the old engine didn’t, like exception handling and GC. On the JetStream 3 Wasm workloads both engines can run, it scores about 7x higher.
In July, we built flap, a small language and compiler for writing LibJS’s interpreter. The Wasm interpreter is written in flap too, so one source builds it for x86-64, AArch64, and Windows x64. Hot functions move from there to the JIT, even in the middle of a running loop.
We’re making great progress on performance. JSLinux, an x86 PC emulator, now boots Alpine Linux to a shell in 1.8 seconds, while Chrome takes 1.5.
Benchmarks
Web Platform Tests (WPT)
On October 26, we passed Safari Technology Preview on WPT. :^) We ended the month at 2,184,722 subtests, a gain of 75,650.
Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing.
A new browser UI
Until now, our UI had grown organically, with tinkering here and there. This was the first time we sat down and mapped out a complete design. We kept it modest and quiet, so the attention stays on the page.
It covers tabs, toolbars, menus, and our own about: pages on macOS and Linux, in light, dark, and a violet dark theme for private windows (#13271, #13169, #12815).
- Tabs: you can pin tabs, search all open tabs, and restore your windows on launch (#12757, #13271).
- Form controls got a new look, and date and time inputs got a picker (#13554).
- Scrolling: smooth mouse wheel scrolling (#12593), elastic overscroll on macOS (#12624), touchpad momentum on other platforms (#12345), and scrollbars that hide until used (#12997).
Sites that work better
- Google Slides: presentations open instead of showing an error (#12497).
- GitHub: Mermaid diagrams render (#12383).
- ChatGPT: the text box grows as you type (#13050).
- nytimes.com and reuters.com get past their bot checks (#12718, #12188).
- Instagram: videos show their first frame instead of staying blank (#12898).
- Gmail: reloading no longer keeps the old page in memory (#12689, #12660).
- x86CSS , an x86 emulator made of CSS, is now usable (#12911).
New browser features
- Screen readers: we’ve added first support for VoiceOver on macOS and Orca on Linux (#9156). There’s still a lot of work to do here.
- Spell checking in text fields on macOS (#12638).
- Picture-in-Picture (#12542).
- Links to text: links can scroll to a piece of text and highlight it, and you can create them from the context menu (#11121, #12744).
- Permissions: sites can now ask for your location and microphone (#13336, #12604).
- DevTools: Inspect Element (#13348), console autocomplete (#13355), and expandable objects in the console (#13360).
- Smaller additions: Find in page can highlight all matches (#12434), ad blocking can be turned off per site from the toolbar (#12695), and we added Reload Without Cache (#13056).
More of the web platform
We rendered this page in Ladybird, using features that landed in October:
From the top left, that’s multi-column (#13026), display: grid-lanes for masonry (#13236), MathML (#13062, #13141), corner-shape (#12942), CSS Motion Path (#13027), much more of anchor positioning (#13021, #13079, #13166), and text-wrap: balance (#13461).
We also added:
-   CSS:  calc-size(), which lets heights animate to and from auto (#13006), plus vertical writing modes (#13103), zoom (#13237), the stretch sizing keyword (#13006), shape() and border-shape (#12942), field-sizing (#13050), view progress timelines and animation-range (#12943), and the start of SVG animation (#12823, #13498).
-   Web APIs and more:  the HTML Sanitizer API (#13185), Touch Events (#13249), Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (#12296), Paint Timing, Event Timing, Largest Contentful Paint (#13110), WebVTT cues (#12895), wide-gamut canvases (#13097), WebDriver BiDi (#13167), JavaScript’s using and await using (#13102), and many execCommand and contenteditable fixes (#13186, #13038).
Security and process isolation
Web pages run in sandboxed renderer processes, so a malicious page that takes over its renderer should be stuck there.
We kept fixing security issues from many sources, including ways around that sandbox. For example, a compromised renderer could ask the browser process to open any file on your computer. Now only a renderer showing local files can read them (#12582, #12590). Renderers could also fake a user click to open popups or read the clipboard. The browser process no longer trusts them on this (#12597).
We also split the browser into more processes, so a compromised one can reach less:
- Cross-site iframes get their own renderer by default (#12647), and so do cross-site popups (#12296).
- Each top-level site gets its own network process, and the HTTP cache and third-party cookies are kept separate per site (#13144, #12424).
- Each renderer has its own audio process (#12604) and image decoder (#12437).
Media and Windows
On Windows, video now plays and YouTube works (#12646, #13195). Hardware video decoding moved to its own process and now works on Linux through Vulkan (#12868). We also read MP4 files ourselves now instead of using FFmpeg, which fixes problems with seeking and buffering (#12641).
More C++ moved to Rust
LibJS’s runtime moved from C++ to Rust just before the JIT landed, so our JavaScript engine is now all Rust, apart from its flap interpreter and the garbage collector (#12492). The new Wasm engine is Rust as well. WebGL, 2D canvas, IndexedDB, Streams, and URL also moved over (#12699, #12935, #13287, #13083, #12998). We also deleted the C++ style computation, so style is now computed entirely in Rust (#12346).
Getting ready for alpha
Our first alpha is planned for later this year. This month we added:
-   Release builds:  macOS archives, Linux tarballs, .deb and .rpm packages, and Flatpak bundles (#13176, #13313, #13340).
- Crash reports: after a crash, you can review a report and choose to send it to us (#12298, #12342).
- A welcome page to pick your tab layout, search engine, and ad blocking (#12333).
- Reporting broken sites from inside the browser (#12880).
That’s it for October. Thanks for reading, and we’ll see you next month!

This Month in Ladybird – October 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
17:59:35 UTC
02:59:35 KST

Hello friends! In October, we moved style and layout off the main thread, built a JavaScript JIT, replaced our WebAssembly engine, redesigned the browser UI, and passed Safari Technology Preview on Web Platform Tests. :^)
Sponsors
Ladybird is entirely funded by companies and individuals who believe in the open web. You can see everyone supporting the project on our sponsors page, and we’re grateful to all of them. If you’re interested in sponsoring, please contact us.
Style and layout no longer wait for JavaScript
Browsers normally run JavaScript, style, and layout on one main thread, one at a time. While a script runs, the page can’t update. A few simple animations can keep going on the compositor, but everything else has to wait.
We moved style and layout to their own thread, and paint recording to another (#12377, #12400). They now run at the same time as JavaScript (#12396, #12432, #12460). If a script asks for layout information, like an element’s size, it waits until pending layout work is finished, so it never gets stale data.
So two things now work during a long script:
-   CSS animations keep running while JavaScript is busy.  This includes animations that change layout, like width and font-size (#12433, #12447, #12451).
- :hover keeps working while JavaScript is busy.  The render thread finds the element under the mouse, applies its hover styles, starts any transitions, updates the cursor, and draws a new frame. When the script ends, the main thread catches up and fires the hover events (#12530).
As far as we know, no other browser can do this today. Here’s a text animation while JavaScript blocks the main thread in 1.5 second bursts, with Ladybird in the top left:
And here’s :hover on a page running JavaScript for 250ms at a time, with Ladybird on the left and Chrome on the right:
You can also try it yourself. The button blocks the main thread for three seconds. Most browsers keep the square spinning, but freeze the bar and the hover target.
transform width :hover A JavaScript JIT
On Linux and macOS, LibJS now compiles hot JavaScript to machine code, on both x86-64 and AArch64 (#12613).
We decided against a JIT in the past, and did what we could to push and tune the interpreter instead. It’s already competitive, so making it twice as fast would be a huge effort, and that would only turn a 300ms hang into a 150ms hang, which you’d still notice. So we needed an optimizing JIT.
The design is deliberately boring: speculative optimization based on runtime type profiling, like other JavaScript engines. For now, we just want to go reasonably fast.
While code warms up, we record things like which types and object shapes it sees (#12588). The compiled code uses those recordings to make guesses, like “this value is always an integer”, and inlines small functions (#12595, #12598).
To find bugs during development, we used a fuzzer that ran the same code in the JIT and the interpreter and compared the results (#12601).
A new WebAssembly engine
We replaced our C++ Wasm engine and Cranelift with a new engine that has its own interpreter and JIT (#12963). It supports newer parts of WebAssembly that the old engine didn’t, like exception handling and GC. On the JetStream 3 Wasm workloads both engines can run, it scores about 7x higher.
In July, we built flap, a small language and compiler for writing LibJS’s interpreter. The Wasm interpreter is written in flap too, so one source builds it for x86-64, AArch64, and Windows x64. Hot functions move from there to the JIT, even in the middle of a running loop.
We’re making great progress on performance. JSLinux, an x86 PC emulator, now boots Alpine Linux to a shell in 1.8 seconds, while Chrome takes 1.5.
Benchmarks
Web Platform Tests (WPT)
On October 26, we passed Safari Technology Preview on WPT. :^) We ended the month at 2,184,722 subtests, a gain of 75,650.
Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing.
A new browser UI
Until now, our UI had grown organically, with tinkering here and there. This was the first time we sat down and mapped out a complete design. We kept it modest and quiet, so the attention stays on the page.
It covers tabs, toolbars, menus, and our own about: pages on macOS and Linux, in light, dark, and a violet dark theme for private windows (#13271, #13169, #12815).
- Tabs: you can pin tabs, search all open tabs, and restore your windows on launch (#12757, #13271).
- Form controls got a new look, and date and time inputs got a picker (#13554).
- Scrolling: smooth mouse wheel scrolling (#12593), elastic overscroll on macOS (#12624), touchpad momentum on other platforms (#12345), and scrollbars that hide until used (#12997).
Sites that work better
- Google Slides: presentations open instead of showing an error (#12497).
- GitHub: Mermaid diagrams render (#12383).
- ChatGPT: the text box grows as you type (#13050).
- nytimes.com and reuters.com get past their bot checks (#12718, #12188).
- Instagram: videos show their first frame instead of staying blank (#12898).
- Gmail: reloading no longer keeps the old page in memory (#12689, #12660).
- x86CSS , an x86 emulator made of CSS, is now usable (#12911).
New browser features
- Screen readers: we’ve added first support for VoiceOver on macOS and Orca on Linux (#9156). There’s still a lot of work to do here.
- Spell checking in text fields on macOS (#12638).
- Picture-in-Picture (#12542).
- Links to text: links can scroll to a piece of text and highlight it, and you can create them from the context menu (#11121, #12744).

A New Go API for JSON
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
17:52:11 UTC
02:52:11 KST

The Go Blog
A new Go API for JSON
Introduction
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!
Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception.
Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.
After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27!
This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment, describing the problems with encoding/json, and an introduction to the new packages.
Problems with encoding/json
Overall, encoding/json has held up well.
The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types
with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to
customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible.
However, in the years since its introduction,
various users have identified numerous shortcomings.
Behavior flaws
There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json:
- Imprecise handling of JSON syntax: Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value. 
  - encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8,
whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8.
The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8,
instead of introducing silent data corruption,
which may cause problems downstream.
  - encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names.
RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names,
so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value,
merge the values, discard the values, or report an error.
The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value
without a universally agreed upon meaning.
This could be exploited by attackers in security applications
and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635).
The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.
- Leaking nilness of slices and maps: JSON is often used to communicate with
programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled
into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object.
Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null,
this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations.
A survey
indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps
are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.
- Case-insensitive unmarshaling: When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.
- Inconsistent calling of methods: Due to an implementation detail,
MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver
are inconsistently called by encoding/json. While regarded as a bug,
this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.
API deficiencies
The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive:
- It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader.
Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v),
which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.
- Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types,
but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions.
Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces
cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack.
For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect
when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method.
- The Compact, Indent, and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer.
This limits the usability of those functions.
Performance limitations
Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:
- MarshalJSON: The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation
to allocate the returned []byte. Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON
and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.
- UnmarshalJSON: The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that
a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data).
This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled
in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON.
Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.
- Lack of streaming: Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate
on an io.Writer or io.Reader, they buffer the entire JSON value in memory.
The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy
and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.
Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method
recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function,
then the performance becomes quadratic.
Trying to fix encoding/json directly
Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.
While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise.
We could in principle declare separate names, such as MarshalV2 or UnmarshalV2,
but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package.
This leads us to encoding/json/v2 (henceforth called v2),
where we can make these changes within a separate v2 namespace
in contrast to encoding/json (henceforth called v1).
Building on encoding/json/jsontext
Before discussing the v2 API, we first introduce the
encoding/json/jsontext package
that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go.
JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components:
- syntactic functionality that is concerned with processing JSON based on its grammar, and
- semantic functionality that defines the relationship between JSON values and Go values.
We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling.
This diagram provides an overview of this separation.
Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods.
The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data.
The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the jsontext package,
contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax,
while the upper half, implemented by the json/v2 package,
contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data
handled by the bottom half.
The basic API of jsontext is the following:
package jsontext
type Encoder struct { ... }
func NewEncoder(io.Writer, ...Options) *Encoder
func (*Encoder) WriteValue(Value) error
func (*Encoder) WriteToken(Token) error
type Decoder struct { ... }
func NewDecoder(io.Reader, ...Options) *Decoder
func (*Decoder) ReadValue() (Value, error)
func (*Decoder) ReadToken() (Token, error)
type Kind byte
type Value []byte
func (Value) Kind() Kind
type Token struct { ... }
func (Token) Kind() Kind
The jsontext package provides functionality for interacting with JSON
at a syntactic level and derives its name from
RFC 8259, section 2
where the grammar for JSON data is literally called JSON-text.
Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level,
it does not depend on Go reflection.
The Encoder and
Decoder
provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens.
The constructors
accept variadic options
that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding.
Unlike the Encoder and Decoder types declared in v1,
the new types in jsontext avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and
semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner.
A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as
a named []byte.
It is identical to RawMessage in v1, which is now a type alias to jsontext.Value.
A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens.
A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque Token type
with constructors and accessor methods.
It is analogous to Token in v1
but is designed represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation.
To resolve the fundamental performance problems with
the MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON interface methods,
we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON
as a streaming sequence of tokens and values.
In v2, we introduce the MarshalJSONTo and UnmarshalJSONFrom interface methods
that operate on an Encoder or Decoder, allowing the methods’ implementations
to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the json package need not
be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by MarshalJSON,
nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value
provided to UnmarshalJSON. These responsibilities belong to the Encoder and Decoder.
Introducing encoding/json/v2
Building on the jsontext package, we now introduce the
encoding/json/v2 package.
It is designed to fix the problems in v1,
while remaining familiar to users of the v1 package.
Our goal is that usages of v1 will operate mostly the same if directly migrated to v2.
Here, we primarily cover the high-level API of v2.
For examples on how to use it, we encourage readers to
study the examples in the v2 package,
the “Working with JSON” tutorial, or
read Anton Zhiyanov’s blog covering the topic.
The basic API of v2 is the following:
package json
func Marshal(in any, opts ...Options) (out []byte, err error)
func MarshalWrite(out io.Writer, in any, opts ...Options) error
func MarshalEncode(out *jsontext.Encoder, in any, opts ...Options) error
func Unmarshal(in []byte, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalRead(in io.Reader, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalDecode(in *jsontext.Decoder, out any, opts ...Options) error
The Marshal
and Unmarshal functions
have a signature similar to v1, but accept options to configure their behavior.
The MarshalWrite
and UnmarshalRead functions
directly operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader,
avoiding the need to temporarily construct an Encoder or Decoder
just to write or read from such types.
The MarshalEncode
and UnmarshalDecode functions
operate on a jsontext.Encoder and jsontext.Decoder and
is actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions.
Unlike v1, options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions,
greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of v2.
There are several options available
in v2 which are not covered by this article.
Type-specified customization
Similar to v1, v2 allows types to define their own JSON representation
by satisfying particular interfaces.
type Marshaler interface {
    MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error)
}
type MarshalerTo interface {
    MarshalJSONTo(*jsontext.Encoder) error
}
type Unmarshaler interface {
    UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error
}
type UnmarshalerFrom interface {
    UnmarshalJSONFrom(*jsontext.Decoder) error
}
The Marshaler
and Unmarshaler interfaces
are identical to those in v1.
The new MarshalerTo
and UnmarshalerFrom interfaces
allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a jsontext.Encoder or jsontext.Decoder.
This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options
can be retrieved via the Options accessor method on the Encoder or Decoder.
See the OrderedObject example
for how to implement a custom type that maintains the ordering of JSON object members.
Caller-specified customization
In v2, the caller of Marshal and Unmarshal can also specify
a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type,
where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods
or the default representation for a particular type.
func WithMarshalers(*Marshalers) Options
type Marshalers struct { ... }
func MarshalFunc[T any](fn func(T) ([]byte, error)) *Marshalers
func MarshalToFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Encoder, T) error) *Marshalers
func WithUnmarshalers(*Unmarshalers) Options
type Unmarshalers struct { ... }
func UnmarshalFunc[T any](fn func([]byte, T) error) *Unmarshalers
func UnmarshalFromFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Decoder, T) error) *Unmarshalers
MarshalFunc and
MarshalToFunc
construct a custom marshaler that can be passed to a Marshal call
using WithMarshalers to override the marshaling of particular types.
Similarly,
UnmarshalFunc and
UnmarshalFromFunc
support similar customization for Unmarshal.
The ProtoJSON example
demonstrates how this feature allows serialization of all
proto.Message types
to be handled by the protojson package.
Behavior differences
While v2 aims to behave mostly the same as v1,
its behavior has changed in some ways
to address problems in v1, most notably:
- v2 reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8.
- v2 reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name.
- v2 marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively.
- v2 unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a
case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name.
- v2 redefines the omitempty tag option to omit a field if it would have
encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are null, "", [], and {}).
- v2 reports an error when trying to serialize a time.Duration,
which currently has no default representation,
but provides options to let the caller decide.
For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option
that can configure the behavior to operate under v1 or v2 semantics,
or even other caller-determined behavior.
See “Migrating to v2” for more information.
Performance optimizations
The Marshal performance of v2 is roughly at parity with v1.
Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower.
The Unmarshal performance of v2 is significantly faster than v1,
with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x.
In order to obtain greater performance gains,
existing implementations of
Marshaler and
Unmarshaler should
migrate to also implement
MarshalerTo and
UnmarshalerFrom,
so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner.
For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in UnmarshalJSON methods
significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes
(see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315),
while switching to UnmarshalJSONFrom improved performance by orders of magnitude.
For more benchmark details, see the
go-json-experiment/jsonbench
repository.
On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the v2 implementation is slower than v1.
You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28.
Compatibility
The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go.
The original encoding/json and new encoding/json/v2 packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise.
Applications using v1 will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to v2.
That said, when designing the v2 packages we wanted to do better than keeping v1 supported.
We wanted to ensure that v1 and v2 are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together.
Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies.
For instance, suppose your package uses v2 to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package.
That package may use the original v1 MarshalJSON method to define its marshaling behavior.
No problem, v2 supports MarshalJSON methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected.
Vice versa, suppose your package uses v1 to marshal the same struct.
The other package may use the v2 MarshalJSONTo method for better performance.
No problem here either, as the v1 implementation supports v2’s MarshalJSONTo method under the hood.
We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, v1 is implemented in terms of v2.
As mentioned above, v2 supports a variety of Options.
Each behavior difference is controlled by one of the these options.
Thus, v1 can be implemented in terms of v2 by passing the full set of v1 compatibility options.
With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., MarshalJSONTo) or new struct tags (e.g., embed) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing v1 users.
Migration
Implementing v1 in terms of v2 options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites.
encoding/json documents the full set of behavior differences between v1 and v2, and which option controls that behaviors.
Many applications can migrate directly to v2 with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on v1 behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on.
For example, we can select all v2 behavior except for allowing duplicate names:
json.Marshal(..., json.DefaultOptionsV2(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateName(true))
Alternatively, we can select all v1 behavior except for disallowing duplicate names:
json.Marshal(..., jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateName(false))
The encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide goes into more detail, covering a variety of scenarios for approaching migration of an application from v1 to v2.
More information
For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see:
- The “Working with JSON” tutorial,
- The encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext package documentation,
- The encoding/json package’s v2 comparison documentation,
- and the encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide.
A long time coming
The planning for a new major version of encoding/json spanned years.
In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package,
Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of encoding/json) first drafted his
thoughts on what a hypothetical v2 package should look like.
Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers,
Joe Tsai was disappointed that the protojson package
needed to use a custom JSON implementation because encoding/json was
neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the
Protocol Buffer specification required,
nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner.
Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable,
Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on v2 and
started to build a prototype
(with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module).
Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt)
joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing.
Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our
recorded meetings and
meeting notes.
Later discussions are available in our encoding/json/v2 working group meeting notes.
This work has been public since the beginning,
and we increasingly involved the wider Go community,
first with a
GopherCon talk and
discussion posted in late 2023,
formal proposal posted in early 2025,
and finally adopting encoding/json/v2 as a Go experiment in Go 1.25
for wider-scale testing by all Go users.
The v2 effort took about 6 years to reach this point,
incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable
empirical experience from use in production settings.
It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem.
Thank you to everyone that contributed!
